en: The Preface to the *Fǎxǐ Zhì* states:

This volume selects the eminent sages of successive dynasties who were satiated with the flavor of the Dharma and weaves them together into a single collection to serve as a clear testimony for future generations.
Indeed, since the Buddha-dharma first reached Zhendan (China) during the Han dynasty, had Zhendan not possessed those who carried the Way...
As for these vessels, by what means have they been transmitted down to this day? Regarding the vessels that carry the Way, there are those who dwell at home and those who have left the home life;
setting aside for a moment those who have left the home life, even among those dwelling at home, they are called sages and men of talent.

If there were one who did not take pleasure in this, how could they perceive that a single drop of flavor from the great ocean possesses the essence of all its rivers? It is said: "Lion’s milk can only be contained in a crystal goblet."
It can store other objects, yet those objects shatter as soon as they are placed within it. However, to carry the Way, one truly requires a person of rare caliber.

Formerly, during the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, sixty thousand bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers, emerged from the earth and made a vow before the Tathāgata:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall remain forever in this realm to propagate the Great Dharma. Since the Buddha-dharma entered this land, the eminent monastics and laypeople here have been...
Flowing [through the ages], is it not those who shoulder the Great Dharma who are the true ones? And who else could possibly do so?

Furthermore, at the end of his life, the Buddha entrusted the treasury of the Dharma to kings and ministers; was this not because in future generations, heterodox views would become dense and thick, and they might exploit such names and power?
Only then can one truly shatter [these views]. This work thus reconciles the divergent tenets of various schools and cuts through the deep-seated delusions of the末代 (final age).
This volume is yet another great instrument for this purpose. Among the talented scholars of today, there are those who have not yet seen Buddhist scriptures and regard them as strange artifacts;
were it not for the guidance of former sages, there would be no way to inspire faith. Thus we know that this volume serves as a guide for future scholars.
This clarifies the realization of the truth. Indeed, from the Han and Jin dynasties down to the Song and Yuan, there have been many who were devoted to the flavor of this Dharma.

Now, I shall simply select those whose brilliance and greatness illuminate the ears and eyes of a thousand ages and list them here; they all provide the sustenance of *dharmaprīti* (joy in the Dharma).

To die without perishing is what is called longevity. Within the teachings, there are two kinds of nourishment: the food of *dharmaprīti* and the food of *dhyānaprīti* (joy in meditation). Consuming these is able to nurture the Dharma.
The physical body sustains the life of wisdom, which is ultimately inexhaustible; these wise and enlightened ones have already been satiated with the joy of the Dharma.
Now, by sharing this collection, their names shall remain imperishable, and one knows that their life of wisdom is likewise inexhaustible. This volume is itself the joy of the Dharma;
it can sustain the life of wisdom of the past, nourish the life of wisdom of the present, and give birth to the life of wisdom of the future—is this not the true joy of the Dharma?
This is indeed the true joy of the Dharma. Composed by Guanheng of the Zilin (Purple Bamboo Grove).
Preface to the "Record of the Joy of the Dharma" by Illustrious Persons.

Now, as for grasses and trees: from their stems to their branches and leaves, from their blossoms to their fruits, they appear in all manner of colors and varieties, with diverse forms and different appearances.
When the sap is exhausted and the blossoms have fallen, everything must ultimately return to its root. As long as the root remains, it will sprout when spring arrives.
It is thus for one year, it is thus for ten years, and even for a thousand or ten thousand years; human beings are likewise but plants and trees.
Their living and dying, their dying and being born—this "dying and being born" is the root, what the Dharma-gate calls the seed.
It is so. Although the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) may undergo the cycle of transmigration, the jewel within one's garment remains sovereign;

this supreme treasure is never lost. It is like planting a *wugu* tree, which yields *wugu*, or planting a *jia* tree, which yields *jia*; according to what is planted, the result remains unchanged for a long time.
There has never been a case of planting an *udumbara* tree and obtaining a *jīmūta* fruit, nor planting a *āmra* tree and obtaining a cluster of *akṣa* fruits. Indeed, since ancient times...
O Sage, the roots of this tree are profound. From its very inception, through two successive generations, that man has repeatedly studied the laws of Zeng and Shi, and the treatises of Shen and Han;

he has inscribed his name upon Mount Qi-lian and shone among the figures on the Linqi Pavilion. Yet he has violated the precepts of both emptiness and existence. At times, he indulges in the refined sounds of stringed and wind instruments, seeking excellence through music;

at others, he conceals his brilliance within the compositions of the *Qusheng* and *Shengmai*. He lingers over the carving of bamboo shoes and engages in polemical debates regarding the "Golden Fortress" and "Iron Wall. Thus he positions himself within the realm of wisdom.
As for those who cherish "this thing" (money), their distance from the Buddha-dharma is no less than that between the Milky Way and the heavens.

Yet, in the ultimate gathering [of the teachings], there is none who has not probed the ocean of awakening or gazed upon the gate of Prajñāpāramitā. Thus, some begin with doubt but end in faith; some appear to turn their backs on the traces [of the Dharma] but are actually in harmony with it;
some reject it verbally while cherishing it in their hearts. In terms of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), such views constitute nineteen cases. Why is this so?
This is because the root remains. Lord Xia was endowed with the nature of wisdom from an early age and was able to perceive the original source.

From the Jin and Wei dynasties down to the Tang and Song, there have been many such individuals among those who understood Chan and the teachings—such as Faxi, Zhi, Xu Xun, Liu Kai, Pang Yun, and Pei Xiu.
It goes without saying that they were disciples of the Buddha throughout their lives; even regarding Han Yu’s "Memorial on Buddhism," [it is clear they were not its adversaries].

He followed You Daodian. Du Qi Gong did not believe in Buddhism, yet upon reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he attained understanding and said, "I regret that I acquired it so late. Thus we know that from the time of Wei-yin until the present, all those scholars, literati, famous ministers, and eminent statesmen— [The text continues:

...bones. And following You Daodian. Duke Du Qi did not believe in the Buddha-dharma; however, upon reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he gained an understanding and said, "I regret that I acquired it so late. Only then did he realize that from the time of Wei-yin until now, all those poets, scholars, famous officials, and great lords—
How could he have ever not come from among the Jetavana Monastery? In the past, Laozi was said to be Mahākāśyapa, and Confucius was said to be the youth Vimalakīrti;

such matters are indeed as they are, and there is no cause for wonder. One who knows meditation does not speak of meditation, just as one who is skilled in the *Yījīng* does not speak of the *Yījīng*.
Thus, those who possess the Dharma do not cling to the Dharma. This is how it is with the people of the world.

To cast aside the Five Precepts as if they were discarded calf-skins and treat the Great Tripitaka as mere chaff, yet still presume to have seen the Buddha—regarding the Dharma as a den of thieves and a thicket of fame and profit—is this no different from the conduct of an icchantika or a low-born slave? How can such a person speak of the Buddha-Dharma?
Try holding up this compilation before them; will they be able to break into a profuse sweat, thereby planting the seeds for realization beneath a single blow of the staff or a shout?
Written by the Layman Chan-ti (Xiandaiguo) Zou Diguang as a Preface to the *Record of Dharma Joy* (*Faxi zhi*).
The Xia County Licentiate Cheng has compiled the *Record of Dharma Joy*. A guest once visited me and spoke of it, saying: "Mao..."
"You, my lord, are so full of the joy of dhyāna (*dhyānāsvāda*). As for the traces you have gathered and plucked, they are all drawn from within loyalty, filial piety, integrity, and righteousness.
Why is it that you cannot leap beyond the portals of the Confucian school? I replied: "Maoqing uses Confucianism to employ Chan; he does not take Confucianism as something employed by Chan.
If one takes Confucianism as being employed by Chan, then even Confucianism is transformed into Chan. But when one uses Confucianism to employ Chan..."
"Thus, Chan itself is transformed into Confucianism. This is Master Maoqing’s hand of forging and molding. [The interlocutor] asked:

"If that is so, why did the Confucian school exclude Chan? [The author] replied: "This was done to preserve the lineage of orthodox learning. Master Maoqing, however, sought to embrace all that is good. One prioritizes strictness; the other prioritizes breadth.
Both proceed side by side without contradiction. [The interlocutor] asked: "Why were the defilements of Master Bo-sheng recorded?"
Xiuwen records those who are sycophants; Chudao records those who are rebellious enemies; Tianjue records those who are his partisans. What is the basis for this selection? I say:
in warfare there is a method, which aims at overcoming the enemy; it need not originate solely with Sun Zi or Wu Qi.
In medicine there is a protocol, which aims at curing the illness; it need not originate solely with Lu Shanfu or Bian Que. The guest said, "Excellent! Then he spoke again to the guest:
I beg you to complete this discourse for my sake. The rise of Chan and the Teachings (Dharma) originally occurred by entering [the world] when Confucianism was in decline.
Yet, that they have been able to endure and not perish for so long is further dependent upon the establishment of Confucianism.
If one were to treat human relations as mere soil refuse and worldly affairs as discarded chaff, leading the entire world into the teachings of emptiness and extinction, the world—
The minds of those on the Way are currently so vacant that they lack any principle to uphold.

As for those practitioners of Chan, even if they wish to sleep amidst the clouds and dine upon the mists, sitting with elegant grace as they brandish the fly-whisk to discourse upon what they call the "Supreme Truth Beyond," how could they possibly achieve it?

Formerly, Wang Zhongzu and Liu Zhenchang went together to visit He the General of the Cavalry (He Piaoqi). While the General was looking over official documents, he did not acknowledge them; Wang then said to He:
[The Emperor] said, "Minister, why do you not set aside your routine affairs to respond with profound words? Why instead do you keep your head bowed, looking at this?
He replied, "I am not looking at this. How could you all exist without it? Those who heard this appreciated it together, considering it excellent.

From this we can see that Minister Mao’s composition of this work was specifically intended to express his deep concern for loyalty, filial piety, integrity, and righteousness; its profundity is such.
"How profound! How deep! The guest told Maoqing, who said, "Excellent. He then took a folded sheet of paper and received it, marking its beginning.
This is the preface titled "Fa-xi-zhi" (The Record of Dharma-Joy).

Originally, all the myriad streams and ten thousand branches are born from the One Source of Heaven; as for the full syllables and single words, which among them lies beyond the Three Representations?

If one can embrace the three to become one, then perhaps the Buddha is none other than this very mind. Thus, from the time his shadow was manifested at the end of the first year of the Zhou dynasty...
Its radiance pervades the sun of Han; beneath Vulture Peak, it expounds the subtle words from the Golden Mouth. Amidst Cock’s Foot Mountain, it unfolds the auspicious colors of the Jade Brow.
The six petals of the lotus bloom together with the White Society; at the twin groves of the Jeta Grove, the profound wind alone flourishes.
Are these not those who uphold the Elephant Dharma (Hastidharma) and draw others toward the Way? Were it not for those of sharp faculties, how could one transcend the fruits of correctness?

With distinct characteristics and distinct names, each brandishes the staff that ascends the hall; with discourses on permanence and discourses on quiescence, all together wield the halberd that enters the chamber.

There is the combined cultivation; there is the single cultivation. Both are intended for the strategic defense and offense at the sacrificial table. There is no need for the contemplation of form (vipaśyanā) nor the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā).

I wish to break down these barriers. Nishi Nantai followed Zhi; the Master [Zhi] likewise had no fixed teacher. As for the "dark" (Daoist) teachings, they return to Yangzi; Yangzi returns to Confucius.

Returning to this, one may receive [the teaching]. Why needlessly divide it into schools or establish separate households? One naturally recognizes the path and knows the home; all belong to a single causal condition (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
When milk and cream flow forth, one speaks of the three successive stages. Both sheep and deer are absent [in the ultimate sense].
The seventy-two rulers were all within the scope of the potter’s wheel. Eighty thousand years are but a fleeting moment. This was the summer residence of Master Zhang Maoqing.
This is to cultivate a resolve for the joy of the Dharma. Maoqing has manifested proof of the One Vehicle and profoundly investigated the Tripiṭaka;

he maintains that this shore is none other than the other shore, and that the Dharmakāya is identical to the Saṃbhogakāya. Moreover, the Confucian virtues of loyalty, filial piety, integrity, and righteousness are in harmony with the purity of the Buddhist path.
The subtle and profound essence has flowed down from afar from the East and more recently from before the Southern Song dynasty.

Regarding all the expositions by officials and lay practitioners (*upāsaka*), as well as the records compiled by minor historians and miscellaneous writers, there are none that do not cite their sources and gather them together.

Even though such individuals were no more than a few per generation and each spoke but a few words, their karmic conditions intersected and stimulated one another like the flashing light of drawn swords. Wisdom...

The treasury is opened and clarified; drawing upon its peripheral insights like the shadow of a whip, it vibrates the golden sound within the garden of awakening and extends the precious path across the arena of rhetoric.

Had this not been a manifesting of the Chan school and a detailed exposition in historical records, how could it have accorded with the metaphor of the *Lamp of Transmission* or achieved the merit of following the same tracks?
Thus we know that those who possess the sinew within their eyes can sport amidst the falling flowers and the jingling bracelets, while those whose tongues have no bone [can speak with such freedom].
These wondrous words serve as a raft for those who see forms and hear sounds; they not only shatter the core of the Three Studies, but may also be called the external protection for the Four Dhyānas.
This unworthy one feels ashamed that his translations fall short of the standards of Linquan, and laments his lack of cultivation in the Pure Land.
My literary power is utterly deficient and my innate capacity for the profound is most shallow. I have merely relied upon the words of Ruan Zhan to append myself to the single remark of Xuan Yan.
Thus ends this self-narrative of the Dharma-joy Vow by the Elder Brother and Lay Disciple Wu Liang. Written at Fanyu.
Wenshi said: "A single bee is exceedingly minute, yet it can travel and observe throughout heaven and earth. A single shrimp is extremely small, yet it can roam freely across the great ocean.
How much more so for a human being, who is paired with the two polarities and transcends all existence—how could such a one lack thoughts of the vast, the boundless, and the far-reaching?
Having attained mastery over both mundane and supramundane dharmas, this is truly the carefree state of the sages of old."
This is intended as a map; it is also the profound essence of the expansive and untrammeled spirit of people today.
The Mountain Man of Jade Couch possesses the *Record of Heroes Beyond the World*, a compilation in which he has gathered from antiquity down to the present those who studied Chan and the Way.

He observed that existing works were such that the voluminous were cluttered and miscellaneous, the concise were desolate and silent, the eccentric were trivial and hyperbolic, and the abridged were incomplete and missing. Before I had even finished reading it, I composed four [sections] for it.

I have reflected upon this with hesitation, yet I have secretly harbored the aspiration to undertake it. On days of leisure while dwelling in the mountains, I cast my mind across the ages and gazed upon antiquity.
From among the various eminent figures, I have selected and gathered their accounts one by one, carefully collating them. For each individual, I have composed a brief biography.

These span from the Jin, Wei, Qi, and Liang dynasties down to the Tang and Song, based upon the official histories of successive reigns or the collected works of those eminent figures, or as they appear scattered elsewhere.
This present biography has been compiled by drawing from various sources within the Tripitaka, the *Chuan deng lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp), and other texts.

By gathering the many and supplementing the few, I have extracted the essentials and probed the profound mysteries, titling this work *Faxi zhi* (Record of Dharma Joy). It is divided into four volumes; for the most part, it describes matters that transcend and excel beyond the mundane world.

They are distinguished as a separate category, yet they accord with human sentiment and do not deviate from the Great Way. In refining their reputation and integrity, they rely upon loyalty and filial piety;
in regulating their advancement and retreat, they prioritize purity and solemnity. When active in the world, they leave a legacy like the qilin, shedding radiance upon bamboo and silk;

when dwelling in seclusion, they follow the tracks of the deer, illuminating the pines and creepers. Some establish their foundation through the study of principle, while others command an age through their literary works.

In short, he renounced glory and returned to simplicity, abiding in spontaneity. This was certainly not a case of aimless wandering or reckless asceticism, nor was it merely the conduct of some aged mendicant.
Occasionally, there were instances where his restraint was not yet complete or where lingering traces of worldly influence remained;

at times, he might leap beyond the boundaries of the round and the square, occasionally deviating from them. Yet, his pure words and subtle principles were also extensively gathered and read, as if [he were a sage].
A water-mirror floats in the void; an ice-pitcher reflects within the seat. Suddenly, it causes the heart and gallbladder to become transparent and the spirit-bones to feel cool and refreshing.

The intent for restlessness and competition vanishes like smoke, while the distress of pent-up emotions disperses like mist. For a student of the Way who wishes to break through the critical juncture and establish a secure dwelling for their life, there is no way other than this.
As the Old Master Laozi said: "Though one may have a carriage yoked with eight horses, it cannot compare..."
To sit and advance upon this Way—this is what is called "Dharma-joy" (*dharmaprīti*). Now, the Dharma is one of the Three Jewels;
when sages emerge in the world, they must surely gaze toward the Dharma. Yet, while there is the Dharma, one does not remain confined within the Dharma.

It is like the ten great disciples of the Snowy Mountain (Śākyamuni), each of whom possessed his own unique creative transformation within his breast; none of them would ever set foot upon the path traversed by the Tathāgata.
This is what is meant by "the Dharma as Dharma," which is not confined by the Dharma. This, moreover, is what those who delight in the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*) should know.

Compiled by the Recluse Bīnglián, Xià Shùfāng. *Fǎxǐzhì*, Scroll One.
Wudou Jushi (The Wakeful Dipper Layman): Feng Ding. He read [the biography of] Dongfang Manqian, Dongfang Shuo.

His courtesy name was Manqian. He was a native of Yanci in Pingyuan. During the reign of Emperor Wu, he submitted memorials that met with imperial favor and served as a *dai-zhao* (waiting for summons).
At the Gate of the Golden Horse, there was at that time Zhengjian Fayen, who was a preeminent master of witty repartee.

In the third year of the Yuankou era, the Emperor excavated the Kunming Pond and discovered black ash. He questioned Dongfang Shuo about it, and Shuo replied, "You may ask a foreign monk from the Western Regions."
At that time, the Indian monk Kāśyapa Mātanga arrived. [The Emperor] questioned him, and Mātanga replied, "This is the ash of the kalpa.

Liu Gengsheng—Liu Xiang, whose courtesy name was Zizheng and also known as Gengsheng—was twelve years old when he followed his father on official duty as a *nianlang* (palanquin attendant). He then presented a fu (rhapsody) to the throne.
He composed several dozen chapters of verse. During the reign of Emperor Cheng, he served as a Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Guanglu Dafu*).

He authored the *Lie nü zhuan* (Biographies of Exemplary Women) to record the licentiousness of Empress Zhao, and wrote the *Hongfan Wuxing Zhuan* (Commentary on the Five Elements of the Great Plan) because the power of the Wang clan had become too great.

The Emperor wished to appoint him to one of the Nine High Ministerial Offices, but he was repeatedly obstructed by the Wangs. He held the rank of a Grand Master for over thirty years. Xiang once served as a librarian at the Tianlu Pavilion.
The green rhi-cane staff illuminated the night, and Buddhist scriptures were frequently encountered therein. His *Biographies of Transcendents* (*Lie xian zhuan*) states:
"I have examined the Tripitaka and searched through the *Illustrations of Transcendents* (*Lie xian tu*) compiled by the Grand Historian, from the time of the Yellow Emperor down to the present day.
I have identified one hundred and forty-nine individuals who attained the Way of the Transcendents; seventy-four of them appear in Buddhist scriptures."
Cáo Zǐjiàn, surnamed Cáo Zhí, was the second son of Cáo Cão. At the age of ten, he was skilled at composing literary works and could recite over one hundred thousand words from the *Shī* and *Shū*.
When Hán Dān Chún saw him, he marveled in astonishment and hailed him as a "Heavenly Man. Whenever Zhí read Buddhist scriptures, he would linger over them in deep admiration and contemplation.
He regarded this as the essence of the Ultimate Way (*zhìdào*). While wandering at Mount Yú, he heard a sound that was exceptionally extraordinary—pure, resonant, and plaintive.

He subsequently imitated that sound to create Buddhist chants (*fàn bèi*). The "Yúshān Chants" found within current liturgical rites are the surviving remnants of his compositions. During his lifetime, Sengzhi did not place much faith in the teachings of Huang-Lao;
he expressed his views in the *Biàndào Lùn* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Way), which is now included in the *Hóngmíng jí* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification) within the Tripitaka.
Yang Shuzi (Yang Hu).
His courtesy name was Shuzi. A native of Pingyang, he was successively promoted to the rank of Shangshu (Minister of the Interior) and served as a Puye (Director of the Secretariat).
Lu Kang of Wu once praised his moral character and capacity, stating that even Le Yi or Zhuge Kongming could not surpass him. When Yang Hu was five years old, he [Yang Xiu] ordered the wet nurse—
He retrieved a golden ring from beneath a mulberry tree belonging to the neighboring Li family. The Li family was startled and said, "This is the very ring lost by our deceased son.
Thus it was known that he was the previous incarnation of Li Hu. During the reign of Emperor Wu, Hu served as the Governor-General (Dudu) of Jingzhou.
He made daily offerings to the temple on Mount Wudang. When someone asked him the reason for this, Xu said, "In my previous life, I committed many transgressions.
It was by relying on the construction of this temple that I obtained deliverance. Therefore, my feelings of devotion in making offerings are particularly focused upon this one."

Wang Maohong (Wang Dao), courtesy name Maohong, was a native of Langya. He served as Grand Preceptor and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Shixing. The monk Jiyou traveled to Jiankang and was skilled at chanting Buddhist hymns (*fanbai*).
Upon seeing him, Wang Dao remarked, "He is one of our own kind. [The text continues with] Yu Liang, the Grand Marshal, and the Court Astrologer...
Zhou Yi and Huan Yi, the Minister of Justice, both visited his door to establish a connection, and his name was registered among the high officials.

Once, while Ji You was conversing with Wang Dao, loosening his belt and acting with unrestrained ease, the Minister of the Interior, Bian Wangzhi, happened to arrive. You immediately assumed a solemn and dignified countenance.

When someone asked him the reason for this change, he replied: "The Duke Wang possesses a discerning spirit that perceives the inner character of men; Minister Bian possesses a standard of judgment that measures the nature of things. I ought to treat them accordingly."
This was his response.

Liu Zhenchang, whose courtesy name was Zhichang, was a native of Pei. From his youth, he was pure and detached; though his family was poor, he remained composed and at ease. Wang Dao held him in high esteem and repeatedly... [honored him].
He was appointed as the Governor of Danyang. At that time, Zhu Fashen’s spiritual influence was loftily manifest and his reputation spread throughout Shandong;
Sengtan had long been one of his disciples. One day, while Fashen was in the presence of Emperor Jianwen, Sengtan asked, "Why does a man of the Way frequent such crimson gates?
Fashen replied, "You see them as crimson gates, but for this poor monk, it is like wandering through a thatched door."
Tao Shixing, whose courtesy name was Shixing, was a native of Poyang. He initially served as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Guangzhou.

While fishing at sea, he obtained a statue of Mañjuśrī and sent it to Hanxi Temple. Although the temple had previously suffered a fire, the hall housing the statue remained unharmed. Later, Tao Kan [Shixing] governed Wuchang.
He sent men to fetch it, but ten men together could not lift it. Subsequently, they exerted all their strength to place it on a boat, yet the boat immediately sank;

thus, the image was lost. At that time, a popular saying went: "Tanyu-kuan is a hero only with his sword; the image is defined by its spirit. It can be brought forth through sincerity, but it cannot be summoned by force.
When Master Huiyuan established the monastery, he prayed for it with all his heart; thereupon, the image arrived of its own accord, as if gliding through the air.
Xie Anshi (謝安石), courtesy name Anshi (安石), was a native of Yangxia (陽夏). From his youth, he enjoyed a reputation for talent, yet he declined all imperial summons despite persistent exhortations.

It was not until he was over forty years old that he finally accepted a command, being appointed as General of the West (Zhengxi Sima, 征西司馬). During the Taiyuan era, he was further promoted to Grand Preceptor (Taibao, 太保) and resided in the East.
At that time, he traveled with Zhi Dun and Xu Xun for excursions among the mountains and waters. He once issued an imperial decree for Zhi Dun to enter the inner palace to lecture on the sutras;
his teachings frequently conformed to the essential spirit of the texts, yet they were resented by those who merely cling to the literal words. Dao’an heard of this and sighed, saying:

"This is like Jiu Fanglao’s method of appraising horses—he overlooks the colors of black and yellow to capture their divine spirit and noble gait. In the second year of the Taihe era, Zhi Dun took his leave of the court and returned to the mountains.
The Emperor issued an edict to establish Wozhou Monastery for him to reside in. At that time, Hui'an was residing in Wuxing and sent a letter to Huidun, saying:
"I have longed for you for many days; my thoughts and yearnings toward you grow ever more intense. Knowing that you intend to return to Shan to manage your own affairs, I am deeply moved by sadness.

Human life is but a temporary lodging. Lately, those matters of refined elegance and worldly success have almost entirely vanished. All day long I am filled with sorrow, and I can only wait [for your return]."
"Once you have come, we shall dispel [our sorrows] with conversation; then one day will be as a thousand years.

Wang Youjun (Wang Xizhi), whose courtesy name was Yishao, was the son of Wang Dao. He was renowned for his forthright integrity. He began his official career as a Secretariat Censor and later served as...
The General of the Right Army and Interior Governor of Kuaiji established Guijong Temple on Mount Lu in the sixth year of the Xiankang era and invited Dharmatrāta from India to reside there.
While Wang Xizhi was in Kuaiji, he heard of Zhi Dun’s reputation but did not yet believe in him.
Later, Huidun returned to Shan. Wang Xizhi went to visit him to observe his character and strength. He said to him, "May I hear your discourse on 'carefree wandering' (xiao yao)?
Huidun composed several thousand words for him; Xizhi then opened his breast and loosened his sash, lingering there until he could not bear to leave.

Wang Mugang Wang Mi, whose courtesy name was Yanyuan, served as the Minister of Education (Situ). He once wrote a letter to Master Huiyuan, saying: "I am forty years old, yet my decline is like that of one who has reached sixty.
Huiyuan replied: "The ancients did not prize a foot-long jade disk as much as they valued an inch of time; observe what they held most dear."

It seems that [longevity] does not depend on years alone. Since you, donor, walk in accordance with the Way and roam within your nature, and govern your mind by riding upon the principles of the Buddha, one may infer from this:
why should you envy a remote lifespan? All people praise your skill in guiding others.
Xi Jabin (Xi Chao).

His courtesy name was Jabin. A native of Shanyang, he possessed a transcendent breadth of character from his youth. He set his aspirations upon the Buddha and was further devoted to the practice of *dāna* (generosity).

Delighting in reclusion, whenever he heard of one who had "shaken off their robes" [to renounce the world], he would invariably build a house for them and provide them with utensils and implements. Zhi Daolin... [text continues]
Liu Lin often remarked that Zhi Dun’s achievement in penetrating the subtle was sufficient to rank alongside the era of the Zhengshi period; he held him in very high esteem.

While serving as a secretary in the administration of Huan Wen, Liu Chao asked Xie An, "How does Zhi Dun’s discourse compare to that of Xi Kang? An replied, "Xi Kang worked hard and only managed to attain half of it.
Chao asked again, "How does it compare to Yin Hao's? An replied, "In terms of tireless debate and argumentation, I fear he may well be a match for him."

His spiritual lineage was profound and eminent; Yin felt deeply humbled by his virtue. Later, he wrote in a letter to his relatives and old friends: "Master Zhi is one who has attained the Way of the Divine Principle (*shenli*).

With his transcendent talent, he achieved solitary awakening. For several hundred years, he has been the sole individual who has sustained and flourished the Great Dharma, ensuring that the True Principle does not perish.

Chao once composed the *Wujie wen* (Treatise on the Five Precepts); having already practiced the five precepts, he further cultivated himself through monthly and seasonal fasts and observances, awaiting the arrival of the midday meal.
After having eaten [the medicine], one may not taste any delicious flavors or sweet fragrances.

Wang Qiao of Langya was a man who possessed the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi), and he composed a poem on it which says: "The wondrous function lies herein; traversing existence, one surveys..."

There is nothing. The spirit proceeds from obscurity to penetration; consciousness employs illumination to discern the coarse. The subtle and refined draw forth one another; their efficacy is fundamentally empty.

When those three contemplations are extinguished, thought turns toward what remains beyond the most sublime. It is further said: "I sigh for my life from its very beginning. My innate wisdom and insight have been entrusted to a person of lofty and profound virtue, so that I may rely upon his hidden power.
As for the function of thought turning toward the sublime, it resides in the unfathomably deep. This is the ultimate of reflections: to fix the mind upon the Western Realm."
Yin Zhongjun, Yin Hao, whose courtesy name was Shenyuan, had not yet fully understood the Buddhist scriptures. He sent someone to welcome Master Zhi.
When Master Zhi wished to go, the Right General (Wang Xizhi) said, "His depth and breadth of thought and refinement are profound and rich; therefore, he is not easily matched."
Yuan Yanbo, whose courtesy name was Yanbo, was a native of Yangxia. From his youth, he possessed extraordinary talent and was highly esteemed by figures such as Xie An.

He served in successive offices until he reached the rank of Governor of Dongyang Commandery. His works, including the "Poems on History" (*Yongshi shi*) and the "Rhapsody on the Eastern Expedition" (*Dongzheng fu*), were widely celebrated in his time.
The *Traditions* (Chuan) once recorded in the *Han Ji*: "In the western regions of India, there exists the Way of the Buddha (*Buddhadharma*). Its transformations penetrate everywhere;

thus it can communicate with all things and bring great salvation to all living beings. Emperor Ming of the Han was moved by a dream and consequently dispatched envoys to India to inquire about the Way.
They returned with his image and several thousand scrolls of scriptures, which excel in their vast and magnificent discourse."
That which is sought lies within the single body; that which is clarified lies beyond sight and hearing.
Worldly scholars regard this as empty and extravagant, yet it ultimately returns to the profound and subtle, being difficult to fathom.
Thus, when princes, dukes, and high ministers contemplate the occasion of the retribution of birth and death, there are none who do not become startled and lose their composure.
Wang Tanzhi, courtesy name Wendu, was a native of Jinyang. During the Ningkang era, he was appointed Director of the Imperial Secretariat and concurrently served as Governor of Danyang.

At that time, as Huan Wen sought to shift the mandate of the Jin dynasty, Tanzhi joined forces with Xie An to provide loyal counsel and support, ultimately securing the stability of the state. He—[and others...]—were [as follows].
He was on friendly terms with Zhi Daolin. Daolin once composed the *Jise lun* (Treatise on the Immediate Nature of Form), which states: "The nature of form does not possess form of itself;
form does not exist independently. Although it is form, it is empty; therefore it is said that form is immediately emptiness. Yet form is not different from emptiness."
He presented his treatise to Tanzhi, who remained entirely silent. Zhi asked, "Do you recognize it through silence?
He replied, "Since there is no Mañjuśrī here, who could appreciate it?"

He was He Cidao (何次道), whose courtesy name was Cidao. A native of Qian in Lujiang, he possessed a refined and elegant demeanor. From his youth, he was renowned for his literary talent and mastery of the principles of the classics.
Both Wang Dao and Yu Liang addressed Emperor Cheng, saying: "He Chong’s capacity and character are as broad and upright as those of ten thousand men."

"May I hope," he said, "that on the day of my death, you will recommend me to serve as an Inner Attendant; then the state will have no cause for anxiety. When Wang Dao passed away, Wang Chong subsequently participated in the administration of the Secretariat of State Affairs.

He was renowned for his ability and diligent service, yet he did not cultivate private favors; thus, he was highly esteemed by the world. By nature, Chong took pleasure in the teachings of the Śākya clan (Buddhism).

At that time, Yu Bing, who was assisting in the governance of the state as the maternal uncle of the Emperor, submitted a memorial stating that śramaṇas should perform full rites of reverence toward the sovereign. Wang Chong and others [opposed this].

He argued that they ought not to be required to perform prostrations, and submitted a memorial stating: "Emperor Wu established the new dynasty through its great brilliance, and Emperor Ming perceived the profound mysteries with his sagely wisdom.
How could it be that at such a time śramaṇas would find it difficult to bend their knees?

It is simply because we do not alter the methods for cultivating goodness that we thereby communicate the will of the whole world. After he presented this petition three times, the official deliberation was consequently shelved.
He was named Youze.
He was the younger brother of [Huan] Chong. Noble-minded and possessing few desires, he did not accept successive summons from the provincial and regional governments.

Initially, when Chong served as General of the Flying Cavalry (Biaoji Jiangjun), he urged Youze to take office. Youze said, "How could the title 'Fifth' be inferior to that of 'General of the Flying Cavalry'? Chong... [resided].

The Prime Minister’s power eclipsed that of his contemporaries; yet Qian Zhun wore his sash loosely at his humble gate, shunning worldly affairs and doing nothing but burning incense and reciting scriptures.
His daughter became Empress Mu.

Xie Renzu, whose courtesy name was Renzu, was the son of Xie Kun. He served the Jin dynasty as General of the West (Zhenxi Jiangjun). Once, while serving as General of the West, Xie Shang dreamed that his father said to him:
"A vapor is approaching from the southwest; whoever encounters it will surely die. You should construct a pagoda and establish a monastery to avert this calamity. If...
"I do not have the leisure [to go]. You may carve the shape of a stupa on the head of your staff; when you see a vapor coming, you can aim at it.
Sengshang then carved a small stupa on the head of his staff. Later, indeed, a strange vapor descended from the heavens and rushed directly toward Shang’s house.
Shang pointed at it with the head of his staff, and the vapor immediately dispersed. His entire family was saved. In the fourth year of the Yonghe era, Shang renounced [the world].
He built a monastery named Zhuāngyán.
Luójūnzhāng, whose courtesy name was Jūnzhāng, was a native of Lěiyáng. In his youth, while once sleeping during the day, he dreamed of a bird with plumage of extraordinary brilliance.
It flew into his mouth. From that time on, his refined thoughts flourished daily. He served as an official (Chongshi) under Jiangxia.

The Governor, Xie Shang, said of him, "He may truly be called a precious jade (linlang) from within the Xiang River. He was fond of reading and devoted to Buddhism, composing the *Shengsheng Lun* (Treatise on Rebirth), in which he wrote:

"The world all laments that what is joined must inevitably separate, yet none offer consolation for the certainty that separation must lead to reunion; everyone knows that what is gathered must inevitably disperse, yet none recognize..."

That which is dispersed must necessarily reunite. Those who speak today merely say, "The 'I' of the past is not the 'I' of the present," yet they do not realize that the 'I' of the present is precisely the 'I' of the past.
To the one of profound insight, birth and death are like waking and sleeping. How true these words are!
Sun Xinggong, whose courtesy name was Sun Chuo, shared with Xu Xun of Gaoyang a lofty aspiration for reclusion.

Initially, he lived in seclusion at Kuaiji, letting his spirit roam among the mountains and waters, and composed the *Suichu Fu* (Rhapsody on the Fulfillment of Initial Vows) to manifest his intent. When Zhi Daolin asked Chuo, "How do you compare [to others]?"
"Agreed. He replied, "Your lofty sentiments and far-reaching ambitions have long been held in high esteem by this disciple. Yet, with every verse and chant, you maintain your original character.
Once, when composing the *Tiantai Fu*, he showed it to his friend Fan Rongqi, saying, 'Try tossing this on the ground; it should produce the sound of metal and stone.
Whenever he reached a particularly fine line, he would invariably remark, 'This must be the language of those like us. During the reign of Emperor Ai, he served as a Court Historian (*Zhuzuo Lang*)."

Lang composed the "Discourse on Illustrating the Way" (*Yudao lun*), which sides with the Buddha; his various writings within the Buddhist scriptures are all found in collections such as the *Hongming ji*.
The court historian praised Chao for possessing the virtue of selfless devotion, noting that he was not merely elegant in literature alone.
Xu Xuandu (also known as Xu Xun), courtesy name Xuandu, was a native of Gaoyang. He was the great-grandson of Xu Yun, the former General of the Central Command under the Wei dynasty.

Having purified his mind through the study of Buddhism, he was universally admired by the high officials and dukes of the Jiangzuo region. Emperor Jianwen held his character in such high esteem that he visited him every month on the night of the full moon.

As for his pure discourse and subtle principles, they were so tireless and profound that Emperor Jianwen unconsciously drew his seat forward to listen. Liu Zhenchang was a preeminent master of contemporary debate;
he formed a friendship with Xun based on their refined conversation, often saying to others, "When the breeze is clear and the moon is bright, how can I not think of Xuandu?
He once debated the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* with Zhi Dun; when Xun raised a difficult objection, the assembly believed that Dun would be unable to resolve it. Dun—

This conveys a single meaning. The assembly said that Xun had nothing with which to refute [the argument]. Xun once established Chonghua Temple at his residence in Yongxing, Kuaiji, and constructed a four-story pagoda there.
Wang Jianqi—
Wang Jin, courtesy name Jianqi, was a native of Langye. He was accomplished in learning and served as the Administrative Assistant (Lu-shi Canjun) during the Qi dynasty.
He composed the "Stele for Tou-tuo Monastery," a work of refined prose and profound reasoning.
Wang Gouzi, whose courtesy name was Gouzi, was at Waguan Temple with Sengyi. Wang Gouzi engaged him in conversation and asked him to expound on the principles of the Dharma.
Sengyi said to Wang, "Does a sage possess emotions? Wang replied, "No. Sengyi asked, "Is a sage then like a pillar? Wang—
He replied, "It is like the calculation of one's lifespan; though there is no sentient being who operates it, there is nonetheless a sentient being. Sengyi asked, "Who then operates the Sage?

Xi Yanwei (also known as Xi Zuochi), whose courtesy name was Yanwei, was a native of Xiangyang. From his youth, he possessed high aspirations and was extensively learned and widely informed in the arts of literature.

He was renowned for his scholarship. He compiled the *Jin Han Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals of the Jin and Han) in fifty-four fascicles. He was summoned by Huan Wen of the Jin dynasty to serve as a *Congshi* (Assistant Official), and through successive promotions, he became a *Biejia* (Vice-Governor).
At that time, there was the śramaṇa Shi Dao’an, who possessed brilliant eloquence and exceptional talent.
When [Xi] arrived in Jingzhou, he met with him. Dao’an said, "Śramaṇa Dao’an, whose fame covers the heavens. Xi replied, "Xi Zaochi of the Four Seas. Thus did the people of the time [recognize them].

He considered this an excellent response. Xi once wrote to Dao’an, saying: "I have learned that you, O Arhat, tread the path of rectitude; your inner clarity is perfectly integrated, and your compassionate instructions shine upon all.

Both monastics and laypeople receive your protection. Those who revere emptiness awaken to the principle of impermanence, while those who dwell in existence realize the skillful means of transcending the self.
It is as if auspicious clouds move eastward and the *maṇi* jewel turns its radiance back, raining down sweet dew upon the lush grass and planting [virtue] therein."
May the teaching of the Tathāgata be restored to its former glory this very day, like sandalwood brought back to the riverbank;
may the profound waves and sublime echoes once again cleanse and purify this entire age.
Dai Andao (Dai Kui).

His courtesy name was Andao. He was a native of Qiao Commandery. By nature he was lofty and pure. When Prince Xi of Wuling heard that he was skilled at playing the *qin*, he sent an envoy to summon him.
Dai Kui broke his *qin* in the presence of the messenger, saying, "Dai Andao cannot serve as a court musician for the gates of a prince."
The man was Prince Yowu, who once visited him while traveling by boat on a snowy night. During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu, he was repeatedly summoned to court but did not accept these appointments.

He once wished to create a statue of Amitābha Buddha; after three years of concentrated contemplation, the carving was finally completed. He then welcomed the statue and enshrined it at Lingbao Temple in Shanyin.
When Xi Chao saw this, he paid his respects. He took some incense in his hand, and suddenly smoke rose up, reaching far beyond the clouds to the horizon.
The assembly all marveled at its divine wonder.
Zong Shaowen—
Zong Bing, style name Shaowen, was fond of mountains and waters and loved traveling afar. He climbed westward to the Jing and Wu mountains and ascended south to Mount Heng.
He sighed with the ambition of Shangping. Due to illness, he returned to Jiangling and lamented, saying: "I fear I shall not be able to behold all the famous mountains;

I must instead clarify my mind to contemplate the Dao and travel through them while lying down. He depicted every place he had visited in his studio and would often say to others: [He would then describe his travels].
He said, "When one strokes the zither and moves its melody, one desires to cause all the mountains to resound. Liu Yao governed Jingzhou and summoned him to serve as his secretary (zhubushi).
He replied, "I have lived among the hills and drunk from the valleys for thirty years. How could I become a servant who bows at the waist before the gates of a king?"
He then entered Mount Lu to build a dwelling and devoted himself exclusively to his religious practice. He once composed the *Míngfó lùn* (Treatise on Clarifying the Buddha).
Zhāng Lèimin—Zhāng Yě, whose courtesy name was Lèimin—lived in Cháisāng in Xúnyáng and shared a marriage alliance with Táo Yuánmíng. [He was] a student of...

He was proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit classics. Despite being repeatedly summoned to office, he did not comply. Yu Yue, noting his poverty, appointed him as an Attendant Censor (Sanqi Changshi).
He laughed and said, "The ancients considered a mere cubit of space sufficient for their comfort; to bend one's will for the sake of official emolument is not my ambition.
Thereupon, he entered Mount Lu, where he relied upon Master Huiyuan to study and savor the Buddhist scriptures.

Tao Jingjie, whose secular name was Tao Qian, was also styled Yuanming and Yuanliang. He served as the Magistrate of Pengze, but after eighty days in office, he resigned his seal of authority and departed.
He composed the "Return My Home" (Guiqulai Ci) poem. When the Song dynasty received the abdication of the throne, he resided in Chaisang and planted five willow trees before his gate.
For this reason, he took "Five Willows" as his own sobriquet. He was leisurely and quiet, spoke little, and did not covet honor or profit. He loved reading books;

he did not seek an exhaustive understanding of them, but whenever he found something upon opening a volume, he would joyfully forget to eat. Seeing trees casting overlapping shadows and hearing the songs of birds change with the seasons, he found contentment.
He was likewise filled with joy and delight. He frequently traveled to Mount Lu, where he had two disciples and his two sons carry him along.
At that time, Master Huiyuan was establishing a community for the West (the Pure Land), and he sent a letter to invite Yuanming. Yuanming said, "If you permit me to drink [wine], I shall go.
This being granted, he eventually visited him. He also composed the *Sou Shen Ji* (Inquiries into the Divine), which recorded many miraculous manifestations of the Buddha.
Liu Yimin, whose courtesy name was Zhongsu, was a native of Pengcheng. Orphaned at a young age, he was renowned for his filial piety toward his mother.

Possessing great talent and integrity, he held himself in high esteem and refused to submit his spirit to the conventions of the age. Though he suffered from cold and hunger, and though power and fortune lay before him, his resolve remained as deep and unwavering as ever.
The Minister of Education Wang Mi, the Chancellor Bo Xuan, the Palace Attendant Xie Kun, and the Grand Marshal Liu Yao successively recommended him.
Chengzhi declined their offers with vigor and retired to Kuangshan, entrusting himself to Master Huiyuan. Huiyuan said, "Your official emolument is most magnificent; why do you not accept it?
Chengzhi replied, "When ruler and subject harbor mutual suspicion, they are like tumors and growths that mutually impair one another. The entire realm lacks the stability of a solid rock."
The nature of things carries the peril of stacked eggs; what could I possibly do? Yuanran agreed with his reasoning and treated him with profound respect and esteem.
The Grand Marshal (Taishou), likewise finding that his resolve could not be bent, consulted with the various lords to honor him with the title "Surviving Man" (Yimin).

He dwelt in the mountains for fifteen years, practicing the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi). Once, while in meditative concentration, he saw the Buddha’s light illuminating the ground, turning it into gold.
Regarding the physical appearance, there was also the distinction of having their heads stroked and being granted robes.

As for those who remained [in the world], they can truly be said to have contemplated the sublime ritual and awakened their minds to true illumination. They let the numinous robes flutter through the eight directions and let the fragrance of incense persist with the wind throughout their lives;
thus, they may perhaps not have failed Huiyuan’s vow. Altogether one hundred and twenty-three people entered into the盟 (oath/bond) of the Lotus Society.

Zhou Xuzhi, courtesy name Tongzu, was a native of Yanmen. At the age of twelve, he studied under Fan Ning and mastered the Five Classics and the Five Wai (Apocrypha), which were collectively known as the Ten Classics;
he was thus acclaimed by the world as the "Yanzi of his time. Later, he entered Mount Lu and served the śramaṇa Huiyuan.
He wore plain clothes and ate simple vegetables, remaining unmarried for his entire life. Together with Liu Yimin and Tao Jingjie, he was known as one of the "Three Recluses of Xunyang.

Xie Kangle (Xie Lingyun) was the grandson of Xie Xuan; he resided in Shangyu and, from his youth, was fond of learning, extensively reading through various texts, and his literary works were highly acclaimed.
The foremost figure of the region east of the Yangtze River, he served as Governor of Yongjia during the Song dynasty and inherited the noble titles of his grandfather and father;

thus, he was known throughout the world as Kāṅlè (Conqueror of Joy). Possessing great talent, Hui-ling looked down upon the world until he met Master Yuǎn at Mount Lú, whereupon his heart was filled with solemn reverence and submission.

He immediately constructed a terrace at the monastery and translated thirty-six fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. He once composed a hymn in praise of the Buddha, which begins: "This Great Awakened One, through the mind..."

Thus, it is numinous. When defilements are exhausted, wisdom shines; when calculations reach their limit, insight becomes luminous. The threefold penetration reveals that there is no self; with a single hand, one assists the multitude of living beings.

The principles are coarse in mental activity, yet the Way transcends form and sound. The Bodhisattva praised him, saying: "If a person looks up to this school, they develop their nature and cast aside discursive thought.

By means of meditative concentration, they nourish wisdom, and thus they harmonize with these principles. Beginning with the four immeasurables, they ultimately abide for a while; their pursuit reaches its ultimate point, yet it remains external."

They all departed. The Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas praised them, saying: "Your weariness with suffering is profound, yet your aspiration for the Dharma is slight. Like that illusory city, you have been granted a provisional treasure;
by luring you with Nirvāṇa, we have rescued you from old age and decay. These three matters from the beginning have now been transformed into a single Way."
Meng Yi, Meng Yi!
While serving as the Governor of Kuaiji under the Song dynasty, he served the Buddha with such profound sincerity that Xie Lingyun mocked him, saying:

"One who attains the Way must be a man of literary talent and spiritual karma; if one is to be born in heaven, it should be before Lingyun; if one is to become a Buddha, it will surely be after Lingyun."
Later, Huiyi deeply regretted these words; nevertheless, his devotion to the Buddha became even more steadfast and vigorous.
Gao Bógōng—Gao Yǔn, styled Bógōng—was a native of Tiáo in Bohai. Possessing extraordinary talent from his youth, Cui Hong marveled at him, saying: "This young man Gao..."
With a yellow complexion moistened from within and a refined brilliance shining outward, he was destined to be a great vessel of his generation.

Serving in the Wei dynasty, he held successive offices culminating in that of Grand Secretary (Zhongshu Ling) and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Xianyang. Although he enjoyed such honor and nobility, his household remained as poor as ever;

when Emperor Wu visited his residence, there were only a few thatched rooms, with coarse woolen blankets and padded robes, and nothing in the kitchen but fermented soybeans and vegetables. The Emperor remarked, "This is the pure poverty of antiquity."
Is it indeed so? He was granted five hundred bolts of silk and one thousand hu of grain.

He once composed the "Ruru Garden Rhapsody" (Lüyuan Fu) and the "Biography of Dharma Master Tanshi," both of which are exceptionally brilliant in style. At the age of ninety-eight, he passed away without illness.

Ming Shengshao (also written as Ming Shao), courtesy name Chenglie, was a native of Ge in Pingyuan. He was a scholar of the classics who lived in seclusion, styling himself the "Gentleman of Pingyuan.
Emperor Gao of the Qi dynasty wished to visit him; at that time, Ming Shengshao was residing at Dinglin Temple under the patronage of Master Huiyuan. Master Huiyuan asked:
Shao said, "If the Son of Heaven were to come, how would you, Master, respond? Huiyuan said, "I am but a man of the mountains and marshes;
my proper course is to retreat by sealing up the earthen door. If I cannot decline his summons, I shall follow the precedent of Lord Dai.

Emperor Gao knew that his will could not be bent, so he sent someone to bestow upon him a bamboo-root *ruyi* (ceremonial scepter) and a hat made of bamboo shoots. During the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, he once...
While traveling to Mount She, a country elder advised him, saying, "This mountain abounds with fierce tigers and venomous snakes; for this reason, human traces have long been severed.
Daoshao replied, "Among poisons, none surpasses the three poisons. If one possesses loyalty and integrity, one can tread upon fire and water; what then can a fierce tiger do?
He then constructed a thatched hut and lived there for some twenty years, unconcerned with the affairs of the world. He once lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* with the Dhyāna Master Fadu.
In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, it is recorded that at night he saw golden light illuminating his chamber.
Lei Zhonglun (whose courtesy name was Zhonglun) was a native of Yuzhang; he withdrew from public life and refused all summons for office, entering Master Huiyuan’s Lotus Society.
He established a residence beside Donglin. Upon the death of Master Huiyuan, he wrote to his sons and nephews, saying:

"I have entrusted my practice to Mount Lu and served the Venerable Shi for thirty years. Now that the profound master has passed away and my virtuous friends have also perished, I am not yet in old age;
I can still exert my will toward the Western Paradise. From this day forward, do not let me hear of household affairs."
Wang Yande (王彥德), courtesy name Yande, was a native of Qixian County. He had long been a devoted follower of Buddhism. Once, he raised troops to campaign against the Wei.

Wang Xuemu (王玄謨) served as General Ningshuo and was under the command of Xiao Bin (蕭斌), the Protector of the State. Xuemu lost discipline in battle and was sentenced to execution; Shen Qingzhi (沈慶之)...

He remonstrated with him, saying, "Fuli’s威 (military might) shakes all under heaven; how could Xu Muzhi’s strategic plans withstand it? Furthermore, killing a battle-hardened general will only weaken us.
Thereupon [the Emperor] desisted. Initially, when Xu Muzhi was about to be executed, he was spared after Guanyin appeared in a dream.
Later, his official rank reached that of Kai-fu-yi-tong-san-si. He died at the age of eighty-two.
Kong Deyang (also known as Kong Zhigui).
His courtesy name was Deyang. A native of Kuaiji, he possessed a refined and elegant demeanor and was fond of literary composition and verse.

When Governor Wang Sengqian saw him, he held him in high regard and appointed him as a Chief Clerk (*zhubushu*). He served alongside Jiang Yan in overseeing official correspondence and literary drafts. He once replied to Xiao Ziyang...
The Preface states: "I, the humble subject, have long since received the benevolence of your guidance and have deeply benefited from your profound instructions.

As for the Great Awakening’s luminous teachings and the true source of Prajñā, you have caused my six obstructions to be suddenly dispelled and my five passions to be properly exhorted. Thus, I have turned my heart to pay homage."
He attained a great awakening.

Jiang Wéntōng (Jiāng Yān), courtesy name Wéntōng, was a native of Kǎochéng. Orphaned at a young age, he gathered firewood to support his mother. He served in the Qi dynasty, holding various offices until he reached the rank of Palace Attendant.

Zhongcheng Shi was a man of stern demeanor whose integrity and majesty were such that he did not shrink from impeaching those of high rank or close proximity to power. Later, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Liling and became renowned for his poetry and prose.
He once composed the "Treatise on Non-Action" (*Wuwei lun*), in which he said: "I have heard that Great Beings descend to manifest their traces, extensively planting the roots of compassion.
They shatter the cage of birth and death and ascend to the further shore of Nirvana. They expound the Two Vehicles to entice sentient beings and eliminate all marks of attachment."
Returning to the truth, those with wisdom do not perceive its coming or going; those with a [discursive] mind cannot know its beginning or end.
It is profoundly still and eternally abiding, forever transcending all divergent paths.
Xiao Yunying (also known as Xiao Ziliang), whose courtesy name was Yunying, was sincere in his sense of righteousness and fond of antiquity.

When Zhu Baian, a man of the commandery who possessed supreme integrity, passed away, [Xiao] sent one hundred *hu* of rice to his widow, provided a servant for her, and supplied her with firewood. He and Crown Prince Wenhui were both devoted to Buddhism.

As for principle, Ziliang frequently summoned renowned monks to lecture on the various vehicles of the Buddhas. The flourishing of his reverence for the Dharma was unprecedented in the region south of the Yangtze River.
He would sometimes personally serve food and distribute water to the assembly of monks.

Ziliang once dreamed of the Tathāgata Heavenly King of the World of Universal Radiance in the East, who preached the Dharma-gate of Pure Abiding and Pure Conduct; consequently, he composed the *Twenty Fascicles of the Son of Pure Abiding* (*Jingzhu zi*). Pure...
"Zhu" (住) is the Sanskrit term *poṣadha*, meaning to abide according to the precepts by purifying one's body, speech, and mind.

Fan Bolun (范伯倫), whose courtesy name was Bolun, was a native of Shunyang. He served the Liu Song dynasty as a Court Secretary (*zhongshu lang*) and subsequently presided over the National Academy (*guozijian*).

Wine. During the reign of the Minor Emperor (Shao Di), there were many transgressions; [Zhu Daoqian] repeatedly submitted memorials to remonstrate earnestly. He had read extensively through the classics and records, compiling twenty-four chapters of "Excellence from Past and Present.
In his later years, he practiced Buddhism with great devotion, constructing a Jetavana Vihāra to the west of his residence.
Fan Weizong, whose personal name was Yan, was the son of Fan Bolen. He served as Secretary of the Imperial Library during the Song dynasty and compiled the *Book of the Later Han*.

In his "Discourse on the Western Regions," he stated: "The divine transformations of the Buddha-dharma originated in India; yet, among the geographical records of the two Han dynasties, there is no mention of it."
As for Zhang Qian, he merely noted that the land was mostly hot and humid and that they fought while riding elephants.

As for Ban Chao, he only recorded their devotion to the Buddha and their practice of non-killing; yet the merits of their refined culture and skillful guidance have not been passed down in any accounts.

I have heard that their country is as prosperous as the Central Kingdom, where the "Jade Candle" [the harmony of the four seasons] and vital energy prevail, a place where spirits and sages descend to gather and where the virtuous and wise are born.

The divine miracles are strange and extraordinary; thus, their principle transcends the realm of human affairs. The responsive manifestations are clear and evident; thus, these events arise beyond the reach of the mundane world.
Yet, as for those who have not heard of such transcendent achievements, is it because the Way was closed during past eras, or that its fortune has opened only in this later age?
He Yan-de (also known as He Shang-zhi):
His courtesy name was Yan-de. During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, he served as Palace Attendant (*shizhong*). The Emperor once said to Shang-zhi:
"Fan Tai and Xie Lingyun often say that while the Six Classics serve to regulate worldly customs, if one seeks the essential truth of the spirit and nature, it must be through Buddhism."
"Principle serves as our guide. Recently, I have seen Yan Yanzhi’s *Refutation of the Discourse on the Attainment of Nature* and Zong Bing’s *Critique of the Discourse on Black and White*;
both clarify the ultimate truth and inspire the human spirit. If the entire realm were to be purified by this transformation, then I would achieve Great Peace while sitting at ease.
Shaoshang said: "Since the crossing of the Yangtze River, there have been Wang Dao, Zhou Yi, Yu Liang, Xie An, Dai Kui, Fu Da, and Xu Xun."
Wang Meng, Xi Chao, and Wang Tanzhi—my High Ancestor’s brothers—all received his instructions and took refuge [in the Dharma].

In a village of a hundred households, if ten people observe the five precepts, those ten will become pure and prudent. In a district of a thousand houses, if one hundred people cultivate the ten wholesome deeds, those hundred will be harmonious and friendly.
If a person can practice even one good deed, they eliminate one evil; by eliminating one evil, [they advance toward liberation].

"Cease one form of punishment. This is what is meant by the profound principle of "attaining Great Peace while seated. At that time, Yang Yuanbao stepped forward and said, "This discourse is not something I am accustomed to hearing.
I privately believe that for the strong armies of Qin and Chu, or for the annexations of Sun Wu, nothing was taken from this.
Shangzhi replied, "If the state honors the recluses, then the warriors will cease their toil; if it prizes benevolence and virtue, then the martial spirit will subside."
Xiao took the states of Sun and Wu as his ambition, and his every move was aimed at annexation;

thus, he would have had no place for the Way of Yao and Shun—how much less for the teachings of Buddhism! The Emperor was pleased and said, "The Śramaṇa community having you is like the school of Confucius having Ji Lu:
evil words do not enter your ears."
Zhang Xiaoshi, whose courtesy name was Xiaoshi, was a native of Wancheng in Hebei. When he was sixteen years old, his grandfather lost his sight.

Xiaoshi wept in grief and anxiety, walking back and forth day and night to pray for divine protection. He also recited the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra*, arriving at the passage concerning those who regain their vision.
He then invited seven monks to light seven-tiered lamps and recite this sutra for seven days and nights. Each day, as they performed their devotions, he made this prayer:

"Originally, because of my grandson's filial impiety, my grandfather lost his sight. Now, by offering these lamp lights throughout the entire Dharma-realm, I pray that my grandfather’s eyes may regain their clarity;
I seek to take his blindness upon myself. That night, he dreamed of a divine monk who used a golden probe to scrape at his grandfather’s eyes.
After three days, he was completely cured.

Liu Lingyu, whose courtesy name was Lingyu, was a native of Nienyang. He maintained his integrity and was fond of learning. During the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, he served as the Magistrate of Dangyang.

Later, he moved his residence to Jiangling. Although the Prince of Jingling repeatedly summoned him, he did not accept. In a letter of reply, he wrote: "I let the lingering echoes of my teachings resonate within the mountains and marshes;

I entrust my late-life sentiments to fish and birds. Consequently, he abstained from grain and consumed only *shu* (Atractylodes), wore hempen clothing and grass sandals, and maintained long-term fasting while performing ritual recitations.
He did not fail in his practice during the six periods of the day. He annotated the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras.
Regarding Zhou Yanlun and Zhou Yong:
Yanlun was the son [of Zhou Yong]. Yong was a native of Jiankang. He established a hermitage on the western side of Mount Zhong; he lived in pure poverty and had few desires.
He maintained a vegetarian diet throughout his life. When Wang Jian asked him, "What do you eat in the mountains? Yong replied, "Red rice and white salt; green chives and purple dock.
Later, he responded to an imperial decree and entered official service, serving successively as a State Academy Doctor (*guozibo*). Emperor Ming was quite fond of metaphysical principles (*xuanli*).
Yet his actions were often cruel and poisonous. Sengyong did not offer him explicit admonitions, but instead recited from the sutras accounts of karmic causes and effects regarding sin and merit.
The Emperor also desisted somewhat because of this. Once, the Crown Prince asked Sengyong, "How does your spiritual cultivation compare to that of [Seng]yin?

Sengyong replied, "The three miserable realms and the eight difficulties are things we have both failed to escape; yet each of us has our own burdens. The Prince asked, "What are these burdens? Sengyong said:
"Zhou’s wife [eats] what meat? Tanyong once established Mount Ci Temple on Mount Zhong; it is the present-day Caotang Temple.
Yan Zhitui, whose courtesy name was Zifen, served as a Gentleman Attendant at the Gate during the Wuping era of the Western Wei. His entire family observed a vegetarian diet.
He held the Buddhist teachings in profound esteem. His *Yan Jiaxun* (Family Instructions of the Yan Clan) circulates in the world; its chapter titled "Turning the Heart Toward the Buddha" states:
"The matters of immortals (*xiānshén*) are largely empty and far-fetched. Even if one were to attain immortality, one would ultimately still face death. I do not encourage you all to study this.

As for the matters of the three periods of existence in the Buddhist tradition, they are credible and supported by evidence. My family has long turned our hearts toward the Buddha; do not harbor thoughts of contempt or negligence. Within it, there are subtle..."
The essential points are fully contained within the sutras and treatises; I shall not further elaborate upon them here.

Dai Zhongruo (戴仲若), whose courtesy name was Zhongruo, was the son of Dai Kui. His talent and skill were equal to those of his father. Once, Jiang Yi requested that Zhongruo construct a Buddhist monastery for him.
Regarding the statue: it had not been completed for many years. One night, he dreamed that a deity said, "Jiang Yi’s karmic affinity with Avalokiteśvara has not yet harmonized;

you should change it to Maitreya. Sengyong immediately dispatched a messenger to report this, yet Jiang Yi’s letter had already arrived. On that very same evening, both were moved by dreams, and as soon as their hands touched the materials, the wondrous image was perfected.
It is now located at Longhua Temple in Kuaiji. Sengyong was exceptionally refined and possessed great talent; because Shan County had many... [text fragment ends].
He was a man of renowned mountains; thus he originally resided in Shan. Since Tonglu also abounds in famous mountains, he subsequently settled in Tonglu.

Later, being fond of the beautiful scenery of the Wu region, he traveled there again. A group of enthusiasts from Wuzhong built a dwelling for him together, even gathering stones and clearing streams to provide a home.
He once composed the *Xiaoyao lun* (Treatise on Tranquility) and wrote commentaries on the "Zhongyong" chapter of the *Book of Rites*. This was during the Jia period of the Yongchu era.
He was repeatedly summoned to office but did not accept.
Regarding Xie Qingsu:
Xie Qingsu’s courtesy name was Qingsu; he was a native of Kuaiji. He held deep faith in the teachings of Śākyamuni. Early on, he entered Mount Taiping and remained there for over ten years.

In his later years, he made the practice of long-term fasting and making offerings to the Buddha his primary vocation. He tirelessly invited others to join him in these activities to guide and transform them.

Because his mother was elderly, he returned to the Nanshan area at the Ruo River. Xiao Neishi (Xiao Yi) submitted a memorial recommending him for office; he was summoned to serve as a *boshi* (Court Scholar) but did not accept. The Minister of the Interior, Xi Shangshu, once remarked:
"Although Xie Qingxu’s insight and discernment do not surpass those of others, he has entirely eliminated all grounds for mental anxiety."
Yan Yanzhi, courtesy name Yanzhen, was a native of Langya. He served as the Minister of Ceremonies (*Taichang Qing*). He lived a life of purity and frugality, never seeking wealth or profit.
Although his son Yan Jun attained high office and his influence eclipsed that of his contemporaries, Yan Yanzhi did not accept any of the resources or provisions provided by him.
Shou’s residence remained as it was before. Seeing that Xun was building a new house, he said to him, "Build it well; do not let future generations laugh at your clumsiness.

Shi Hui-liang crossed the Yangtze River and stayed at Heyuan Temple, where he lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, and other texts.

Yan Zhi was deeply moved by their virtue and remained lingering in admiration, often sighing and saying: "Seng'an and Fayu have yielded pearls and jade before us; Sengbin and Daoliang now vibrate with golden sounds behind them.
These pure words and wondrous lineages, which were nearly extinguished, are now flourishing once more."
He Zixi (何點), styled Zixi, was the son of He Yan and the grandson of He Shangzhi. He had bright eyes and elegant eyebrows; his appearance was dignified and refined.
He did not boast of his family lineage. Sometimes he drove a wooden cart, and sometimes he wore straw sandals, wandering wherever his whim led, always ending in intoxication.
He returned home. People called him "The Recluse of Penetrating Insight. Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty bestowed upon him a deerskin cap and summoned him for an audience.

He was led into the Hualin Garden, where the Emperor issued an edict appointing him as a Palace Attendant. The Emperor pointed at his own beard with his hand and said, "Do you wish to serve as a minister to this old man?
Thereupon, he took his leave. At that time, renowned scholars such as Xie Yao of Chenjun, Zhang Rong of Wuguo, and Kong Dezhang of Kuaiji were [his contemporaries].

They were inseparable friends. The family of Wang Dian had long been devoted to Buddhism; because Mount Kuaiji was filled with spiritual wonders, they went there to travel and dwell. They resided at Yunmen Monastery on Mount Ruoye.

Dian’s elder brother, Qiu, and younger brother, Yin, both followed him in their reclusive seclusion. The world referred to Dian as "Mount Dà" (the Great Mountain), Yin as "Mount Xiǎo" (the Small Mountain), and Qiu as "Mount Dōng" (the Eastern Mountain).

Liu Shiguang (also known as Liu Xiao), courtesy name Shiguang, was a native of Pingyuan. He was renowned for his filial piety toward his mother and brotherly devotion to his elder brother. Whenever his mother was ill, she would dream that Xiao approached her with medicine;

the following day, when someone asked about it, [she would explain]. His younger brother, Liu Xu, frequently wore a turban made of grain husks and donned a *nà* robe whenever he went wandering in the mountains.
He frequented the mountains and marshes, lingering there so long that he forgot to return home. He was profoundly good at profound discourse and was especially versed in the Buddhist scriptures.
Together with his elder brother, Xu Yao, he attended lectures at Mount Zhong, whereupon they jointly built a hermitage with the intention of spending their final years there.

Xu Yao authored the "Treatise on Ending Life" (*Gezhong lun*), in which he maintained that the physical form is but a lodging-house for the spirit; once the spirit has departed, the lodging quickly decays. The world praised him for his profound understanding.
He was posthumously titled Master Zhenjie.

Yuan Jingqian (袁景倩), whose courtesy name was Jingqian, was orphaned at a young age and devoted himself to reading. As he grew up, he possessed refined character and integrity. He once composed the *Miaode xian*...

Sheng’s biography states that he served the Song dynasty and held successive offices up to the position of Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs. While serving as the regional commander stationed at Shitou City, he was killed by Liu Sengjing.
His son Zui died protecting his father with his own body. Before dying, Sheng said to Zui, "I have not failed to be a loyal minister."
"You have not failed in being a filial son. The reclusive scholar Gu Huan was a partisan of the Daoist teachings.

[Hui]can composed a treatise to refute him, asserting that while the teachings of Confucius and Laozi take the governance of the mundane world as their foundation, the teachings of Śākyamuni take transcendence from the world as their primary principle. Since their initial departures differ, their ultimate goals are likewise distinct.

Furthermore, the Way of the Immortals prizes the transformation of the physical form, whereas Nirvāṇa prioritizes the cultivation of the spirit. As for the transformation of the form... white... [text fragment].

He reached the ultimate depths of the profound mysteries, yet was unable to transcend death. As for those who cultivate the spirit, their worldly delusions diminish daily, and they abide in a state of serene permanence.
Wang Huai zhi, whose courtesy name was Yuanhui, was a native of Langye. His family had long followed the Confucian tradition and did not believe in the Buddha-dharma; he often said that the body—
When both body and spirit perish together, how can there be three periods of existence? During the Yuanjia era, he served as the Magistrate of Danyang.

When his illness reached its terminal stage and he had barely regained consciousness, He Daoli, the Magistrate of Jiankang, went to visit him. Zhi said to Daoli, "The body dies, but the spirit survives; only now do I know that the teachings of Śākyamuni are not false.
Daoli replied, "Throughout your life, Your Excellency’s philosophical positions were not such as this. What have you seen today that causes you to suddenly [change your view]?"
Was this not extraordinary? Huai composed his countenance and replied, "The spirit is truly inexhaustible; one cannot but believe in the Buddha.
Having spoken these words, he passed away.
He Zi-ji... [text ends]
He Yin, styled Zijì, was fond of learning from his youth. He served as a disciple under Liu Yan of Pèguó, receiving instruction in the *Yì*, the *Lǐjì*, and the *Máoshī*.
From time to time, he would enter Zhōngshān Dìnglín Sī to study the Buddhist scriptures (*nèidiǎn*). During the Qi dynasty, he served as the Governor of Jiàn'ān.

Whenever the fast days of the伏 (fú) and 臘 (là) occurred, he would release prisoners to return home, and they invariably returned according to the appointed date. He Yin once discussed vegetarianism with his disciples; the disciples submitted [their views].
