The Commentary states: Among great transformations, none surpasses birth and death; among what is most weighty in birth and death, nothing exceeds one's nature and destiny (*xingming*).
Nature and destiny are of the utmost urgency for that [other world], whereas the flavors of the palate are merely matters of personal indulgence that may be postponed.

If one were to say that coming and going is but a constant occurrence of life and death, then even the most heart-wrenching sorrow would eventually reach them. Consequently, in his final years, Sengyin finally renounced the taste of blood.
Su Qiong, courtesy name Zhenzhi, was a native of Wuchang. He served as the Governor of Qinghe. Once, an elderly man from the commandery presented him with two melons;

Su Qiong placed them upon a beam and never cut them. By nature, he delighted in the principles of Chan (meditation). When a śramaṇa came to visit him, his intention was to inquire about [the state of the Governor’s practice].
The debt was settled. Throughout the entire day, [Wang] Qiong conversed with him on the profound mysteries (*xuan*), leaving the śramaṇa unable to open his mouth.
When a disciple asked for the reason, the śramaṇa said, "Whenever I see the Lord of the Prefecture, he takes me straight into the azure clouds. How could I possibly discuss matters of this earth?
Thereupon, he burned the promissory note.
*Fǎxǐzhì* (Record of the Joy of Dharma), Volumes One and Two.
Compiled by the Daoist Bīnglián (Ice Lotus), Xià Shùfāng.
The Layman Wudou, Feng Ding, read the work of Tao Zhenbai (Tao Hongjing). His courtesy name was Tongming.
He was a native of Danyang. His mother, Lady Huo, dreamed that a celestial being descended, holding an incense burner in his hand.
In his family, there was one who became pregnant and gave birth to Hongjing. At the end of the Song dynasty, he served as the tutor to various princes.

During the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, he removed his court robes and hung them at the Shenwu Gate, submitting a memorial to resign from his emoluments. The high officials and nobles held a farewell banquet for him at the Zhenglu Pavilion with great magnificence;
both the court and the commonalty regarded this as an honor. He settled at the Huayang Cave on Mount Jiuqu, where he constructed a three-story watchtower and dwelt upon it himself. One hundred...
He should have completely severed [worldly ties], listening only occasionally to the blowing of the *sheng* flute. He planted pine trees throughout his courtyard;

whenever he listened to the sound of the wind in the pines, he would find joy and delight within himself. He shared a long-standing friendship with Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty from their days as commoners. After the Emperor ascended the throne, he issued a hand-written edict summoning him. Hongjing painted two oxen:
one was let loose to graze on water and grass, while the other wore a golden headstall and halter and was being driven by a whip. The Emperor laughed.

The Emperor remarked, "How can this be less than the story of Zhuangzi cutting off the tail of the turtle? Thereupon, he ceased all further requisitions. Regarding the great affairs of state, there was nothing that did not await his decision.
Whenever the Emperor received a letter from Hongjing, he would invariably burn incense, wash his hands, and read it with devotion.

From Shen Yue, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, downward, all set aside their usual respect for teachers and seniors. At the time, he was popularly known as the "Minister of the Mountains. He once constructed a white stupa for a Bodhisattva.
At Mount Sanmao, he again dreamed that the Buddha bestowed upon him a prophecy, naming him Bodhisattva Śrī-bala.

He then proceeded to the Aśoka Stūpa in Mao County, where he took a vow to observe the five major precepts. At the time of his death, he refused to bathe; instead, he covered his bedding with a great *kāṣāya* robe.
His disciples followed his instructions. He was eighty-five years old at his passing, and was posthumously titled Master Zhenbai.

Xun Gongpu, whose courtesy name was Xun Xu, served as Director of the Imperial Secretariat during the reign of Emperor Wu. He obtained the bamboo slips from the tomb at Jiji County and compiled them into the *Zhongjing* (Central Canon), which was subsequently cataloged in the Imperial Library.
When he was promoted from the Office of the Central Secretariat to the position of Minister of the Interior, people congratulated him, saying: [The text continues with the congratulatory remarks.]
"You have snatched away my Phoenix Pond; how can you all offer congratulations? In the second year of the Taishi era, Xū fashioned twelve golden images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in Luoyang.
They emitted great radiance, and the people of the capital flocked together to gaze upon and worship them.

Liu Huifei, courtesy name Xuánwén, was a native of Péngchéng. He was widely learned and skilled in literary composition. He began his official career as a *cānjūn* (attendant counselor) to the Prince of Ānchéng under the Liáng dynasty.

Later, he retired to live in seclusion at Dōnglín Monastery, where he constructed for himself a small garden named Lígòu (Free from Defilement). Consequently, people of the time referred to him by that name.
The Master Ligou traveled with Zhang Xiaoxiu; they were in perfect harmony and took great delight in one another.
Commentators remarked that it would be nearly two hundred years after the time of Dharma Master Huiyuan before there would again be such a flourishing period for the Zhang and Liu families.

Lu Zuogong (陸佐公), whose courtesy name was Zuogong, was diligent in his studies from a young age and excelled at composing literary works. During the Yongming era, he served alongside eight others, including Xie Miao, as a close attendant for his literary talents.
He was successively promoted to the rank of Jishi Huangmen Silang. At the beginning of the Tianjian era, together with Liu Xiao...

Chuo went on a pilgrimage to Longmen and once composed an inscription for the stupa of Master Zhi, which reads: "His ancestral lineage is difficult to ascertain, and his place of residence is rarely seen.

He is like something emerging from the depths, or as if appearing out of space. His words leave no fixed traces; his conduct transcends ordinary ranks. He vanished while sitting and appeared while standing; his body dissolved and his spirit divided.
When he moved his feet, walls stood up; when he spoke, the wind bowed down. People merely recognize his spiritual wonders, but none can fathom his profound depth."
Qian. Kong Yanshen (also known as Kong Chunzhi).
His courtesy name was Yanshen. He resided in Shan County, Kuaiji. By nature he loved mountains and waters; whenever he traveled, he would invariably...

Having exhausted the mysteries of its secluded heights, he once encountered the śramaṇa Fachong while traveling in the mountains; he invited him to stay and ascend together, and so they remained for three years.
Thereupon, pointing toward Fachong, he sighed and said: "I have longed for those beyond the mundane world for thirty years, and only now do we meet under this same canopy."
He was unaware that old age was approaching. Xie Fangming, the Governor of Kuaiji, earnestly sought to invite him but could not succeed.
The messenger said to him, "If you will not enter my commandery, why do you enter my outskirts? Zhunzhi laughed and said, "One who swims in concealment does not concern himself with the waters;
one who nests in the heights does not distinguish the forests. As for where the flying and the diving go, why ask about their master? Yuan.
At the beginning of the Jiā period, he was summoned to serve as an Attendant Gentleman of the Secretariat but did not accept the appointment.

Liáng Jìngzhī—Liáng Sù, whose courtesy name was Jìngzhī—was promoted to Palace Secretary of the Crown Prince for his elegant and refined literary style. He compiled the National History and held successive offices.
He served as a Hanlin Academician. He studied the Tiantai teachings under Master Jingxi and attained a profound mastery of their essential principles.
Because the texts of *Zhiguan* were so vast in both wording and meaning that readers would waste much time upon them, he edited and condensed them into six fascicles for circulation in the world.
He also authored the "Stele of Tiantai Chanlin Monastery," the "General Principles of Tiantai Zhiguan," and the "Biographical Treatise on Master Zhiyi."

Wei Boqi, whose courtesy name was Boqi, was Wei Shou. From his youth, he was quick-witted and capable of composing literary works. After the Northern Qi dynasty received the abdication of the throne, all the imperial edicts and the history of the Wei were compiled by Shou.
He held office as the Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs and was posthumously honored with the title Wenzheng. It was he who authored the *Wei shu*.

The *Folao zhi* states: "Among all classes of living beings, the spiritual consciousness (*shen-shi*) of the three periods of existence never perishes. Whatever good or evil one performs will inevitably entail retribution.
By gradually accumulating superior karma, one refines away coarseness and vulgarity; through the various forms of the scriptures, one bathes and tempers the divine spirit."

It extends even to attaining the Buddha-way through non-arising. It includes the discourse on the three refuges and the five precepts; rebirth within the six realms; the progressive cultivation of the six perfections;

as well as the true and responsive bodies of the Buddha, which are neither born nor extinguished; and the meaning of the widespread propagation of teaching through stūpas and temples dedicated to Śāriputra.
This is most profound and esoteric.
Liu Kai—Liu Kai was the great-grandson of Liu Yanzhi; he served as the Governor of Jian’an. His old friend Ren Fang sent a poem to Kai requesting [something].

There was but a single garment. When Kai searched his bag, he found nothing with which to present a gift. [The other] replied: "My clothes are originally but a hundred patches; the people of Min raise but eight silkworms a year.
Though my official rank reached that of Minister of Personnel, at home I subsist on vegetarian food, sleep upon a straw mat in an empty room, and have no female attendants by my side."

Morning and evening, he followed the monks in ritual recitation. Emperor Wu provided him with three days of vegetarian fasting each month, and all the stipends he received were dedicated to the two temples at Mount Jiang.
When he passed away, his countenance remained as if alive; he departed this life while bending two fingers.
Shen Xiwen (Shen Yue), courtesy name Xiwen, was a native of Dongyang in Wuzhou. In his youth, he served as a scholar and enjoyed great renown in his time.

He was celebrated for his refined elegance, yet his physique was so slender that people of the era remarked, "The waist of Master Shen is thin. He once devised an innovative method for composing verse based on tonal prosody.

He revised the ancient *Shijing* according to the rules of prosody, which later generations adopted as a standard; this was titled the *Sisheng* (Four Tones). He established his residence on a suburban mound and composed the "Fu on Suburban Dwelling" (*Jiaojufu*) to describe himself.
His official career reached the rank of Minister of the Interior (*Shangshu Puye*). Xiao Xiuwen was exceptionally refined in his understanding of Buddhist principles;

he authored one scroll of the *Zhongshi lun* (Treatise on Midday Meals), in which he stated that there are three things that obstruct the Way: first, power, profit, glory, and fame; second, the allure of beauty and luxury; and third, delicious delicacies.
Fatty and rich foods both cause the mind and spirit to become clouded and disordered; yet one becomes sweetly addicted to them, which constitutes a most urgent source of affliction.

Since the Buddhas of antiquity did not eat after midday, one should infer from this that late meals should be consolidated into the period before noon. From the time after midday until the following morning, one remains pure, empty, and free from affairs;
thoughts naturally become simplified. At first, one may not yet be focused, but with persistence, it becomes a habit. This is truly a means [a "trap"] for casting off worldly burdens.
*Zhen*: A swift shortcut for attaining the Way.
Liu Yanhe (Liu Xie), whose courtesy name was Yanhe, was a native of Dongguan. He was highly esteemed by the Crown Prince Zhao Ming. He composed the *Wenxin Diaolong*.
Lóng composed fifty treatises. Being poor, he did not marry and lived in dependence upon the śramaṇa Sēngyù, through whom he became extensively versed in the sūtras and śāstras.
He categorized the various schools and wrote prefaces for them; the collection of scriptures at Dinglin Temple was his own arrangement.

Shěn Yuè, the Minister of the Central Secretariat, held his writings in the highest esteem and would always place them upon his desk. Regarding all the temples, pagodas, and monuments of famous monks in the capital...

The inscriptions on all [the monuments] were produced by his hand. He held successive offices as a *tongshi sheren* (Attendant-in-Ordinary). He submitted a memorial requesting to leave the household life;
he first burned off his own beard as a vow, which the Emperor praised. The Emperor bestowed upon him the Dharma name Huìdì.
Cui Ziyue, Cui Ziyue:
at five years of age he lost his father and refused to eat meat. Later, while observing the mourning period for his mother, he was so grieved and emaciated that he became a mere skeleton.

When his elder brother’s son, Du, died, he did not enter his private chambers for one hundred days. Standing over eight chi tall, his appearance and spirit were exceptionally refined and extraordinary; he served as the Attendant Gentleman (Pingyuan Gong) to the Prince of Pingyuan.
The Grand Master of the Household (Kaifu Jijiu) and his nephew Zhan went together to Jinyang to reside in a Buddhist temple.

Zhan was two years older than Zijue; whenever he retired from court and stood for a long time, Zijue would lean against a couch to face him. The refined elegance of these two men was truly magnificent.
Various śramaṇas secretly observed him and considered him to be one of the two celestial beings.
Liu Shiyin—Liu Ji’s courtesy name was Shiyin—was of an exceptionally filial nature. At fourteen, he lived in mourning for his father; every time he wept, he would vomit blood. His family was poor.

Together with his younger brother Xiāo, he resolved to apply himself diligently to learning. He was widely read and possessed extensive knowledge. During the Tiānjiān era of the Liáng dynasty, he served in succession as the Magistrate of Xīchāng and Hǎiyán.
When his mother, Lady Míng, fell ill, he wept as he recited the name of Guānyīn tens of thousands of times; his mother’s illness was cured. When she passed away, [he continued his practice].
He dwelt in a hut at his father’s grave, wailing in mourning; a pair of white cranes flew alongside him. His extant works include the *Shisuyu* (Explanations of Colloquial Terms) in eight fascicles.

Yuansizong, whose courtesy name was Shizong, was a native of Chenliu. His father, Yanzhi, served as the Secretary of the Imperial Household (*Chongzhonglang*) under the Grand Marshal (*Taiwei*) of the Song dynasty. [Xu] Xiaoxu...
At thirteen years of age, Xu mastered the essential principles of the Five Classics. At sixteen, he encountered a family tragedy; he entered Mount Zhong to attend lectures.
When his mother fell ill, Xu returned home from the lecture hall with a heart full of alarm. Medicine was required that included fresh *renshen* (ginseng).

He went into the mountains to seek it but had not yet found it when, suddenly, a deer appeared before him. Finding this strange, he followed the deer to where it rested and indeed discovered the *renshen*. Once the medicine was prepared, his mother... [recovered].
His illness soon abated. Wang Yan, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, came to visit him; Xu detested this man and slipped away by breaking through his fence.

When Wang Yan was subsequently executed, Xu escaped punishment because he was not an associate. He once used a deer forest as a hermitage, surrounding it with woods and ponds, and cut himself off from social visits so that few in the world could see him.
When Ren Fang, the Vice Minister of the Imperial Chancery, wished to meet him, he would simply gaze toward the hermitage from afar.
He returned and pointed toward Luk-lin, saying to his elder brother, "The dwelling is near, but the person is far away. From that time on, the court nobles ceased visiting him;
he maintained friendship only with Fei Ziyě. Toward the end of the Tianjian era, though summoned repeatedly, he did not go.

He said, "If even common deer such as the *jūn* and *jiā* could all be employed in the imperial chariots, how would they differ from the *lù* and *jì* steeds? He once composed the *Qīlù* (Seven Records), which catalogued internal and external books and documents;
its sixth section was titled the *Fófǎ Lù* (Record of the Buddha-Dharma). Upon his death, his disciples conferred upon him the posthumous title of Wenzhen Chushi (Wenzhen Hermit).

Yu Yanshi, whose courtesy name was Yanshi, was a native of Xinye. From childhood, he was intelligent and quick-witted; there were no classics, histories, or works of the hundred schools that he did not master. By nature, he delighted in forests and springs;
he lived simply on vegetarian food and plain clothing, never engaging in worldly occupations. During the Putong era, he was summoned to serve as a Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gate.

He did not serve [in office]. In his later years, he followed the teachings of Śākyamuni and established a *dharma-śālā* within his residence, where he performed prostrations and recitations during the six periods of the day.
Upon his death, he was posthumously titled Master Zhenjie (Master of Upright Integrity). — Du Fuyan.

Du Bi, courtesy name Fuyan, was a native of Zhongshan. From childhood, he was intelligent and quick-witted; as his family was poor and lacked books, he attended the regional academy to pursue his studies, where he was highly esteemed by his contemporaries.
At the beginning of the reign of Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty, he was appointed as a Doctor of the Imperial Academy.

Upon entering the Northern Qi, he was sent on a diplomatic mission to Western Wei by Gao Huan (Shenwu). When the Wei Emperor saw him in the Jiulong Hall, he remarked, "You are profoundly learned in the study of Buddhism. Let me... [text continues]
Question: "In the sutras, are Buddha-nature and Dharma-nature the same or different? Bi replied, "They are but a single principle.

He asked again, "Those who speak say that Dharma-nature is broad and Buddha-nature is narrow; how is this so? Bi replied, "When it resides in the broad, it becomes broad; when it resides in the narrow, it becomes narrow.
If one discusses the essence of nature itself, it is neither narrow nor broad. The Emperor said, "Since you say it becomes broad and becomes narrow, why..."
"It is neither narrow nor wide. Bi said, "If one says it is wide, then it cannot constitute narrowness; if one says it is narrow, it likewise cannot function as width.
Because it is neither wide nor narrow, it is able to be both wide and narrow. Although that which is produced differs, the producer is one.
The Emperor praised this as excellent.
Xu Xiaomu (Xu Ling):
His courtesy name was Xiaomu. A native of Shan, he served as a Court Gentleman Attendant (*sanqi changshi*) under the Liang dynasty.

When Hou Jing invaded the Liang and his father, Xu Shixiu, was besieged, Ling maintained a vegetarian diet and wore plain cloth garments, appearing as if he were in a state of profound mourning. Upon his return from Qi, he was appointed... [text ends]
He served as the Censor-in-Chief (*yushi zhongcheng*). At that time, Prince Ancheng, Wang Xu, was the Minister of Works (*sikong*), and his power dominated both the court and the commonalty;

no high official dared to speak out against him. Xiao Ling impeached and prosecuted him, causing both the court and the commonalty to be struck with solemn awe. He held successive offices until he reached the rank of Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince (*taizi shaofu*). At the age of eight, Ling was already capable of composing literary works.
The śramaṇa Baozhi rubbed the crown of his head and said, "This is a stone qilin from the heavens. He once attended lectures by Zhiyi.

While lecturing on the sutras, he established five vows: first, to maintain right mindfulness at the moment of death; second, not to fall into the three miserable realms; third, to take rebirth among human beings;

fourth, to leave the household life as a celibate youth; and fifth, not to become a monk who succumbs to worldly customs. Later, during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, he was born into the Zhu family of Jinyun.
When he was eighteen years old and about to take a wife, he encountered a foreign monk on the road who said to him, "Young man, what is your intention?"
Wishing to break his former vow, he revealed his five aspirations; thereupon, [the king] was moved to realization and no longer returned home.

He immediately went to Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai, where he entered the service of Dharma Master Zhang’an to inquire about and receive the essentials of the mind. He realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra and was given the name Zhìwēi.
Xu Xiaoké, Xu Xiaoké:

the younger brother of [Prince] Ling. He was filial by nature, mastered the Five Classics, and was skilled at composing literature. During the Taicheng era of the Liang dynasty, he began his official career as a *boshi* (Doctor).

Amidst the chaos caused by Hou Jing’s rebellion and the resulting famine, Xu Xiaoké supported his mother; as even thick gruel and rice porridge could not suffice for their sustenance, he shaved his hair and became a monk.
The śramaṇa supported himself by begging for alms. Later, he was honored at court, and Emperor Gaozong summoned him to serve as the Chief Libationer (Jijiu).

Whenever he attended banquets and received rare fruits, he would return with them to present to his mother. Emperor Gaozong sighed in admiration and commanded the relevant authorities to provide provisions for his mother.
It was during this period that a divine monk from India named Fazheng arrived.

Li Zhiyue, whose courtesy name was Zhiyue, was a native of Pingji. Orphaned at a young age, he served his mother with filial piety. His paternal uncle, Li Zhang, praised him, saying, "This is our family’s Zengzi.
Although his clan and relatives were powerful and prosperous, Li Shiqian alone donated his residence to establish a temple, conducting himself with constant vigilance and frugality.
He was simple by nature and abstained from wine and meat. After the Sui dynasty took control of the realm, he remained steadfast in his resolve not to serve in office.
He once had a thousand *shí* of millet that he had lent to his fellow villagers; when a famine struck, he burned the promissory notes before a crowd and did not demand repayment.

The following year there was another great famine, and Sishuan exhausted his family’s resources to provide gruel and distribute medicine, saving the lives of tens of thousands of villagers. Someone said to him: "You..."
"You have performed many deeds of hidden virtue (*yīn dé*). In the future, your lineage will surely flourish and become great. Sishen said, "Hidden virtue is like ringing in one's ears;
one knows it oneself, but no one else knows. Since you now know of it, what merit is there in it? Sishen was skilled at discussing the profound principles (*xuán lǐ*) of the Way.

Once, while he was seated with guests, there was one who did not believe in the Buddhist doctrine of karmic retribution. Sishen exhorted him, saying, "The accumulation of goodness brings forth blessings; the accumulation of evil brings forth calamity..."
Are these not the retributions for the lingering calamities of past evils?

As for Gun becoming a yellow bear, Du Yu becoming a *tíjué* (cuckoo), Bao Jun becoming a dragon, Niu Ai becoming a tiger, Peng Sheng becoming a boar, Rui Yi becoming a dog, and Deng Ai becoming an ox—these are all such instances.
Xu Bo became a fish; Yang Hu was the son of Li Zi in a previous life. Is this not what the Buddhist tradition calls "transforming and receiving a different form"?
The guest said, "Xing Zicai asked: 'How could the latter incarnation of a pine or cypress tree transform into a *chū* or *lì* tree?
I believe this to be true. Shishen said, "This is a discourse on what is dissimilar. Transformation is entirely created by the mind; how could a tree [be otherwise]?"
"Does he have a mind? The guest was unable to challenge him further.

Yang Su, Duke of Yang, whose courtesy name was Chudao, was a native of Huayin. With extraordinary strategies and sublime compositions, he was a preeminent talent of his time. He held successive offices as high as...

He served as a Zhuguo (Commander-in-Chief) and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Yue. He held the Buddha-dharma in profound esteem and constructed Guangming Temple. He also built Siqiao Temple on Mount Hua.
Once, while practicing the Way in a monastery, he observed a painted image on the wall. A Daoist said, "This is the 'Diagram of Laozi Transforming the Hu People into Buddhas.
Xu Su replied, 'I have heard that when Laozi transformed the Hu people, they would not accept him. Therefore, Laozi manifested himself as a Buddha.'"
The Hu people were then able to receive [the teaching]. This demonstrates that the Buddha was able to convert the Hu, whereas the Dao could not. Why, then, do you say that Laozi converted the Hu?
Furthermore, for what purpose would Laozi have converted the Hu into Buddhists? Why did he not convert them into followers of the Dao? The proponents of the Daoist tradition were unable to respond.
Zhang Shiheng was a native of Leshou. He lost his mother at the age of nine and grieved so deeply that he violated the prescribed mourning period.

When the wars broke out at the end of the Sui dynasty and scholars were forced to abandon their studies, Zhang Shiheng resumed teaching in his hometown. Crown Prince Chengqian welcomed him there and introduced him to Emperor Taizong, who held him in high esteem.
The Erxian Scholar was asked by the Crown Prince about how to serve the Buddha and cultivate merit. He replied: "Serving the Buddha lies in purity, benevolence, and forbearance.
If one is greedy, arrogant, and vain, even if one exhausts their wealth to serve him, it will not diminish one's calamities.

Furthermore, good and evil must inevitably be requited, just as a shadow follows a form. If you are an enlightened ruler, a loyal minister, and a filial son, then your fortune and blessings will endure forever."
To act contrary to this brings disaster. At that time, the Crown Prince harbored rebellious intentions; therefore, [the Emperor] used the response as a means to admonish him.
Sun Simiao, Sun Simiao, was a native of Huayuan. From childhood he was intelligent and wise, memorizing ten thousand words a day. Du Guxin marveled at him and said, "A sage!"

He was a youth who excelled in the works of Laozi and Zhuangzi and was also proficient in the principles of Yin and Yang, as well as in calendrical calculation and medicine. He investigated all aspects of the Buddhist scriptures without exception.
Residing on Mount Taibai, he was summoned by Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty as a Doctor of the National Academy but did not accept the appointment.

When Emperor Taizong summoned him to the capital, he was already old; though the Emperor wished to grant him office, he refused and eventually returned to the mountains on the pretext of illness. He once transcribed the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* by hand.
The Taizong asked Miaoyi, "Which sutra is the greatest? He replied, "The Avataṃsaka Sūtra is that which the Buddha honors as the greatest.
The Emperor said, "Recently, Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang translated the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra in six hundred fascicles;

why is this not considered the greatest, while the eighty-fascicle version is instead regarded as such? He replied, "The Dharma-realm of the Avataṃsaka encompasses all gates. Within all these gates..."
One may say that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* is but a single gate of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, which can unfold the great scroll of the trichiliocosm. The Emperor was enlightened;
from then on, he received and upheld [the teachings]. Lu Zhaolin once praised him, saying: "When he speaks loftily of the One True Principle (*Zhengyi*), he is the ancient Mozi and Zhuangzi."
To enter deeply into non-duality is to be the present-day Vimalakīrti.

Wang Zhongyan—whose courtesy name was Zhongyan—was a native of Longmen. Having reached the age of majority, he was filled with a profound resolve to broadly rescue the masses of living beings. To the west...

He traveled to Chang’an and presented twelve strategic memoranda for the establishment of peace (*Taiping shier ce*), but they were not adopted. He composed the "Song of the Eastern Expedition" (*Dongzheng ge*) and returned home.

Thereupon, he studied the *Shi* and *Shu*, rectified ritual and music, compiled the *Yuan jing*, and expounded upon the Way of the *Yi*. Within nine years, his work on the Six Classics was largely completed.
Disciples came to him from afar, including Du Ruhui of Jingzhao, Li Jing of Zhaojun, and Pi Shou of Hedong. The middle...
Shan Jiaqiong, Fang Yuanling of Qinghe, Wei Zheng of Julu, Wang Gui and Wen Yanbo of Taiyuan—all claimed to have received the way of a royal minister from him while serving under him.
In the thirteenth year of the Daye era, he fell ill; upon hearing that Emperor Yang had been killed, [he passed away].
He rose with tears falling and said, "The people have long been weary of turmoil. Heaven may perhaps be about to inaugurate an era like that of Yao and Shun;
yet I shall not participate in it. It is my fate. He then passed away. He once composed the *Zhongshuo* (Discourses of the Center) as a counterpart to the *Lunyu* (Analects).

In its chapter on the Duke of Zhou, he wrote: "The flourishing of the Odes and Documents led to the destruction of the Qin dynasty; this was not the fault of Confucius. When metaphysical abstractions (*xuánxū*) grow long..."
The chaos of the Jin dynasty was not the fault of Laozi and Zhuangzi. The fall of the Liang state despite the observance of fasts and rituals was not the error of Śākyamuni.
Does the *I Ching* not say: "If it is not the right person, the Way will not manifest"? Someone asked about the Buddha, to which Wen Zhongzi replied: "He is a sage. The questioner asked:
"What is his teaching like? He replied: "It is the teaching of the West; in the Middle Kingdom, it would be mired in formalism."

Chu Suiliang of Henan, courtesy name Dengshan, was a native of Qiantang. In the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era, when Emperor Taizong proclaimed that Master Xuanzang’s translated scriptures were to be circulated, Suiliang entered the court and memorialized, saying:
"The Buddha-dharma is profound and mysterious; neither gods nor men can fathom it."
The essence is profoundly deep; the gates of language are difficult to enter. Your Majesty protects the five vehicles and establishes the Three Jewels.

Born with noble character during this age of decline, you have emerged as a preeminent figure after a thousand years. You have traversed perilous precipices to seek the scriptures and walked upon treacherous paths to inquire after the Way.

Having encountered rare wonders in foreign lands, you have fully obtained the authentic texts. Returning to your kingdom to translate and proclaim them is like the first appearance of the *amra* fruit.

This exquisite text and profound meaning are as if the golden mouth [of the Buddha] has newly opened its teaching. How much more so, since Your Majesty’s benevolence is vast and far-reaching, causing it to be spread throughout the nine provinces, so that all the common people may partake of the wondrous Dharma.
For us ministers, such an opportunity is difficult to encounter in ten million kalpas; we cannot contain our joy and good fortune.

Suiliang was widely versed in literature and history and was skilled in the regular and clerical scripts. He served successively as Palace Counselor (Jianyi Dafu) and concurrently as Recorder of the Court (Qiju Zhu). The Emperor Taizong said: "I..."
"Are there instances of misconduct? Do you, Minister, also record them? Su Lian replied, "It is my duty to hold the writing brush; whatever the Sovereign does must be recorded.

Later, when he received the charge of regency to assist Emperor Gaozong, he was promoted to Right Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs. When Emperor Gaozong wished to establish Empress Wu as empress, Su Lian remonstrated with all his might, but his words were not accepted.
He then placed his ceremonial tablet (hu) at the palace steps, struck his head until it bled, and said, "I return this tablet to Your Majesty; I beg to retire to my fields."
Li. His loyalty and integrity were such as this.
Yu Wenyi (Yu Shinan), courtesy name Boshī, was a native of Yaojiang. During the Zhenguan era, he served as a Scholar of the Hongwen Hall. His portrait was depicted on the [Ling]... [Walls].

Yanke. Shen Nan deeply revered Buddhist affairs. He once composed a preface stating: "As a disciple, I suddenly encountered a grave illness in my early years and vowed to provide a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks.
Now, I respectfully offer vegetarian food to a thousand monks at this place of practice.

By the power of this vow, I hope that in life after life I shall always be free from sickness and affliction. May this same wish extend to seven generations past and distant times, and to all those—whether enemies or kin—within the six realms of existence."
Later, Fang Xuanling passed away. The Emperor personally issued an edict to Prince Tai of Wei, saying:
"With the death of Fang Xuanling, there is no longer anyone within the halls of Shiqu and Dongguan. Not long after, he composed a poem on the rise and fall of past dynasties and sighed:
"When Zhong Ziqi died, Boya never again played the lute for the rest of his life. To whom shall I show this poem of mine? He then ordered Chu... [the remainder of the text is missing].
Suiliang took it to the spirit altar of Yanshou’s memorial hall and burned it after reading it through, hoping that his consciousness might attain awakening.
The following year, he dreamed of Yanshou offering forth upright counsel as if in life. Consequently, he issued an edict stating:

"The late Minister of Rites, Duke Wenyi Yu Yanshou, was pure and complete in his virtuous conduct and maintained a will devoted to loyalty and benefit. Having suddenly passed away into the realm of things, I feel this all the more keenly."

I am deeply grieved. You may immediately prepare a vegetarian feast for five hundred monks at his residence and commission one statue of the Buddha to provide merit for his posthumous welfare, thereby expressing my intention to honor our old friendship.

Kong Yingda, whose courtesy name was Zhongda, composed the *Wujing Zhengyi* (Correct Meanings of the Five Classics). During the reign of Emperor Taizong, he held successive offices and eventually served as the Director of the National University (*Guozijiao*).
At that time, the monk Huìjìng was discussing Buddhist doctrine with the Daoist Cai Huáng; Huáng was repeatedly defeated in debate, while Kong Yingda remained inwardly attentive.
Daodang said to Huijing, "In the Buddha's teaching there is no contention; why do you, O Dharma Master, repeatedly provoke such difficulties?
Huijing replied, "The Buddha refuted the non-Buddhists, but they could not respond. Instead, they turned around and said to the Buddha: 'You always say for yourself that you are impartial.'"
"Now that you have refuted me with difficult arguments, this is itself unjust. What is meant by 'equality'? The Buddha explained to him:
"I use my own lack of injustice to refute your injustice; if you attain justice, then I am likewise just. He continued: "It is the same now as well:
I use the dispute of purity to refute your dispute; if they attain freedom from dispute, then that is the purity of non-dispute."
Du Keming, whose courtesy name was Keming, was a native of Duling. He was brilliant and decisive, possessing the talent of a minister who assists a sovereign.

When Emperor Taizong ascended the throne, he was promoted to Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (*you puye*) and, together with Fang Xuanling, managed the affairs of state. He honored the Way of the Dharma Master Yuankuan.
He once inquired after the essential Dharma. At the time of his death, he summoned Sengwan, wishing for her to be his teacher in every successive life.
Sima Qiaqing, a native of Henei, served as a Judicial Rectifier at the Court of Judicial Review. By nature he was pure and prudent, possessing the most exemplary conduct. [Yong...]

While serving as the Assistant Magistrate of the Judicial Department in Yangzhou during the Huichun era, he encountered the mourning period for his mother. During his period of bereavement, he became so emaciated that he was reduced to a mere skeleton.

He drew blood from his own body to transcribe the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Not long after, two stalks of *zhicao* (mushroom) grew from within his mourning hut; they were one foot and eight inches tall, with green stems and crimson caps.
One *sheng* of its juice was extracted daily; its flavor was as sweet as honey, and once taken, it would grow back again.
Qiao Qing and several of his colleagues witnessed this event together.
—Prince Wenzhang of An.

Wang Bo, courtesy name Zian, was a native of Longmen. At the age of six, he excelled in literary composition. During the early years of the Linde era, he ranked high in the imperial examination on statecraft and was appointed as a Chao-san-lang.
He frequently presented memorials at the palace gates. His elder brothers, Wang Mian and Wang Ju, both passed the jinshi examinations and were renowned for their talent;
Lin Yijian praised them as "three pearl trees. Wang Bo also composed the *Record of the Śākyamuni Portrait* and the *Stele of the Vimalakīrti Portrait*.
The *Rulai chengdao ji* (Record of the Tathāgata’s Attainment of Enlightenment) is composed entirely of refined gold and exquisite prose; it is abundant, comprehensive, and detailed.

Luo Binwang, whose courtesy name was Binwang, was a native of Yiwu. At the age of seven, he was already able to compose poetry. During the reign of Empress Wu, he submitted several memorials to address matters of state. He was subsequently appointed... [text fragment ends].
As the Sub-prefect of Linhai, he was dissatisfied and frustrated, resigning his office and departing.

When Xu Jingye rose to suppress the rebellion, Fang Bingwang composed a manifesto on behalf of Jingye to proclaim throughout the empire, denouncing the crimes of Empress Wu. After Jingye’s defeat, Fang Bingwang fled and his whereabouts became unknown.
At that time, Di Renjie employed indirect means to plan for a great achievement, while Xu Jingye expressed his lofty sense of righteousness with resolute spirit;
Lu Binwang was one who assisted and supported Jingye. It is erroneous for some to claim that because Jingye rebelled and Binwang was executed [for it], [the latter] must have been complicit.
The *Tàipíng Guǎngjì* records this in great detail. According to the record, [he served as] the Vice Director of the Office of Personnel Evaluation under the Tang dynasty...

Liang Song Zhiwen, having been demoted and exiled due to accumulated offenses, was released to return to Jiangnan. While visiting Lingyin Temple, the moonlight was exceptionally bright; as he strolled along the long corridors, he began composing a poem, saying: "The Vulture Peak rises steeply and loftily; the Dragon Palace is locked in silence. He lingered over the second couplet, unable to complete it, when an old monk sitting upon a large meditation seat lit a "long-life lamp" and spoke in response: [The rest of the verse follows: "The golden light illuminates the world; the jade river flows through the void. Zhiwen was profoundly moved by these words. He further composed a poem: "The mountain path is steep and the valley deep; the temple gate is secluded and quiet. The moonlight shines brightly upon the peaks; the clouds drift slowly across the sky. The golden light illuminates the world; the jade river flows through the void. I have come from afar to seek the Way; I fear that my life will soon end. The old monk replied: "Your talent is truly extraordinary. You shall surely attain fame in this world. Zhiwen subsequently passed the imperial examination and rose to high office. Later, when he was about to depart for the capital, he returned once more to bid farewell to the old monk. The monk said: "You are now leaving to serve at court. Be careful not to forget your former vows. Zhiwen asked: "What do you mean? The monk replied: "In the future, when you reach the age of sixty-two, you will fall ill and die. Your body will be placed in a coffin, and you will be buried in the mountains. At that time, you must remember me. Zhiwen wept bitterly and took his leave. Later, when Zhiwen reached the age of sixty-two, he indeed fell ill and passed away. His remains were interred in the mountains. One day, while out hunting, Zhiwen encountered a monk who called out to him: "Do you still remember the promise you made to me? Zhiwen looked up and saw the old monk from Lingyin Temple. He bowed deeply and apologized profusely. The monk said: "I have already told you before. Why do you still ask? Now, take this staff and follow me. Zhiwen followed the monk and entered a cave. Inside, he saw a stone bed, upon which lay a corpse. The monk pointed to it and said: "This is your own body. Zhiwen was startled and wept uncontrollably. The monk then struck the corpse with the staff, whereupon the corpse suddenly sat up and spoke: "I am the one who composed the poem for you at Lingyin Temple. Because I had not yet attained the Way, I was reborn here. Today, I have finally achieved liberation. You should now go back and spread the Dharma. Zhiwen bowed again and departed. From that time on, he devoted himself to propagating the teachings. It is said that he lived to be over ninety years old. This account is recorded in the *Xu Gaoseng Zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks). It is a rare example of a monk manifesting his spiritual power to transform a person's mind. It also demonstrates that the Buddha-Dharma is truly inconceivable. One should never underestimate the efficacy of the Triple Gem. Thus, we know that even those who have committed grave offenses can be transformed by the power of the Dharma. How much more so for those who cultivate themselves with sincerity! This is why the sutras say: "Even if one has committed the five grave offenses and the ten evil deeds, if they encounter a good friend and hear the Dharma, they can still attain liberation. We should therefore take this as a warning and strive to practice the Way with diligence. Do not let the opportunity pass you by. This is the true meaning of the Buddha’s teaching. "Why not say: 'The tower overlooks the sun rising over the blue sea; the gate faces the tide of the Zhejiang River'? Shen Quanqi was startled and marveled at its vigor and elegance.
He then completed the final verses, saying: "The cassia seeds fall from within the moon; Celestial incense drifts beyond the clouds.

Climbing the distant pagoda by grasping at vines, Carving wood to fetch spring water from afar. Frost is thin and the flowers bloom all the more; Ice is light and the leaves have not yet withered. I await entry into Tiantai."
On the road, I watched as he crossed the stone bridge. The verse the monk had presented to me was truly a "whip-stroke" (a masterful exhortation) for an entire composition.
At dawn, I went to visit him again, but he was no longer there. A temple monk who knew him said, "This is Luo Binwang.
When I questioned him further, he replied, "At the time of Xu Jingye’s defeat, I fled together with Binwang. We were pursued but not captured; the generals..."
Fearing that the leader might escape and his crime remain unpunished, they sought out two individuals resembling him and presented their heads in a casket as an offering;

thus, Jingye was able to become a monk on Mount Heng. He died at the age of ninety-odd years. Lu Binwang also shaved his head and traveled extensively through famous mountains, passing away at Lingyin after one year.
Although they were defeated at the time, they did so under the pretext of restoring the Tang dynasty.
Therefore, many in the world took pity on him and released him. Wupingyi and Wuzhen were natives of Taiyuan.

They were well-versed in the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals) and skilled in literary composition. During the reign of Empress Wu, fearing the consequences of political turmoil, they went into seclusion at Mount Song to cultivate themselves.
Futu repeatedly summoned [him] but did not respond. During the reign of Emperor Zhongzong, he was appointed as a Scholar of the Xiuwen Pavilion.

Song Guangping—Song Jing’s courtesy name was Guangping; he was a native of Nanhe. He was upright and possessed great integrity; his demeanor was solemn and profound. This was during the era of Empress Wu.

He served as a Palace Attendant (Sheshen) of the Fengge Pavilion. Whenever he encountered matters of state, he spoke with direct candor, disregarding his own personal interests or safety. During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong, he was appointed as Chancellor.
He governed with integrity and impartiality in administering justice, thereby upholding the rectitude of the empire; among the eminent ministers of the Restoration, Zhang Jing is preeminent.
While serving as the Prefect of Guangzhou, he entered Caoxi to pay homage at the stupa of the Sixth Patriarch and made this vow: "I, your disciple, pray that throughout my life..."

Outside, the State Preceptor Hugong prayed for an auspicious sign. As soon as he finished speaking, a wondrous fragrance permeated the air and sweet rain poured down. Jing was filled with joy and leaped for happiness;
he composed a poem and departed.
Fáng Guǎn, courtesy name Yǐlǜ, was appointed Minister of Personnel during the reign of Emperor Xuanzong and served as a Participant in the Administration of State Affairs.

Initially serving as the Magistrate of Tónglú, he once accompanied the Immortal of the True Person, Hé Pó, on a stroll through the countryside. As they passed a ruined temple, [they came upon] pine trees...
The bamboos were lush and dense. Huopu sat beneath them and struck the ground with his staff, instructing an attendant to dig several feet deep.
There they found a jar, inside of which were letters from Lou Shide to Master Yong. Huopu said to Guan, "Do you understand this?"
Master Yong was indeed the previous incarnation of Guan. His father was Fang Rong, who was intelligent and fond of Buddhism.

During the reign of Empress Wu, he served as a Palace Counselor (Jianyi Dafu) and participated in the deliberations of state affairs. It happened that the Indian monk Paramiti arrived carrying the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*;
Fang Rong translated the text while acting as the scribe for its oral transmission. Later, he was exiled to Qinzhou.

Yuan Lushan, whose given name was Dexiu and courtesy name Zizhi, lost his father while young and served his mother with filial piety. He passed the jinshi examination and was appointed as the Magistrate of Lushan.

Upon the completion of his term, he departed in a carriage made of firewood. The world held his conduct in high esteem and thus referred to him by the name of his county, Lushan. When his mother died, he lived in a hut beside her grave.
He pricked his veins to transcribe sutras. Upon his death, he was posthumously titled Master Wenxing. Yuan Jie lamented for him, saying:
"In his sixty years of life, you never once knew the sight of female beauty; you never possessed even ten mu of land; you never wore clothing made of finished silk or cloth;
and you never ate food prepared with the five flavors. That I mourn you is because you served as a warning against debauchery, greed, flattery, fine silks, and rich meats."
They were merely his disciples. Fang Guan also once sighed, saying: "To behold the brow and countenance of Zizhi causes one's heart for fame and profit to vanish entirely."—Wang Youcheng.
Wang Wei, courtesy name Mojie, served as Right Reminder and Censor-in-Chief during the Kaiyuan era, and was appointed as Secretariat Drafter at the end of the Tianbao era.

He subsequently held the office of Vice Minister of the Department of State Affairs. Both he and his younger brother Wang Jing were deeply devoted to Buddhism and regularly maintained a vegetarian diet.
He abstained from pungent vegetables and meat. In his later years, he observed a lifelong fast. He did not wear patterned or colorful garments.
Having acquired Song Zhiwen’s villa at Lántián near Wǎngkǒu, he traveled by boat with his dharma-friend Fèi Dí, playing the zither and chanting in song, lingering there all day long.

Upon the death of his mother, he was so emaciated by grief that he stood like a mere skeleton. He submitted a memorial to the court requesting that land in Wangchuan be established as a Buddhist monastery.
In the capital, he provided daily meals for ten or more monks, finding joy in profound discourse.

Within his hall there was nothing at all, save for a tea kettle, a mortar for medicine, a desk for scriptures, and a rope bed. After retiring from court, he would sit alone burning incense, dedicating himself entirely to meditation and recitation.
He devoted himself to his religious practice. When his wife passed away, he did not remarry. For thirty years, he lived alone in a single room, severing all worldly ties.
He died in the seventh month of the second year of the Qianduan era. As death approached, knowing that Jing was in Fengxiang, he suddenly asked for a brush and wrote a letter of parting to him.

He also wrote several scrolls of farewell letters to his relatives and close friends; most of them emphasized the principles of befriending others, revering the Buddha, and cultivating the mind. Having relinquished...
He wrote until his brush snapped. He once composed an inscription for Master Neng, which says: "There is nothing that can be abandoned; this is reaching the source of existence.

There is no emptiness in which one can dwell; this is knowing the root of emptiness. Every step taken and every foot set down is always within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Whether it be the mind or the emotions, they all return to the ocean of nature."
Zhang Yan-gong, Zhang Yue, styled Daoji, was a native of Luoyang. During the Kaiyuan era, he served as Chief Secretary (Zhongshu Ling) and was enfeoffed as Duke of Yan.
Most of the great compositions produced at court were his work. He possessed a refined fondness for the Buddhist scriptures; regarding the stele for Princess Xie, he personally [inscribed it].

He transcribed the *Sanskrit-Script Golden-Syllable Sutra* and once sought the essentials of the Dharma from Chan Master Shenxiu. The Master said, "All Buddha-dharmas are inherently possessed within one's own mind;
to seek them elsewhere with the mind is like abandoning one's father and fleeing. Later, he composed the *Brief Commentary on the Heart Sutra of Prajñāpāramitā*, which states:
The myriad practices arise from the mind; the Three Vehicles converge into One. To know that the mind has nothing to be attained is true attainment;
that this One penetrates all is perfect penetration. Later, he served as the Regional Inspector of Xiangzhou and the Circuit Intendant of Hebei.
He was diligent in alleviating the hidden sufferings of the people and implemented benevolent governance.
Yan Tingzhi (嚴挺之).

His given name was Jun (浚), but he was known by his courtesy name. A native of Huayin, he possessed a noble and refined bearing. He valued friendship and commitment, remaining steadfast in life and death.
Zhang Jiuling held him in high esteem and would often remark, "Yan is truly firm and resolute. He passed the jinshi examination and rose through successive ranks.

His eminent achievements were manifest, and the people of the world looked toward him with bated breath, hoping he would serve as Chancellor. The Emperor also recognized his worthiness and intended to appoint him to that office;
however, he was later suppressed by Li Linfu and remained despondent, unable to fulfill his ambitions. At this time, he composed a preface for his own tomb inscription.
In the first year of the Tianbao era, Tingzhi submitted a memorial from his post as Imperial Governor of Jizhou, petitioning for imperial grace to retire and recuperate from illness.
He concurrently served as the Prince’s Chief Steward (*Kumārabhṛtya*). Throughout his career, he held thirty-five successive offices.
At the age of seventy, finding no further means to serve, he became an object of lamentation for the high officials. In the ninth month of this year, he fell ill in his private residence in Luoyang.
He intended to select a burial site to the west of the stupa of the Great Master Dazhao, so that his life of loyal service to the sovereign might be recorded in the national history.

He diligently applied himself to his tasks; at times he would circulate popular songs among the people. Since mountains can become valleys and valleys mountains, these may serve as a record for oneself—what need is there for ornate literary compositions?
Initially, Zongting served as a disciple to Chan Master Daizhao Huiyi and attained a profound understanding of the Buddhist scriptures.
When Daizhao was interred in the pagoda, Zongting composed a memorial inscription to demonstrate that he did not forget the master’s virtue; this is recorded in the *Jiushi* (Old History).
Li Qinglian, whose courtesy name was Taibai, was a native of Chengji and a scion of the Tang imperial clan. At the beginning of the Tianbao era, he went to Chang’an to visit He Zhizhang.
Upon reading his writings, He Zhizhang sighed and said, “You possess the talent of a celestial exile. He reported this to Emperor Xuanzong, who summoned him for an audience.

At the Golden Imperial Hall, he was granted a meal, during which the Emperor personally prepared the soup for him. An edict was issued appointing him as a Palace Attendant of the Hanlin Academy. Bai once composed the *Praise of the Western Pure Land*, which says:
"In the direction where the sun sets, I gaze afar upon the countenance of Great Compassion. His eyes are as pure as the waters of the four seas; His body’s radiance is like a mountain of purple gold.
Through diligent mindfulness, one is reborn there; Therefore, it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss. With nets of pearls and trees of precious jewels, The heavens..."

Flowers are scattered upon the fragrant pavilion; the painted images remain vivid before my eyes. I pray to entrust myself to that place of enlightenment, so that by this ocean of merit, you may secretly bestow blessings as a bridge and raft.
May the transgressions of eighty-one kalpas be swept away like wind driving off light frost, so that I may behold Amitāyus and forever long for the light of his jade-like brow.
Li Gongdu, whose courtesy name was Gongdu, served as the Prefect of Qianzhou. In his youth, he prided himself on his integrity and conduct. Du Fu composed a poem of thirty-six stanzas to see him off;
it begins with the lines: "In the north of the realm there is a noble falcon / That bears sons whose feathers are entirely crimson. This refers to Li Zhiu, who once...

In a letter to his younger sister, he wrote: "If Śākyamuni had been born in the Middle Kingdom, he would have established teachings like those of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius; if the Duke of Zhou and Confucius had been born in the Western Regions, they would have established teachings like those of Śākyamuni.

As for the heavenly realms—if they do not exist, so be it; if they do exist, then the gentleman shall ascend them. As for the hells—if they do not exist, so be it; if they do exist, then the petty man shall enter them.
Those who understand this consider it a famous and eloquent statement.
Su Jin, Su Jin.

A native of Lantian, he was the son of Su Xiang, Minister of the Ministry of Revenue. At the age of several years, he was able to compose literary works, including a treatise on the Eight Trigrams (*Bagua lun*).
Fang Yingshu and Wang Shaizong marveled at him, saying, "He is the Wang Can of a later age. He frequently received instruction from the foreign monk Huishen.
Tancheng had a copy of the *Maitreya Buddha Sūtra*. Jin Baozhi said to him, "This Buddha loves to drink rice gruel;
this perfectly accords with my own nature. I wish to serve him alone; I do not care for other Buddhas."

Wei Suzhou, whose courtesy name was Wei Yingwu, was a native of Jingzhao in Chang’an. He was a descendant of Wei Qiong, the Duke Xiaoyao. Li Zao’s *Guoshi Bu* states: "Wei was by nature lofty and pure;
he ate sparingly and had few desires. Wherever he stayed, he would burn incense and sweep the ground before sitting. This was during the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty.

At that time, he accompanied the Emperor on imperial excursions. During the Yongtai era, he served as the Director of the Office of Works for the Prefecture. During the Dali era, he served as the Magistrate of Hu and the Magistrate of Luoyang.
At the beginning of the Jianzhong era, he was appointed as the Prefect of Chuzhou, and later as the Prefect of Jiangzhou. During the Zhenyuan era, he served as the Prefect of Suzhou.

Throughout his official career, he served the Buddha with refined devotion and formed a transcendent friendship with the monk Jiaoran. Those of the Tang dynasty said that he composed [his works] through the medium of literature.
Regarding Buddhist affairs, all [writers] merely imitated its external outlines like shadows and echoes;
only three—Wang Mojie, Liu Zhitou, and Wei Suzhou—were able to penetrate deeply. Li Xatou...
Li Hua, courtesy name Xiashu, was a native of Zannang. He passed the examination for "Eloquence in Broad Learning" (*bóxué hóngcí*). During the Tiānbǎo era, he was appointed as Censor-in-Chief.
He submitted a memorial impeaching the consort relatives of Chancellor Yang Guozhong for their横行暴虐 (arrogant and violent conduct), whereupon the prefectures and commanderies were brought into order.
He once studied *zhíguān* (stopping and contemplating) under Chan Master Rán of Jīngxī, who composed for him a treatise on the Great Meaning of *Zhíguān*, which encompassed [the entire system].

The great master was then joined by his contemporaries, the Court Gentleman for Ceremonial (Sanqi Changshi) Cui Gong and the Palace Counselor (Yanjian Yidafu) Tian Dun, who together promoted and extolled him.
When Yuan Su, the Master of Mount Jing at Heilin Monastery in Runzhou, passed away, Hua composed the inscription for his stele.
Its conclusion states: "I, your disciple, have studied the Way under Mount Jing, much as Yue Zhengzichun did under the Master Confucius."

Du Zixun, whose courtesy name was Zixun, was a native of Puzhou. While serving as the regional governor of Ba and Shu, he dispatched an envoy to Mount Baiya to invite Chan Master Wuzhu to enter the city to inquire about the Dharma.
The Master replied, "Your disciple has heard the Master speak of non-recollection, non-thought, and non-..."
Regarding the Dharma-gate of the three phrases of "delusion" (*mṛṣā*): I do not yet understand whether these are one or three. Wuzhu said: "Non-recollection is called precept (*śīla*);

non-thought is called concentration (*samādhi*); non-delusion is called wisdom (*prajñā*). However, when the single mind does not arise, it is complete with precept, concentration, and wisdom; it is neither one nor three. [The interlocutor] asked:

"In the final phrase, does the character for 'delusion' (*mṛṣā*) not derive from the radical for 'mind' (*citta*)? Wuzhu said: "That which derives from the character for 'woman' (*nǚ*) is correct. [The interlocutor] said: "There is..."
Wuzhu said, "According to the *Dharmapada*, it says: 'If one gives rise to a mind of diligent effort, this is delusion, not diligence.
If one can remain without a deluded mind, diligence will be boundless. At that moment, a crow was crying in a tree in the courtyard. The Master asked, 'Teacher, did you hear it?'"

Wuzhu said, "I hear it. [The official] said, "The crow has gone. He asked again, "Do you hear it now, Master? Wuzhu said, "I hear it. The official said, "The crow has gone and there is no sound; why do you say you hear it?
Wuzhu replied, "Hearing and not hearing have nothing to do with the nature of hearing.

Originally they were not born, and now they do not perish. When there is sound, it is the object of sound that arises of itself; when there is no sound, it is the object of sound that perishes of itself."
Furthermore, this nature of hearing does not arise following sound, nor does it perish following sound. The Master asked again:

"What is meant by 'recognizing the mind and seeing the nature'? He replied: "All practitioners of the Way drift along with their thoughts because they do not recognize the true mind and do not see their original nature.
As for the true mind, when thoughts arise, it does not follow them in arising; when thoughts perish, it does not depend on them in perishing. It neither comes..."
It is neither fixed nor distracted; neither grasping nor rejecting; neither sinking nor floating. It is unconditioned and signless—vibrant, ordinary, and sovereign.
This essence of mind is ultimately ungraspable. Whatever meets the eye is suchness; there is nothing that is not the manifestation of the nature of seeing.
On the same day as Du Huangchang was appointed as Chancellor, he resigned from his post due to illness. Three days after relinquishing his position, he passed away.
He was commanded to wear his court robes over his *saṃghāṭī* and, having shaved his beard and hair, he passed away. His final instructions were that he be buried according to the Dharma of a śramaṇa.

Hongjian was a meritorious official who served as the strategist for Lingwu; his family had followed the Buddha for generations. Observing this final act of his, it is clear that his thorough realization of the Great Matter was no mere coincidence.

Lu Hongjian, whose courtesy name was Hongjian, was originally a śramaṇa who found him by the water’s edge and raised him. Once he had grown up, he divined for himself using the *Yījīng* (Book of Changes) and obtained the hexagram Jian (Obstruction) changing into Jian (Gradual Progress).
He read the line: "A wild goose gradually advances upon the land; its feathers may be used as a model. Thereupon, he took "Lu" (Land) as his surname.
He had a surname and was given a name and a courtesy title (*zi*). His teacher instructed him in the *pāṅ-hang* script (Brahmi).

He replied, "If one has no brothers and severs his lineage, can this be considered filial piety? He fled and became a performer. During the Tianbao era, the Prefectural Governor Li Qiwu marveled at him and taught him writing.
Though his appearance was humble and his speech stammered, he was eloquent. During the Shangyuan era, he lived in seclusion at Tiexi, where he associated with a śramaṇa.

His reputation was widely known as preeminent; he styled himself the Old Man of Mulberry and Bamboo (Sāngchù Wēng), and was also called the Son of Jingling, the Son of East Ridge (Dōnggāngzǐ), and Master East Garden (Dōngyuán Xiānshēng).
When summoned to serve as a Court Scholar to the Crown Prince, he declined the appointment.
He shut himself within his gate to compose writings, or wandered alone in the wilds, chanting poetry and striking wooden clappers, strolling at ease as he pleased.
Li Yuehou Li Mi, courtesy name Changyuan, was a native of Jingzhao. At the age of seven, he knew how to compose literary works;

Emperor Xuanzong summoned him for an audience and called him a "prodigious child," enlisting him as a commoner friend to the Crown Prince. Later, he attended upon Suzong at Lingwu and entered the council to deliberate on state affairs.

He accompanied the imperial carriage and litters during the restoration of the two capitals, for which his assistance and counsel were predominant. Initially, he had no wife and abstained from eating meat;

however, Emperor Daizong forcibly issued an edict compelling him to eat meat and marry. During the reign of Emperor Dezong, he was promoted to Minister of the Ministry of Rites and concurrently served as a Chief Councilor.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ye. Hearing that Chan Master Zan resided at Mount Nanyue and was known to people as "Lan Can" (the Lazy Remnant), Li Bi went to visit him.
Upon hearing the sound of his recitation, it was first sorrowful and then joyful; Bi knew from this that he was a person who had been demoted for his transgressions and would soon depart.
He waited for a long time before crawling forward to ask about the Way. The Master said, "Only after you have smashed your brush and inkstone may you discuss this.
He then poked at the fire and pulled out a taro root for him to eat. Later that night, Li Mi requested instruction again, saying, "Do you not have a single word of teaching for me?
The Master patted his back and said, "Take this as the appointment of a Chancellor for ten years. When Li Mi came to power, he spoke of the Master’s noble conduct to the Emperor.

An imperial edict summoned him. When the envoy arrived at Shiku to proclaim the appointment, Huizang wept with tears falling down to his chest; yet he sat upright and motionless, regarding the matter with indifference.
The envoy returned and reported this to the throne, and Emperor Dezong marveled at him all the more.

Yan Lugu Gong, Yan Zhenqing, styled Qingchen, was the younger cousin of Yan Gaoding. He was extensively learned and skilled in poetry. Renowned for his filial piety toward his parents, he passed the jinshi examination and served in successive offices until he became the Governor of Pingyuan.
When An Lushan rebelled and the region north of the Yellow River fell entirely into enemy hands, Pingyuan alone maintained its defenses.
He held various offices and was eventually appointed as Right Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs (*Shangshu Youcheng*). He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Lu County.

When Li Xilie occupied Ruizhou, the imperial court dispatched Zhenqing to go there and persuade him; he refused to submit and was subsequently martyred. The Duke had previously received the precepts from Huiming of Huzhou and further sought instruction in the Way from Yanjun of Jiangxi.
In the third year of the Qianyuan era, Suzong established the empire upon the "pool of life" (*shengchi*).
Eleventh Site. The Duke received the imperial decree to erect a stele, the inscription of which read: "In the past, Tang of Yin was perfected in benevolence and lowered his net on one side;
Emperor Wu of Han bestowed kindness and received the reward of the 'pearl-bearing' [dragon]. The flowing water saved the parched; the *Bao-sheng* [Temple] acquired its fame.

Indeed, these matters were limited to their respective times, yet they still brought blessings unto eternity. How much more so for us today—beings that move and things that grow, those dwelling in the water..."
Dwelling in the midst of aridity, he takes all under heaven as his moat; encompassing the realm within its borders, he bestows blessings upon all.

Relying on the power of the empowerment of *dhāraṇī*, he dries up the ocean of afflictions and the fords of birth and death. Measured against the ancients of yore, how could there ever have been even a faint resemblance?

Pei Jinguo, Pei Du, styled Zhongli, was a native of Wenxi. He passed the jinshi examination at the beginning of the Zhenyuan era and served successively as Minister of the Central Secretariat (Zhongshu Shilang).

He led the military forces that suppressed and pacified Huai and Cai, whereupon he was enfeoffed as Duke of Jin. Later, due to the incitement of tyranny by eunuchs, he retired to Jixian Ward, where he spent his days...
He enjoyed the pleasure of wine and poetry with Bai Juyi and Liu Yuxi, never inquiring about matters outside their immediate circle.

He once visited Master Daqin of Mount Jing to seek the Way, observing the etiquette of a disciple and requesting the teachings for transcending the mundane world. As he approached his death, he said to his disciples:
In my death, I have nothing to which I am attached. It is only a matter of regret that the pines and clouds on Wugqiao Estate have not yet been completed;
that the "Soft Green" pond has not yet seen the embroidered tails of its fish grow long; and that the *Book of Han* has not yet reached its final chapter.
Páng Dàxuán, whose courtesy name was Dàxuán, was the son of Páng Yùn. His father served as the Governor of Hénghuáng. The family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.

At the beginning of the Zhēnyuán era, he went to visit Master Shítóu. They attained a wondrous accord beyond words. One day, Shítóu asked him, "Since you first saw me, what have been your daily activities?"
"How is it? [the Master] asked. He replied, "If one asks about the affairs of daily life, there is no place for opening one's mouth. Thereupon, he presented a verse, saying:
"The affairs of daily life are no different; Only my own verses harmonize with them. At every turn, there is nothing to accept or reject; In every place, do not allow discord to arise."
Who would designate them as crimson or purple? Amidst hills and mountains, not a speck of dust remains. Spiritual powers and wondrous functions are used to carry water and haul firewood.
Shitou said this. Later, while visiting Master Bailin, he encountered him on the road. Bailin asked about the verse by which Shitou had attained his realization in the past:
"Do you still remember it; can you recite it for me? The Layman replied, "I remember it; I can recite it. Bailin said, "Recite it for me."
"Who has come? The layman pointed to himself with his hand and said, "I am Master Pang. Lingyun said, "Truly this is Wondrous Virtue (Miaode) and Empty Birth (Kongsheng).

Liu Liuzhou, whose given name was Zihou, was a man of understanding who passed the jinshi examination and the Examination for Broad Learning and Magnificent Prose (Bóxué Hóngcí Kē). During the Zhenyuan era, he was appointed to office.

Censor-in-Chief. During the Yuanhe era, he served as the Prefect of Liuzhou. Later, he was demoted to the position of Assistant Commandant of Yongzhou, where he withdrew into the mountains and marshes.
His pent-up sorrow and indignation were all channeled into his writings. In the inscription he composed for the Monk Panzhou, he wrote:

The Master’s mind was vast and his conduct was subtle; his demeanor was humble yet his Way was honored. He held that wisdom is generated from meditative concentration and that this must necessarily rely upon the *vinaya*.
Thereupon, on a lofty ridge, he constructed a meditation cell called the Pratyutpanna Terrace (*Banzhou Tai*).

Alas! Because there is nothing to be attained, mindfulness is the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*); because no phenomena are grasped, the *vinaya* is the Mahāyāna. Thus, while the myriad practices are strenuously cultivated, entry into the nature of reality remains eternally as it is.
The limits of quiescent function cannot be grasped. This is the preface sent with Master Hào-chū:
"Hán Tuí-zhī reproached me for my fondness for the words of the Buddhists and censured me for associating with them. There are indeed aspects of Buddhism that cannot be dismissed;
they often accord with the *Yì* and the *Lùn-yǔ*. I truly delight in this. However, it does not differ from the Way of Kǒng-zǐ. Tuí-zhī is a lover of Confucianism..."
I have not yet been able to surpass Yangzi. In Yangzi’s writings, there is much that is drawn from Zhuangzi, Mozi, Shen Buhai, and Han Feizi.
Is it then the case that the Buddhists are even more eccentric, perverse, treacherous, and cruel than Zhuangzi, Mozi, Shen Buhai, and Han Feizi? I reply: It is because they are "barbarians" (Yi).
If one judges by their status as barbarians, would one then befriend the likes of Erali and Daodi, while deprecating Jizha and Youyu? That which I find acceptable [in them] is...
This accords with the *Yi* and the *Lunyu*; even if a sage were to arise again, he could not refute it. Your letter, Master Zihou, extols the teachings of Śākyamuni to the ultimate degree.
This is evident in your "Preface to the Return of Monk Jun to Visit His Parents" and your composition of the "Record of the Jingtu Monastery."
The Stele Inscription for Vinaya Master Daming of Nanyue is fully recorded in the History of the Tang Dynasty and cannot be enumerated here.

Liu Mengde, whose courtesy name was Yuxi, was a native of Zhongshan. He passed the jinshi examination and attained the degree of "Broad Learning and Eloquence" (Bóxué Hóngcí). He served in various official capacities.
He served as a *zhixueshi* (Director of the Hanlin Academy). In his later years, he amused himself with literary composition; Bai Juyi ranked him among the "poetic heroes.

He once composed the Stele Inscription for the Sixth Patriarch, the Chan Master Dajian, stating: "Five hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa Matanga and Dharmaratna arrived with the scriptures.
For the first time, the people of China heard their words, like those in deep darkness suddenly beholding the dawn. Later...

Five hundred years later, Bodhidharma arrived with the Dharma; the people of China began to transmit his mind-to-mind teaching, like those who, though previously obscured, finally behold the bright sun.
From Bodhidharma’s six transmissions down to Da Jian (Huineng), it was like a string of wish-fulfilling pearls:

there was a sequence of before and after, yet no difference in essence. What the world calls the True Doctrine is known as the Sudden Gate. Initially, Bodhidharma came together with the Buddha’s robe.
The transmission of the Way was conferred as the "Mind-Seal" (xinyin). Yet when the Great Mirror [Huineng] arrived, he set it aside and did not transmit it.

Was it because he regarded it as mere straw dogs? Furthermore, he composed the *Inscription on the Buddha’s Robe*, saying: "Were there not a vessel of faith, how could sentient beings find their refuge? This opens the convenient gate."

It is not merely that the transmission of the robe must have an end; how could its transmission ever be without cessation? All things must ultimately reach their exhaustion. Why, then, do you rely so long on this robe?

To know the end through the end is to ensure that its utility is inexhaustible. My Way is imperishable; what need is there for a robe? Since its utility has already been exhausted, what further use is there for it?
Who among them was not like a straw dog?

As for the Cishi Yu Di, his courtesy name was Yunyuan; he was a man of the Dai clan. In the fourteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, he was appointed as the Regional Inspector (Jiedushi) of Shandong. Initially, he...
He served as the Prefect of Huzhou and presented the collected poems of the śramaṇa Jiaoran of Zhushan to be preserved in the Imperial Calligraphy Hall.
He was on very friendly terms with Pang the Layman of Xiangyang. One day, he went to visit the Layman to inquire after his illness, whereupon the Layman said to him:
"I only wish to empty all that exists; be careful not to reify what does not exist. Furthermore, he once asked Master Ziyu, "What is a Zen master?
The master replied, "A black wind blows a ship so violently that it drifts and falls into the land of rākṣasa demons.
Yu Di said, "Master, you are a hired laborer asking such a question! At that moment, Yu Di turned pale with fear. The master pointed and said, "This very moment is precisely what it means to drift."
[This would mean] falling into the realm of rākṣasa demons. Having heard this, Yi accepted it with faith.

Li Yuanbin (Li Guan), whose courtesy name was Yuanbin, was a nephew of Hua. During the Zhenyuan era, he was selected for the *Hongci* examination and was skilled at composing prose, having thoroughly cleansed [the literary style].
Qian Ren was a contemporary whose poetic style ranked alongside that of Han Yu. He died at the age of twenty-nine, for whom Tuizhi composed a tomb inscription.
While observing the mourning period for his father, he drew blood to transcribe the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*;
a wondrous fragrance emanated from his residence, lingering intensely for many days, its scent reaching his neighbors.
Li Xizhi, whose courtesy name was Xizhi, was a native of Zhaojun. He was highly esteemed for his literary compositions during his time.

Having passed the jinshi examination, he served as a compiler of the National History (Guoshi Xiuzhuan) at the beginning of the Yuanhe era. By nature, he was upright and outspoken; on one occasion, he publicly rebuked the errors of the Chancellor Li Fengji.
He was dispatched to Langzhou. Admiring the spiritual influence of Master Youshan Weiyen, he entered the mountains to pay him a visit. Youshan held up a sutra and paid him no attention.
Haowei then shook out his robes and said, "Meeting you in person is not as good as hearing of your reputation. Youshan, however, called out, "Governor! Haowei responded, "Yes?
Youshan asked, "How can you hold my ears so dear while despising my eyes? Haowei apologized and then asked, "What is the Way? Youshan [responded with]...
The Master pointed to his fingers up and down and asked, "Do you understand? Xuefeng Aowang replied, "I do not understand.

The Master said, "Clouds in the blue sky, water in the pitcher. Aowang joyfully responded with a verse: My body has been refined until it resembles the form of a crane; Beneath a thousand pine trees lie two cases of scripture.
When I came to ask about the Way, there was no further teaching— Clouds in the blue sky, water in the pitcher. One night, the Master ascended the mountain.
Suddenly the clouds parted and the moon appeared; he let out a great roar, a sound that fell for eighty or ninety *li* across Liyang.
When Hào heard it, he sent another verse, saying: "I have chosen this secluded dwelling to satisfy my rustic sentiments; Throughout the year, there is neither seeing off nor welcoming.
Sometimes I ascend alone to the peak of a solitary mountain, And beneath the moon, I part the clouds and let out a roar."

Quán Cǎizhī, courtesy name Cǎizhī, was a native of Qīnzhōu. In his youth, he was renowned for his literary talent. When Emperor Dēng heard of his abilities, he summoned him to serve as a Left Assistant in the Palace Secretariat (Zuǒ Bǔquè).

He was subsequently promoted through various ranks until he became the Minister of the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū). Regarding the classics and arts, there was nothing that Quán Deyú had not mastered. Although...
