In his movements and stillness, he was devoid of external affectation, yet possessed a refined and elegant grace that was naturally admirable.

He once composed the "Record of Chan Master Cao Yi’s Seated Meditation," which states: "The Master resided on Mount Nanyue for thirty years; his feet never trod upon the ground, and his mouth never tasted flavors.
Regardless of the heat or cold of the season, he occupied nothing but a single rope bed. While the myriad phenomena were clamorous, this body remained unmoving. As for what was within..."
The five aggregates of the three periods of time all arise from deluded fabrication. Thereafter, one uses the existence of phenomena to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination.
Within right wisdom, one attains the true, eternal, and true self. In this square inch of the mind, all is profoundly still and void. Both body and wisdom are equally pure.
Subtle words and gentle speech are occasionally heard, like rain moistening the myriad things or wind blowing through the air.
As they stepped across the threshold of his gate, all were able to enter.

Xu Dai, Xu Dai—originally from Suzhou—was one who was proficient in all branches of learning and possessed sharp, incisive debating skills. Whenever the Emperor encountered his birthday, [he would summon him].
An imperial edict was issued for the two schools of Buddhism and Daoism to engage in a great debate with the assembly of ministers at the Linqide Hall.

Zhang Dai initially argued that the three teachings were as contradictory as a pair of opposites, yet he ultimately demonstrated that they all converge upon the good. The Emperor was greatly pleased; Dai’s official rank reached that of School Librarian (Jiaoshu lang).
Li Yishan, whose courtesy name was Yishan, was a native of Henei. He passed the jinshi examination and served successively as an Assistant Director of the Ministry of Works.

His poetry and prose were characterized by a spirit that transcended the extraordinary and the ancient; his poetic style was known to the world as the Xikun Style. He composed a hymn in praise of the Buddha which says: "We Confucians..."

His teacher was called Zhongni of Lu. Zhongni took Nantuo as his teacher; as for Long, I do not know him. Nantuo took Tianzhu as his teacher, who was skilled at entering the state of non-action (*wuwei*).
I bow my head to this Great Awakened One, the Teacher of my Teacher. Shangyin admired the Way of National Preceptor Zhi Xuan of Wuda and served him with the etiquette due to a disciple.
Once, suffering from severe eye disease, he prayed in secret; Zhi Xuan then sent him three stanzas of the "Heavenly Eye" (*Tianyan*) verses.
Upon finishing the reading, his illness was cured.
Lu Yuanyi, whose courtesy name was Lushiyan, came from a family of official lineage; he held office for over thirty years, serving through eight successive reigns.

He served in the various provincial governorships, where he managed all matters of great urgency. By nature, he was robust and vigorous, never attending to trivial or obscure details. Consequently, he was framed by an official and demoted to Jianzhou.

There, a man of extraordinary character secretly transmitted to him the core of his realization; thereafter, [the master] vanished into the unseen. His son searched for him exhaustively for many years without success.
One night, among a group of *dhūtas* at a Buddhist monastery on Mount Heng, he recognized him by the light of a lamp. He cried out and wept.
He had no regard for his own life; it was clear that he had lost his [original] head. Previously, the multitude had thought this was the "Shang" ascetic, but by this time they knew it was Lu.
In the first year of the Yuanhe era, Yuan Weizhi paid his respects to Zhang Zhongchen at Xiangtan. It happened that Shi Yan was present in the assembly;

that very day, Yuan went to the Eastern Temple where [Zhang] resided, and upon seeing him once, they laughed together. Yuan then obtained the original text in its entirety and subsequently presented it as a gift.
A heptasyllabic pentameter poem: Lushi speaks deeply of the origins of his renunciation: He has shaved away the flowers of the mind before shaving his head.
The horses weep on the green mountains as he parts from Chandaka; Crows fly past the conch-like topknot as he meets Rāhula. He returns once more to his former place of walking meditation.
It is as if separated from my former life, like wandering in dreams; may I tell this to the Eight Dragon Brothers: that in another birth there is extinction, while in this life there is rest.
By Pei Kuan.
Pei Kuan was a native of Wenxi. He served as the Prefect of Hezhou; whenever the prefecture suffered from prolonged drought, rain would fall as soon as he entered its borders.

He was subsequently transferred to the post of Governor of Henan, where he refused to bend before powerful officials. He was appointed Minister of Rites of the Board of Rites. A devotee of Buddhism, he associated with śramaṇas and studied their scriptures, becoming increasingly steadfast in his practice as he grew older.
*Fǎxǐzhì* (Record of Joy in the Dharma), Volumes II and III,
compiled by the Daoist Bīnglián (Ice Lotus) Xià Shùfāng.
The Layman Wudou, Feng Ding, read this for the Junior Grand Master Bai Shao-fu, whose courtesy name was Le-tian.
At the age of seventeen, he passed the jinshi examination. During the reign of Emperor Xianzong, he was held in the highest favor and esteem. At that time...

There was nothing he would not speak of, which led to his being resented by those in power. Consequently, he was marginalized and excluded from official service. He then gave himself over to literature and wine;

at his residence in the Eastern Capital, he dredged a pond, planted trees, built a stone pavilion on Fragrant Mountain (Xiangshan), and excavated the Eight-Section Rapids (Bajietan). He styled himself the "Madman Who Sings in Drunkenness" (Zuiyin xiansheng).

In his later years, his devotion to Buddhism became particularly intense, to the point that he would abstain from meat for as long as a month. In the second year of the Changqing era, he was appointed... [text ends].
In Hangzhou, he sought the Way from Chan Master Niaoke. Seeing that the Master was dwelling atop a bird’s nest, he asked, "The place where you reside is extremely perilous.
The Master replied, "Your Excellency, your own danger is even greater. Bai Juyi said, "As a disciple whose rank governs the mountains and rivers, what danger could there be?
The Master said, "Fuel and fire intersect; if the nature of consciousness does not come to rest, is this not perilous? Bai Juyi was convinced by his words.

He spoke thus, prostrated, and withdrew. He once asked Chan Master Weikuan, "How should one cultivate the mind? The Master said, "The mind is fundamentally without injury; why then do you seek to repair it?
Whether defiled or pure, do not give rise to any thoughts whatsoever. He asked again, "If one must not think of defilement, may one likewise have no thoughts of purity?
The Master replied, "It is like the surface of a person's eye: there is not a single thing [upon it]."
"One may remain [in this state]. Although gold dust is a precious treasure, it acts as a cataract when in the eye. From this, Letian attained awakening and entry.
He further consulted Master Ning on the essentials of the mind and obtained eight words, which he expanded into eight verses. The eight words are: "Contemplation" and "Awakening."
It is called concentration and wisdom; it is called clarity and penetration; it is called salvation and relinquishment. The verse for contemplation says:

With the eye of the mind, contemplate the appearances outside the mind—from what do they arise, and from what are they lost? Contemplate again and again, and you will distinguish the true from the delusory.
In his final verse of renunciation, he said: "Since all sufferings have been transcended, great compassion is also relinquished. Since suffering is not real, compassion is likewise provisional.

Therefore, among sentient beings, there is truly no one who delivers others. At the age of seventy-five, he was posthumously granted the title of Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Emperor Xuanzong composed a poem to mourn him. After his death, the residence where he lived was donated to establish a Buddhist monastery.

Li Junzhi (also known as Li Bo). His courtesy name was Junzhi. Initially, he lived in seclusion on Mount Lu, and later followed [the teachings] at Shaoshi Mountain. At the beginning of the Yuanhe era, Li Xun and Wei Kuang submitted joint memorials recommending him.
He was summoned to serve as a Right Reminder (You Shiyi), but he did not accept the appointment. Han Yu, the Magistrate of Luoyang, sent him a letter saying: "The court..."

The scholar turned his neck to gaze eastward, as if competing with the morning star and the phoenix for the joy of beholding them. When he first emerged [into public office], he was appointed Counselor of Remonstrance (*jianyi dafu*).

Whenever there were deficiencies in the administration, he would immediately submit memorials. Standing alone and relying on himself, though repeatedly dismissed from office, he never diminished his integrity.
During his tenure as Prefect of Jiangzhou, he once asked Chan Master Guizong: "How can Mount Sumeru contain a mustard seed?"
He did not ask [the question]. [The Master asked], "What is it like to contain Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed? The Master said, "People say you, Lord, have read ten thousand scrolls of books;
is this true? Bo said, "Yes. The Master said, "From the crown of your head to your heels, you are no larger than a coconut.
Where, then, are those ten thousand scrolls of books? At these words, Bo attained realization.
Du Yanzhi, whose courtesy name was Yanzhi, was the son of Du Mu. He passed the imperial examinations during the Dazhong era and served as a Hanlin Academician.
His residence enjoyed the scenic beauty of Xianglin. He befriended Gu Yun and other worthies, and styled himself the "Man of Jiuhua."
A collection of his poems circulated in the world. One of his poems sent off a monk reads: "What reliance can there be on the gates of profit or the paths of fame?

A hundred-year life is but a flickering lamp before the wind. I only fear that though you have become a monk, your mind is not yet resolved; If your mind as a monk is truly resolved, you have surpassed all other monks."
Wei Nankang, Wei Gao by name, styled Chengwu, was a native of Wannian. When Gao was first born, his father offered a meal to the *saṃgha* to pray for blessings. Suddenly, an Arhat arrived.
After the meal was finished, the wet nurse took the child in her arms and requested a consecration prayer. The Arhat rose and said to the assembly: "This..."
"This child is Zhuge Wuhou. In the future, he will bring fine governance to Shu; you should name him 'Wu'.
Having finished speaking, he vanished. Subsequently, Gao’s official career, conduct, integrity, and achievements were generally similar to those of Wuhou.
Originally, Li Bai wrote "The Difficulty of the Road to Shu" to censure Yan Wu; later, Lu Yang wrote "The Ease of the Road to Shu" to praise him.
He governed Shu for twenty-one years, holding office as high as Grand Marshal and Chief Secretary of the Palace Secretariat, and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nankang Commandery.
He was deeply devoted to the teachings of Śākyamuni. When the stone image of Maitreya Tathāgata at Jiazhou was first completed, Gao composed an inscription for it, stating:
"The circumference of the head is seven feet; the width of the eyes is twenty feet; all other marks of excellence are likewise proportionate. The world praised this for its brevity and elegance.
Furthermore, he once instructed a parrot to recite the Buddha’s name. When the parrot died, he enshrined it within a shrine according to the traditional rites of the *śramaṇa*.
He obtained more than ten grains of śarīra. Gao composed a record for them; its rhythmic praise and eulogy captured the subtle essence of dhyāna quite well.
(Huángfù Shí)
Huangfu Shi, courtesy name Chizheng, was a native of Xin’an. During the Yuanhe era, he passed the jinshi examination. He devoted his mind to the Inner Canon (Buddhist scriptures).

In his "Preface to the Account of Master Jian," he wrote: "With the feathers of a phoenix and the fur of a qilin—these are but birds and beasts; yet the Classics and Commentaries use them as metaphors for the Sage."
Although this Master followed the teachings of the Buddha, his conduct was Confucian; although his clothing was that of the barbarians, his heart was rooted in benevolence and righteousness.
Even had he not been ranked among the scholar-officials, he would have been their equal, like a phoenix or a qilin.

Is he not far superior to those who wear the mourning cap or court robes yet leak out depraved and怪异 (strange/superstitious) doctrines, thereby corrupting the eternal patterns of human relations? He served as an official up to the rank of Director of the Bureau of Works. Han Yu admired him...
Cai [was] renowned as an equal to Li Ao and Zhang Ji. Han Changli, whose courtesy name was Tui-zhi, was a native of Nanyang.
He lost his father at the age of three and was raised by his aunt, Lady Zheng; from a young age, he knew how to read.

He kept a diary of several thousand words. Having grown up, he mastered the classics, histories, and the works of the hundred schools. He passed the jinshi examination and served successively as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice.
When Emperor Xianzong welcomed the Buddha’s relics, he submitted a memorial offering vehement remonstrance, for which he was demoted to the post of Prefect of Chaozhou.
Having arrived at Chao, he heard of the fame of Chan Master Dadian and sent a letter inquiring about the Way. After the letter had been sent three times, Dadian finally entered the city;
Han Yu paid him reverent homage and invited him to stay for ten days before returning home. Later, while performing a sacrifice to the gods on the sea, he ascended Mount Ling.
He further built a residence for him and inquired after his well-being; subsequently, he changed his post to Yuanzhou and presented two sets of robes as a parting gift.
Later, Zhou Maoshu went to Lingshan Temple to visit the remains of Dadian and saw the story of the "Pavilion of the Robes Left by Master Wen. He inscribed a poem on the wall, saying:
"Tuoji claimed for himself to be like Confucius, And in 'The Origin of the Way' deeply refuted the errors of Buddhism and Daoism. Yet he did not recognize Dadian..."
"What is it like? [He replied: "I have frequently written to you with deep respect and have further left behind this robe.

Pei Gongmei—his courtesy name was Gongmei; he was a native of Mengzhou. In his childhood, he lived in seclusion together with his brothers. By day he lectured on the sutras, and by night he composed [writings].

Shu remained within his door for years without venturing out. When a deer was presented as a gift, his students offered it to him; Xiu would not eat it, saying, "Even my vegetarian diet is insufficient;

if I were to consume meat now, what would I have to sustain me hereafter? He passed the jinshi examination and served as a Censor and concurrently as a Chief Councilor of the Secretariat and Chancellery.
He was devoted to the teachings of the Buddha and sought out their doctrines, even though those of his time mocked him for it.

Yet his fondness for it did not diminish. During the days when the Duke was governing Xin’an, Master Yun had recently left the assembly at Huangbo Mountain and entered the Dà’ān Vihāra, mingling among the laborers.
When the Duke entered the temple and observed a painting on the wall, he asked what kind of image it was.
The attendant replied, "It is the true likeness of a noble monk. The Duke said, "The true likeness is indeed worthy of contemplation; [the noble monk...]"
"Where is the Sangha? The monks all remained silent. The Official asked, "Is there any Chan practitioner here? They replied, "Recently a monk has come to serve in this temple;
he bears much resemblance to a Chan practitioner. The Official ordered him to be brought before him.

Upon seeing him, he was pleased and said, "Just now I had a question, but the virtuous ones were too parsimonious with their words. I now request that you, Master, provide a response on my behalf. Yun said, "Simply speak it. The Official then—
He raised the previous question. Yun朗 (Yun Lang) called out in a resonant voice, "Pai Xiu! Pai Xiu responded, "Yes. Yun asked, "Where are you?

At that moment, Pai Xiu understood the essential meaning, as if he had recovered the pearl from his topknot. He then invited him into his residence, where they discussed the Dharma morning and evening. Later, when Pai Xiu was transferred to the commandery of Wanling, he also took him along.
Through this, Pai Xiu deeply penetrated the source of the Dharma and further established a karmic affinity with Chan Master Guifeng Mi.

He was particularly reclusive. He passed away at the age of seventy-four. Xiu was capable in composition; his calligraphy, both in the regular and cursive styles, was forceful and elegant, adhering to the formal rules of the tradition.
As a person, he was grave and upright in his integrity, and his deportment was dignified and composed. Emperor Xuanzong once remarked, "This is truly a Confucian scholar.

He never consumed wine or meat during his life and authored tens of thousands of words of Buddhist literature, such as the *Exhortation to Generate the Bodhicitta* and the *Complete Enlightenment* [Sūtra Commentary].
The prefaces to the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*, the *Chan-yuan-ch'üan*, and the *Ch'an-yüan* are all esteemed by the world for their essentiality.
Ding Fan, who served as a Court Secretary (Shang-shu-lang), attended upon Master Lingdu; he resigned from office to seek the Way, subsisting on only two portions of coarse grain (*tu-su*) per day.
A single bowl of water; during summer nights while practicing *dhyāna*, even when flying mosquitoes bit and fed upon him, he never stirred.
Chen Chou (Chen Chou), the son of Hong, served as an aide in the retinue of the Vice Minister of Justice Guo Changshi at Xu during the Xian-tong era. By nature...
He was upright and resolute; he would not associate with anyone who did not meet his standards.

There was a man surnamed Wu in the same administrative district, a descendant of the Prime Minister Yuanheng and a son-in-law of the Duke of Fenyang. Li Chuo felt no inclination to be his companion, so he moved his family to Mount Zhu.
He lived separated from his wife and children by the mountain, wearing coarse cloth garments and a simple sash, merely burning incense and practicing meditation. While serving in office...
At that time, only the elder of Liugou Monastery received him with cordiality. [Huineng] personally recounted the three fascicles of the *Platform Sutra*, which are now preserved in the canon.
Upon his departure, he left behind a verse for the monks, saying: "Traveling like a single-wheeled cart, one always fears overturning on the great road."

In stillness, he was like a vessel with a rounded bottom, always fearing contact with other objects; since both his conduct and stillness were thus, how could he not remain apart from the secular world?
During the Qiánfú era, his younger brother Liàn again served under Bì Néng’s command in Xù.

Lord Bì held him in high regard for his character and invited him into the city, but [Dàchǔ] firmly declined, saying, "I have already taken a vow never to tread upon your lordship's gate. Lord Bì then took a boat and departed.
He constructed it. They engaged in refined conversation throughout the day and departed without staying overnight.
Cui Qun:

a native of Wucheng. Before reaching the age of twenty, he was recommended for the jinshi examination and served in successive offices as a Hanlin Academician. He frequently submitted forthright counsel.

Emperor Xianzong graciously accepted his advice. Later, having been slandered, he was sent out as the Inspector of Huguang. Upon arriving at his post, the Duke visited Chan Master Ruyi of Hunan and asked, "By what means did you attain realization?
The Master replied, "I attained it by seeing my nature. At that time, the Master was suffering from an eye ailment.
The Duke said, "If you say it is 'seeing one's nature,' what then of this eye problem? The Master replied, "Seeing one's nature is not the eye; it is the eye that is ill."
"What harm has been done? The Duke bowed his head and expressed his thanks. During the reign of Emperor Muzong, Chao was promoted to Minister of the Ministry of Personnel (*Li-bu Shang-shu*).

Siku Table Sheng, surnamed Si (Si Kong Tu), was a native of Henei. He passed the jinshi examination at the end of the Xian-tong era and was appointed as Censor-in-Chief (*Jian-yi Da-fu*). However, he did not [accept].

He traveled to Guangu Valley in Mount Zhongtiao, where he built the Xiuxiu Pavilion (The Pavilion of Rest) and took delight in the joy of meditation (*dhyāna*). He styled himself the "Gentleman Who Endures Insult. He composed a poem that says:
Yesterday it was the warbling oriole; today it is the cicada. Having risen, once again it is the day of the setting sun.
The six dragons’ galloping chariot always press me hard; How much more must I endure this peril and spur myself on?

Lord Lü Xugong, Lü Mengzheng, styled Shenggong, was the first among those selected for the jinshi examination during the reign of Emperor Taizong. He served in succession until he attained the rank of Chief Councilor (Canchizhengshi) and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Xu.

In his youth, he lived as a boarder in a Buddhist monastery, which allowed him to devote himself to the study of the classics and histories. Later, he held the office of chief councilor for ten years.
For several years, he did not accept any stipends for the suburban sacrifices. When the Emperor asked him the reason, he replied that his private gratitude had not yet been repaid.

The Emperor questioned him further, and he answered truthfully. The Emperor remarked, "Is there such a person among the monks? He then bestowed upon him a purple robe and conferred a title to honor him.

Thereupon, he bestowed all his honorary stipends upon the monks of the monastery to repay their long-standing virtues. Whenever the Duke rose at dawn to worship the Buddha, he would offer this prayer:
"May those who do not believe in the Triple Gem never be born into my family; may my descendants enjoy official emolument from generation to generation and protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
His nephew Yi-jian, the Duke of Shenguo, would always burn incense after returning home following his morning prostrations before the family shrine on New Year’s Day.
He sent a letter to the Venerable Guanghui Liai to pay his respects. Gongzhu, the son of Lord Shen, was also enfeoffed as the Duke of Shen.
On New Year’s Day, he sent a letter to Chan Master Tianyi Huai; Hao Wen, the Vice President of the Left, was the recipient. On New Year’s Day, he sent a letter to Chan Master Yuanzhao;
Yongzhong, the son of the Vice President of the Left, was the recipient. On New Year’s Day, he sent a letter to Chan Master Fozhao. As for his family lineage:
His devotion has a long history.

Li Wenjing, whose given name was Li Han and courtesy name Taichu, served as Right Assistant for Deficiency during the reign of Emperor Taizong and was appointed as Chancellor during the reign of Emperor Zhenzong. Every day he drew water...
When reports of drought and banditry reached the throne, he said, "The ruler, being young, should be made to understand the hardships of the four quarters;
otherwise, his attention will be diverted toward matters of construction and the worship of spirits. Later, these words proved true.
Public Minister Wang Wenzheng sighed and remarked, "Master Li Jing was truly a sage. He was usually upright, silent, and spoke little, yet he had a profound mastery of the Buddhist scriptures."
He was particularly weary of honor and profit. When his family members urged him to renovate their residence because it was cramped and dilapidated, the Duke said:

"I receive a generous salary and occasionally receive extraordinary gifts; by calculation, I could certainly afford to renovate it. However, I reflect that according to the Inner Canon, this world is considered defective."

"How could one obtain fulfillment according to one's wishes? How could one seek personal satisfaction? When the flower stands beneath the hall became tilted and damaged, she did not inquire about them for years.
When someone requested that they be repaired, she said, "How could I move even a single thought because of this? She passed away lying on her right side.
At that time, during the height of summer, her body remained for seven days without its complexion changing, and it emitted a fragrance like that of a lotus flower. People said that she had...
The evidence of this practice is found in the cases of Xie Zongyuan and Xie Bi.
Zongyuan’s courtesy name was Zongyuan; he passed the jinshi examination and served as the Right Censor-in-Chief. During the reign of Emperor Taizong, he oversaw the reconstruction of the Main Hall.
Li Bi remonstrated that it was improper to use colored paintings and suggested that vermilion and whitewash be used instead; the Emperor then rewarded him for his loyal devotion.

Lord Gong knew how to identify talent and attract men of worth; whenever he submitted a memorial of recommendation, he would invariably face the imperial palace, prostrate twice, and say, "This old servant has once again found a man for Your Majesty.
Both the Duke Wengzheng Dan and Cha Daizhi Dao were individuals whom Lord Gong had recommended.
He was extensively versed in the Buddhist scriptures. At the time of his death, he bathed and solemnly donned his cap and robes; without illness, he passed away sitting upright.
Former Commissioner Zeng Hui, courtesy name Zongyuan, was a jinshi of the second year of the Duan-gong era and served as Hanlin Academician. When Ding Wei constructed the *huan*... [text fragment].

Regarding the sea embankment: the authorities were excessively urgent in their demands on the people, yet at that time there was no one daring to speak out. The Master [Chang Shang-ying] argued the matter most forcefully in his memorial and had it abolished; both the military and the commoners were thereby granted peace.
In his youth, he shared quarters with the Chan Master Xuedou Xian; once they reached adulthood, they took different paths. At the beginning of the Tianxi era, they met again in the Huai region.
The Master then took the *Zhongyong* and *Daxue*, cross-referencing them with the *Lengyan jing* and the sayings of the Chan school to test his understanding against Xian’s. Xian...
He said, "This [teaching] is not even in accord with the scriptural vehicles (śāstra), let alone the *Zhongyong* or the *Daxue*. A scholar must investigate directly and decisively.
Then, snapping his fingers once, he said, "Just realize it in this way. He took Gong’s understanding of the essential meaning from beneath these words.

Chá Zhànrán (查湛然), whose courtesy name was Zhànrán, was compassionate and filial by nature. When his mother fell ill and craved soup made of mandarin fish (*guìyú*), there was no one in the market who could sell it. Chá Dào wept and prayed by the river;

he cut through the ice and obtained the fish. His mother’s illness soon abated. At the beginning of the Duāngǒng era, he passed the jinshi examination and served as an official until reaching the rank of Long... (the text is incomplete).

Director of the Imperial Library (Tugede taizhi). When the public served as Governor of Guozhou, bandits from Dong rose in rebellion; they warned one another, saying, "Governor Cha governs this region with benevolence and righteousness;
we must not provoke him. Upon reaching the city walls, the rebels fled. He authored a collected works in twenty volumes.
Formerly, when I composed the "Record of the Sangha Hall" for Master Shimen Cong, I wrote:

"Since the Buddha-dharma spread widely and Bodhidharma came from the West, those who possessed the faculty of faith sought to realize the fundamental source. They wore robes that could not ward off the cold and ate food that did not fill their bellies.

Lately, however, Zen monasteries have vied with one another to plan halls of vast magnificence; young beginners now lie at ease within them, while those who understand cause and effect feel as if they were lying upon iron."
As for the bed: if one were to encounter a mortal enemy, would one not personally nurture the sacred embryo (āryagarbha) day and night and secretly seek liberation?

Yet, if the mind is turbid and entangled by afflictions, and while the body enjoys warmth and comfort, one fails to examine ignorance and instead devotes oneself solely to the study of words and letters, claiming this to be the ultimate realization—only to find that when life ends and one passes away, one falls into those evil realms.
Would a man of fierce resolve not be moved to alarm by such a prospect?

Yang Wengong Yang Yi, courtesy name Da-nian, was a native of Pucheng. He served successively as Court Gentleman for Scholarly Attainment (Chao Lin Xueshi). By nature he was upright and incorruptible, and he esteemed reputation and integrity.
His literary style was powerful and robust; scholars took him as their model. He was posthumously titled Wen. His collected works comprise one hundred and ninety-four scrolls.
In his collected works, the Master once remarked that in his youth he was keen on pursuing official advancement, and it was as if something were constantly obstructing his chest.
Upon studying the teachings of the Śākya clan, that obstruction suddenly shattered and dispersed; no longer hindered by anything, his mind became serene.

Chao Wen-yuan, whose given name was Chao Jing and courtesy name Mingyuan, was a native of Qingfeng. He served through the three reigns of Emperors Taizong, Zhenzong, and Renzong, retiring from office as Grand Master of the Crown Prince’s Household (Taizi Shaobao).
He died at the age of eighty-four and was posthumously honored with the title Wen-yuan. Jing was by nature broad-minded and simple; when he held office and presided over affairs...

He never allowed personal emotions to harm living beings. His extant works include the *Hanlin Ji* (Collected Works from the Hanlin Academy) in thirty fascicles, the *Daoyuan Ji* (Collected Works from the Daoist Retreat) in fifteen fascicles, and the *Fazang Suijin Lu* (Record of Glimpses of Gold from the Dharma Treasury) in ten fascicles.

Regarding the *Platform Sutra* read by the Master, his seventh-generation descendant Zikan saw a postscript at its end which stated: "At the age of eighty-one, read for the sixteenth time. This was when the Master was in his early twenties.

He encountered the eminent scholar Liu Yiyi and questioned him regarding the matter of birth and death. Liu said, "People do not truly die. The Master was startled by this. Liu continued, "The physical form dies, but the nature does not perish.
Only then did the Master begin to understand his teaching. From that time on, he devoted himself to Zen contemplation;

even in his later years, he remained diligent in studying the *Platform Sūtra* with such earnestness. Furthermore, I once saw an account of the Master’s life in the *Congbao lu*, which records one particular incident concerning him. The Master—

After retiring from office, he lived in leisurely seclusion, dwelling alone in a Daoist cloister and attending to no other affairs. He cautioned his family members not to make any requests of him on his behalf.
When his son, Zongke, was promoted to the jinshi degree, he changed into his official robes to visit and pay his respects; the Master, however, paid him no heed.
His wife observed him secretly and saw only that he sat upright with eyes closed, his beard and hair swaying in the breeze, as motionless as a wooden puppet. He once composed a poem: [Poem omitted]
He said: "Refining ore into gold, one obtains precious treasure; refining emotion into nature, one attains true spontaneity.
Among those who meet and converse upon this principle, there is not a single person among a thousand or ten hundred. He also once remarked:
"I observe that the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* concludes by saying: 'If that bhikṣu, regarding all dharmas, takes up but a single practice that is most conformable, namely...'"

"Non-arising—this is the practice of dhyāna. Having examined these words in detail, if there are those who clearly understand the principles of dhyāna and study the Buddha-dharma, this single section alone will suffice for them.

Wang Wenzheng, whose personal name was Wang Dan and courtesy name Ziming, served in successive offices up to Minister of Works and Concurrent Chancellor. He was posthumously honored with the title Duke of Wei and the posthumous epithet Wenzheng.
Because he had previously used his own blood to transcribe the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and established a religious society to cultivate purity, [he attained this merit].

Karma is the foremost of all things. On the first day of the ninth month in the first year of the Tianxi era, he passed away. One day prior, he entrusted his wishes to Yang Yi of the Hanlin Academy, saying:
"I am deeply weary of this toilsome life. I wish that in a future existence I may become a monk, sitting in meditative repose among the forest trees, taking joy in contemplating the mind."

Zhu Yan, whose secular name was Zhu Yan, served as a *jiedu panguan* (military governor’s administrative judge) during the reign of Emperor Zhenzong. Having studied the *Haiyan* (Ocean Eye) for a long time, he did not yet know how to enter its profound meaning.
One day, he asked the lecturer-monk Yijiang, "After this body dies, where does this mind reside? Jiang replied, "Before this body has even died."
"Where does this mind reside? Gong Qizhi composed a verse in response: "The four elements need not be awakened to sequentially; The six sense organs are empty when they function.
It is difficult to present it through speech or silence to the Master; It resides only within ordinary speech and silence. Jiang said: [This is the meaning.]
Furthermore, one must expel [these faults].
Zhu Zhengyu (style name:
Juzhi) was a native of Jingnan. During the reign of Emperor Zhenzong, he served as a Hanlin Academician; he was a man of vast learning and pure virtue.

In his later years, he requested to return home. Emperor Zhenzong issued an edict to detain him, awaiting the cool season of autumn. At that time, Wu Shu presented a poem for his departure, which said:

"The night grows cool in the Bath Hall as you first set down your brush; at the dusk of autumn in Zhugong, you await the suspension of your carriage. Yang used the stipends he had received throughout his career [to purchase a carriage].

He purchased rare books daily, saying he took pleasure in them himself; he was especially fond of Buddhist scriptures. He composed his own funerary inscription, and his disciples conferred upon him the posthumous title "Master Zhengyu.
His younger brother, Xie, served as the Director of the Court of State Ceremonial and likewise retired to live among the common people; they were known by the people as the "Two Shus of Zhugong."

Wang Zhongli, styled Wang Zhongli, was a native of Ke’lan Prefecture. His family was wealthy, yet he provided all his resources for hosting guests while maintaining a very frugal lifestyle for himself.

After his wife died, he did not remarry; he lived alone in a single room like a divine monk and only emerged after several years, at which time people noticed the refinement of his speech and conversation.
He was unusual. When struck, he did not speak. In his later years, he changed his name to Yunhe and styled himself Ni xu. He passed away at the end of his life according to a pre-announced date.
He composed many poems on Chan.
Wang Suishi, styled Zizheng, was a native of Henei. At the beginning of the Tiansheng era, he was transferred from Runzhou to serve as the Governor of Jiangning Prefecture.

During a year of great famine, the Commissioner of Transportation ordered the prefectural administration to open the Changping granaries to provide daily rations of rice based on population counts. Suishi would not permit this.

He said, "The people are starving because merchants are hoarding grain and closing their stores to drive up prices. Thereupon, he distributed a large amount of government grain, and private prices were subsequently stabilized;
those among the people who were saved from death numbered in the tens of thousands.

He had always admired the character of Pei Xiu, and while serving as Censor-in-Chief stationed at Qiantang, he went to Xingjiao Temple to pay his respects to Chan Master Xiaoshou. Their exchange of words and spiritual resonance were in perfect accord.
From then on, his practice deepened further until he finally clarified the Great Dharma. Together with Yang Dainian, he was renowned as a Chan practitioner.

Previously, Dainian had compiled the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) in thirty volumes; [Fenyang] subsequently abridged it to fifteen volumes, titling it the *Yu Ying Ji* (Collection of Jade Blossoms).
At the time of his death, he wrote a verse: "The lamp in the painted hall has already been extinguished; To whom shall I point my finger and speak? Leaving or staying..."
This is quite ordinary. The spring breeze sweeps away the lingering snow.
The elder Fu was Zhongfu Bi, styled Yanguo; he was a native of Henan. During the Qingli era, he served as Chancellor alongside Wen Yanbo. The whole world praised them—

He was posthumously titled the Duke of Zheng and granted the style name Wenzhong. While the Duke was serving as the regional governor of Beizhou, he welcomed the Master Huayan Yong and hosted him at the provincial seat.
After they had attained mutual realization and parted ways, the Duke later wrote a letter to Master Yong, saying:

"Regarding what you have instructed me on this matter, I have heard that one who encounters the Buddha must surely possess past causes. Now that I, Bi, have met the Venerable Master, it is as if I have recovered what I had forgotten since beginningless time."
Once this matter is recognized, from that point forward you must certainly pull yourself out of the sea of birth and death; this is no ordinary favor.

Even if you exert your full strength, you cannot transcend the Way by cutting it off. Although you may receive a hundred thousand instructions from the Master, what benefit would their number have for the matter?
It would amount to nothing more than gaining a reputation as a man who has produced an old, sickly layman under the assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, which can only benefit the Master himself.
This matter is indeed profound; what you say regarding the vast amount of refinement required is truly so.
I often reflect that when the ancient patriarchs were first with their own teachers, they remained for twenty or thirty years, or at the very least, for ten or more years.

Only by attending upon them day and night, following their guidance, and hearing the Dharma, could they finally penetrate to the ultimate limit and reach the very bottom. Yet, I recall how twice I have been graced by the Master’s [compassionate] favor.

I have reflected that we were able to seek instruction together for two months; had it not been for the Master’s skillful deployment of expedient means and your diligent efforts to provoke my realization, how could I have seen even a glimpse of the ultimate boundary?
Although I exhaust my head and feet, it is difficult to repay your kindness.
I do not yet know when I shall again behold you, but morning and night I remain filled with longing.

Wen Lugu (style name Yanwen, courtesy name Kuānfú) was a native of Jiexiu. He passed the jinshi examination and served through four successive reigns. For over fifty years, he held positions both as a military commander and a high minister.
When he was appointed as Grand Councillor for the second time, he was invested alongside Fu Bi; the scholar-officials celebrated this event, considering it a great honor.

He attained high office, serving as Grand Preceptor (Taishi) and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Lu. He lived to the age of ninety-two and was posthumously honored with the title Zhonglie (Loyal and Valiant).

While the Duke was governing Luoyang, he once went to Long’an Temple to pay homage to the sacred images. Suddenly, he saw that one image had fallen to the ground in a state of ruin, yet he showed it no sign of reverence;
he merely looked at it and departed. A monk standing nearby asked, "Why did you not prostrate yourself? The Duke replied, "The image has already..."

"It has been destroyed. What ritual shall I perform? The monk said, "It is like the earth of an official road. A person digs it up to fashion an image. The wise know it is merely road earth; ordinary people say an image has come into being.
Later, when the officials wish to travel, they take the image and fill the road again with it.

The image was never born nor does it perish; the road likewise has neither newness nor antiquity. Upon hearing this, the official attained a realization. From then on, he pursued the Way with even greater diligence, focusing his mind exclusively upon it.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha. Whether at dawn with incense or sitting at night, he never slackened for even a moment.
He would frequently make this vow: "May I always be diligent and energetically cultivate all virtues; may I realize the essence of the mind and bring all sentient beings to vast awakening.
The Master Ruru composed a verse in praise, saying: "I know your courage is as vast as heaven; I vow to form a hundred thousand karmic ties with the West. Not for the sake of...
Seeking a livelihood for one’s whole life, everyone boards the ferry at the crossing together.
Du Qigong, whose courtesy name was Shichang, was a native of Shanyin. During the Qingli era, he served as Chancellor alongside Fu Bi, Han Qi, and Fan Zhongyan.
Together with Yan An, he reformed corrupt practices to restore the state's discipline; Yan was particularly resolute in suppressing favoritism, returning all imperial favors granted by special edict.
Later, he retired from office as Grand Master of the Crown Prince (Taizi Shaoshi) and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Qi. Upon his death, he was posthumously titled Zhengxian.
He was commonly known as the "Pure and Frugal Chancellor. The Duke had long privately marveled at Zhang Fangping’s devotion to Buddhism. There was once a physician...
The gentleman Zhu moved between these two masters. One day, the master summoned Zhu to examine his pulse. When he arrived late, the master questioned him.

Zhu replied, "I had not yet finished reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. The master said, "The subtle words of the sages do not exceed those of Confucius and Mencius; what kind of language is there in the *Śūraṅgama*?
Zhu said, "If you have not read this sutra yourself, how can you know that it does not equal Confucius and Mencius? Thereupon, he produced from his sleeve—
The Duke looked at it and, before he realized it, had finished the entire scroll. Greatly astonished, he said, "Fangping knew of this, yet he did not tell me.
He immediately ordered his carriage to go and see him. Fangping said, "It is like losing an object and suddenly finding it; one should simply rejoice in its recovery."
There is no need to regret being late.
Fan Wenzheng,
whose courtesy name was Zhongyan and style name Xiwen, was reading among the Longbai Mountains when he discovered a cache of gold in a temple one day.
He covered it up and did not take it. Later, when he attained high office, he told the monks to produce gold to repair the temple.

During the reign of Emperor Renzong, he served successively as a Grand Master of Remonstrance (Shumimi) and Acting State Councilor (Chanzhi Zhengshi). He was posthumously titled Wenzheng and enfeoffed as Duke of Chu.

While serving as Pacification Commissioner (Xuanchu) in Hedong, the Duke stayed at an inn in Baode and obtained a scroll of ancient scriptures titled *The Verses on the Cause and Effect of the Ten Original Arhats*, which was not recorded in the Tripitaka.
The Duke composed a preface for them, stating: "These are seven hymns by one Venerable, all of which are words concerning awakening to the fundamental nature and attaining Buddhahood.
As I read them, each hymn brings a new realization; only then do I know that within the human world there exists boundless, sacred Dharma, yet its texts have been lost from the Great Canon.
Therefore, I entrust them to the Śramaṇa Huizhe so that they may circulate in the world. While the Duke was serving as Governor of Wu, Langye...
Master Jue went to visit him and stayed for several days. Under the Master’s words, he realized his true home. He presented the Master with a verse, saying:
"Throughout these consecutive days we have conversed, dissolving the knot of doubt; Who would have thought that in this floating life there was half a day of leisure?
I wish to remain in leisure with you until old age, Completely gathering the nature of consciousness into the Mysterious Barrier."

Yin Shilu (尹師魯), whose courtesy name was Shilu, was a man of broad learning with profound expertise in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*. Since the end of the Tang dynasty, literary style had gradually declined;
Yin Shu and Mu Bochang (穆伯長) championed the revival of ancient prose. From that time on, the literary climate underwent a slight transformation. During the Qingli era, he held various official posts.
The起居舍人 (Attendant-in-Ordinary) was once traveling with the venerable monk Fayan while he was in exile in Daliang.
One day, he said to Fayan, "Recently, I have come to consider that withdrawing into stillness is the attainment of the Dharma. Fayan replied, "Why not forget both withdrawal and stillness?"
The Duke immediately attained realization. On the day of his passing, he first wrote a letter by hand to bid farewell to Fan Wenzheng Gong.
Just then, Zhu Chongshi Yan arrived; the Duke said to Yan, "I have long studied Buddhism under Chan Master Fayen, and it is precisely this that serves as my support now.
When Wenzheng Gong arrived in haste and wailed in grief, the Duke opened his eyes and said, "I have already bid you farewell. Why [do you weep]?"
"Come again! Life and death are the constant law; how could Xiwen not understand this? Having spoken these words, he sat upright and passed away.
Feng Dangshi (Feng Jing), styled Dangshi, was a native of Jiangxia. He passed the jinshi examination, ranking first from the provincial selection through to the imperial court examination.
When Ou Yang Jing served as Director of the Imperial Chancellery, Han Qi was the Chancellor. For several months, Jing did not see him even once.
Han Qi took this to mean that Jing was arrogant. Upon hearing of this, Jing said to Han: "That you, a Chancellor, do not visit me without cause is precisely what honors you;
how could it be arrogance? While serving in Bingzhou, he once wrote in a letter to Wang An-guo: "The songs and dances of Bingmen..."
Miaoli closed her eyes and would not look out; she made the practice of discussing Chan her highest priority. An-guo said, "If it is as you argue, you have not yet mastered the principles of Chan.
To close one's eyes and not look is already a single kōan."

Xia Yinggong, whose personal name was Xiǎ Sǒng and courtesy name Zǐqiáo, was a native of Dē'ān. During the reign of Emperor Rénzōng, he passed the *zhìkē* (imperial examination for special talents). In the Huángyù era, he served as a Participant in State Affairs (*cānzhī zhèngshì*).
Having already found his spiritual affinity at Gǔyǐn, he spent his days in the company of elderly monks. Once, when the Chan Master Làn Pǔ arrived, the Duke went up to meet him.
The Duke asked, "When the hundred members of the body dissolve and scatter, which one is the Elder's own self? Lan said, "I left Qiyang on the twentieth day of last month.
The Duke stopped him there. Lan, however, asked back, "When the hundred members of the body dissolve and scatter, which one is the Governor's own self?
The Duke then gave a shout. Lan said, "There is no doubt that you shouted; but ultimately, which one is the Governor's own self?"
The Master replied with a verse: "Do not mistake this for the foremost pivot before the wind; In the vast void, where can one harbor thoughts?
If this mountain monk wishes to convey the message, It is when the moon rises over ten thousand miles of cloudless sky."

Li Gou, courtesy name Yanli, was a native of Nanyang. He was thoroughly versed in the Five Classics and had several hundred students. Both Zeng Gong and Deng Runfu were his younger brothers in commerce.
Li Gou once authored the *Qianshu* (The Hidden Book), in which he exerted great effort in refuting Buddhism; this was brought forth by Master Song.
Upon reading the *Fujiao bian* (Compilation for Assisting the Teachings), he first began to pay close attention to Buddhist scriptures.

He then sighed regretfully, saying, "The discussions of those like us do not even reach the level of a single scroll of the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*. How can the Buddha-way be easily spoken of? During the Huángyù era, Fàn Zhōngyǎn recommended him to take the examination for the position of *shuōshū* at the Imperial Academy.
After his death, Yúnrǔ submitted his *Luìgǎo* (Collected Drafts from Retirement) and the *Huángyù xùgǎo* (Continued Drafts from the Huángyù Era). By imperial decree—
The official had one son, Zhao Qingxian (Zhao Bian), whose courtesy name was Yuedao.
His bearing was pure and detached; people could not perceive his joy or anger. He styled himself "The Man Who Knows His Errors."

During the Zhizhi era of the Song dynasty, he served as a Court Censor (*shiyushi*). In his official duties, he prosecuted and impeached without avoiding even the high-ranking relatives of the imperial family.
He habitually kept a tortoise and a crane with him; later, he released the tortoise into the Bian River, from which arose the verse: "A tortoise released into the Longhuai will not return again.
While the Master was in Chengdu, a monk presented a poem to him which said: "One must walk upon the crown of Vimalakīrti’s head. Subsequently, [the Master] followed [the monk] to Tianbo Monastery.

When Master Chongyuan asked for the essentials of the mind, [Zhaozhou] was serving as the Governor of Qingzhou. While leaning on his armrest in the public hall, he suddenly attained great realization upon hearing the sound of thunder.
Later, returning to Sanchu as the Imperial Tutor (Taizi Shaobao), he associated with mountain monks and country elders without interruption.

He named his residence "Gaozhai" (The High Studio) and expressed himself through a poem, saying: Beyond the window is the long stream; beyond the stream are the mountains. Rolling up the curtains, all is empty.
Amidst the vast waters and clouds, when someone asked about his high study quarters, he replied: "At night I sleep peacefully; by day I am at ease.

During the Yuanfeng era, one day he took leave of all his relatives and friends. His son, Shanji, noticing that his father’s appearance and demeanor were extraordinary, questioned him regarding his future affairs.
The Duke rebuked him with a stern voice. After a short while, his speech returned to its usual state, and he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.

Chan Master Faquan praised him with this verse: "In office, he was an auspicious sign for the realm; returning home, he became a model for the world. Now that the Golden Grain has departed from the human world, the Jade Tower is completed in heaven.
His sword of wisdom is without the slightest flaw; his crystal pitcher is clear to the very bottom. Upon the waters of the Hui Canal in the spring breeze, a solitary moon."
Poyunming died at the age of seventy-seven; his posthumous title was Qingxian.
Ouyang Yongshu, whose courtesy name was Yongshu, was a native of Luling. During the reign of Emperor Renzong, he served as a censor, discussing state affairs with incisive and direct candor. Later...
He was appointed as a Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs. Vowing to assist and rectify the administration, he collaborated with Han Qi in the enthronement of Emperor Yingzong.

At the beginning of the Xining era, he retired from office with the rank of Junior Master of the Heir Apparent. His posthumous title was Wenzhong. Initially, the Duke did not believe in Buddhism; when he learned that Cheng Jingzhao had written a poem for him, he remarked:

The Buddha said, "I do not study. This has caused you, Master, to labor in vain knocking at my gate. I am currently preoccupied with benevolence and righteousness; you, however, find leisure amidst the waters and clouds.
Later, while he was guarding the Hao community, Xu Changling came to visit the Taiqing Palace. The Master invited him to his residence in the prefecture to converse with him.
Suddenly, he attained enlightenment. While residing in Luoyang, he traveled to Mount Song. Leaving his attendants behind, he went forth with unrestrained ease until he reached a temple.
Tall bamboos filled the courtyard, and the scenery was fresh and beautiful. The Master rested upon the steps of the hall; nearby, an elderly monk sat reading a sutra with composure.
The Master asked which sutra he was reciting. "The Lotus Sutra," the monk replied. The Master said, "In ancient times, when eminent monks faced the threshold of life and death..."

"In every case, they depart with laughter and ease. What path leads to this? [The Master] replied, "It is simply the power of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*. He asked again, "Nowadays, people are desolate and lack these; why is that?
The old monk smiled and said, "In the past, people were in a state of concentration and wisdom at every thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*).

How could they be distracted at the moment of death? Nowadays, people are in a state of distraction at every thought-moment. How could they attain concentration and wisdom at the moment of death? The official sighed in great admiration.
Later, while residing in Yingzhou, he renounced alcohol and meat and distanced himself from sounds and sights. With his mind extinguished, he sat in silence.
He ordered an old soldier to go to a nearby temple to borrow the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and read it up to the eighth fascicle; then, having settled into his seat, he passed away.

Simma Wen Gong, surnamed Sima Guang, styled Junshi, was a native of Xia County. He passed the jinshi examination at the beginning of the Baoyuan era and served successively as Academician of the Endming Hall.

He submitted a memorial vehemently stating that the Green Sprouts Law was disadvantageous. He retired to live in Luoyang for fifteen years. When Emperor Zhezong first ascended the throne, he was summoned back.

He was summoned and appointed as Left Vice President of the Department of State Affairs. He abolished the Green Sprouts Law. Contemporaries remarked that Prime Minister Fan’s achievements during the Yuanyou era possessed the merit of turning heaven and earth upside down.

Upon his death, he was posthumously honored with the title of Grand Preceptor, enfeoffed as the Duke of Wengu, and bestowed the posthumous name Wenzheng. Throughout his life, his writings were extensive.
I once composed six verses on the interpretation of Chan (Zen). I observed that those in the world who discourse on Chan delight in using obscure language to bewilder one another;
therefore, I have expanded upon the words of Wenzhongzi to explain them. The first verse says: "Thoughts and anger are like a blazing fire; profit and desire are like sharp blades.
To be perpetually sorrowful throughout the day—this is called the Avīci Hell. The second verse says: "Yan Hui found peace in the humble alleyway."

Mencius nurtured the "vast and courageous" spirit; to him, wealth and honor were like floating clouds. This is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The third says: Filial piety and fraternal respect penetrate the divine spirits;
loyalty and trustworthiness prevail even among the barbarians. Performing good brings down a hundred blessings. This is called the law of cause and effect. The fourth says:
Words become teachers for a hundred generations; deeds become laws for all under heaven. Over time, these cannot be obscured. This is called the indestructible.
The fifth is: "It is the peaceful dwelling for the benevolent and the straight path for the righteous. To practice it with sincerity and over a long duration—this is called the Treasury of Radiance.
The sixth is: "Cultivating the Way and righteousness within one’s own person, so that merit and virtue cover all things;
becoming a worthy one or a great sage—this is called a Buddha or a Bodhisattva."

Zhang Wending, whose courtesy name was Andao, was a native of Songcheng. He served successively as Grand Master of the Crown Prince (Taizi Shaoshi) and was posthumously honored with the title Wending.

He shared a close friendship with the father and son from Meishan. Having gained the favor of Emperor Shenzong, he remained steadfast and impartial while Wang Anshi held power. At that time, the public was resolute and remained unaffected [by partisan influence].

He moved. His reputation rose for a time. During the Qingli era, he once served as the Governor of Chuzhou. While traveling to Langlang Mountain, he arrived at a monastery and happened to see a copy of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
Upon picking it up and examining it, he suddenly awakened to the events of his previous life. As the scroll entered his hands, he felt a sense of clarity, as if recovering an old possession.

Before he had finished opening the volume, his long-standing karmic obstructions were dissolved like melting ice. When he read the passage: "The world is free from birth and death; it is like empty space..."
"Flowers in the Sky. He then clarified his own realization with this verse: "A single thought abides in arising and ceasing; A thousand mechanisms bind one to existence and non-existence.
Where the divine blade is lightly raised, It passes through and escapes like a bead rolling from a platter.

In his later years, he bestowed this scripture upon Su Zigan, providing him with three hundred thousand coins to print and distribute it throughout the Jianghuai region. Zigan then transcribed it and had it carved into woodblocks.
Fan Zhongwen, whose courtesy name was Jingren, was a native of Huayang. He served successively as Hanlin Academician.

During the Xihuang era, when gentlemen of the court discussed the most worthy men in the realm, they invariably pointed to Sima Guang and Fan Zhongwen. Guang once remarked that he himself lacked the courage and decisiveness [to act].
Jingren died posthumously with the title Zhongwen (Loyal and Civilized). He had a collected works in one hundred volumes. Someone once asked Jingren why he did not believe in Buddhism.
Jingren replied, "Do you expect me to join my palms and prostrate myself before you, and only then will I be considered a believer?
One day Huang Shan谷 (Shangu) visited Jingren; they sat facing each other for the entire day, both sitting upright and straight, never looking back and showing no sign of weariness.
Jingren said, "For twenty years, not a single thought has ever arisen in my breast. For the past two or three years, I have not read much of the books.
When there are no guests, I sit alone all day long; I do not sleep until the second watch of the night.
Even when my children shout and play within arm's reach, I do not hear them. Huangzhou remarked, "You, sir, are truly a master of Buddhist practice."

Shao Kangjie, whose courtesy name was Yaofu, was a native of Fanyang. He resided in Luoyang for forty years, living in poverty while delighting in the Way. In winter he used no stove, and in summer he used no fan;
for several years he did not go to his mat at night. He named his place of rest the "Anlewo" (Cottage of Peace and Joy) and styled himself [the Master of the Anlewo].
Reverend Anle, you have a Buddhist verse that says: "Eating to satiety and wearing fine clothes are not easy to sustain; as the days grow long, what can one do with this sorrow?
In my youth, seeking fame, I turned to Confucius; in my old age, fearing death, I draw near to Śākyamuni. I vainly wish to sever worldly ties, yet they only become heavier;
I seek to rid myself of illness, yet the ailments only multiply. The vast expanse of the Long River is as level as a roll of silk; fortunately,"

"Even when there is no wind, waves may arise again. At the beginning of the Xining era, he was summoned as a Court Historian (*zhuzuo lang*) but did not go; upon his death, he was posthumously titled Kāngjié.

He authored the *Huangji jingshi shu* (Book of the Supreme Ultimate Governing the Ages) in twelve fascicles, and the *Jixiang ji* (Collection of the People Striking the Earth) circulated in the world.
Master Cheng praised him as a heroic figure of all antiquity.

Wang Jiefu, whose courtesy name was Anshi, was appointed as Prime Minister during the reign of Emperor Shenzong and enfeoffed as the Duke of Jing. One day, he visited Chan Master Yuan of Mount Jiangshan.
During their conversation, they discussed and evaluated matters of antiquity and the present. The Master said, "The breath from the Prime Minister’s mouth is overwhelming; I fear..."
"Exerting one's spirit in literary composition causes the mind and breath to become unbalanced. Why not sit in meditation to realize this great matter? The Master followed his advice.
One day he said to the Teacher, "Sitting in meditation truly does no harm to a person. For several years I have wished to compose the 'Eighteen Taps of the Hu-hu Flute,' but had not yet finished it.
Suddenly, while sitting at night, I attained it. The Teacher laughed heartily. Later, when the Master was reading at Dinglin, he once...
He asked Master Yuan about the essential meaning of the Patriarchs' intent. Yuan did not answer. He pressed him further, and Yuan said, "You have three obstacles to the Prajñāpāramitā;
you are merely close to the Way in one respect. He asked, "I wish to hear the explanation of these. Yuan said, "Your received nature is stern and grand, and your worldly attachments are deep.
Because you possess such a stern and grand vessel while encountering deep worldly attachments, you will inevitably feel compelled to take responsibility for the whole world."
The gravity of this matter is such that one harbors the ambition to govern the world; yet if the application of this ambition is not pure, the mind will not be at peace.

To maintain the ambition of governing the world with a mind that lacks peace—when could such a person ever achieve "ten thousand years in a single thought"? Furthermore, excessive anger leads to much contention with others; this is the third point.
One must regard fame and profit as if shedding one's hair, and find sweetness in the simple and meager as a *dhūta* ascetic does. This is...
"The Way is near; it should be nourished and made flourish through the vehicle of the teachings. The Duke bowed twice. Later, he attained the essential meaning through the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.

In the eighth year of the Xīníng era, the Duke entered the相位 (the position of Chancellor) once again. One day, after retiring from a memorial to the Emperor, the Sovereign asked, "Does the Buddha-dharma provide any benefit to our Middle Kingdom?
The Duke replied, "When both the noble and the common people know to revere [it] and do good, how could this be anything less than a great benefit?"
When the Duke resided in Jinling, his former residence lay halfway between Mount Jiangshan and the city. Later, he requested that his house be converted into a monastery,
which was consequently named Bāngshàn (Halfway).— Sū Duānmíng.
Sū Shí, whose courtesy name was Zǐzhān, stayed overnight at Dōnglín Temple. While discussing the "discourse on insentient beings" with Zhàojué, he attained a realization and offered this verse:
"The sound of the stream is the broad and long tongue; The color of the mountains is surely the pure body. Last night, eighty-four thousand verses were born;
How shall I explain them to others in days to come? He also said: "Seen from the front, they form ridges; seen from the side, they form peaks. Everywhere..."
"Looking at the mountains, they appear different; one does not recognize the true face of this mountain. It is simply because one’s body is within the mountains.
Once, while Gōng was visiting his disciple Zīyóu at Gāo'ān, on the eve of his arrival, Zīyóu and the Chan Master Zhēnjìng Wén were together.
Chan Master Shouchengcong and [Zhenjing] were engaged in a night conversation on their shared bed. When it reached the third watch, they finally fell asleep.
Zhenjing suddenly woke with a start and said, "In my dream, I visited Chan Master Wuzu Jie. That he appeared in my dream without prior thought—what auspicious omen is this?
Ziyou shook Master Cong, who said, "I have just dreamed that Chan Master Jie arrived and is sitting here beside me. At dawn, news was suddenly reported of the arrival of Dongpo.
Having already arrived at Fengxin, after a short while Dongpo arrived. They discussed the matter of Master Li’s dream. Dongpo asked where Master Jie was born; he replied, “In Shaanxi.
Dongpo said, “When I was about ten years old, I frequently dreamed of coming and going with this monk in Shaanxi.
He then asked what Master Jie’s physical appearance was like; he replied, “Master Jie has lost one eye. Dongpo said, “When my late mother was pregnant, she dreamed that a monk arrived.”
Men were emaciated and one-eyed. He was asked again, "Where does the Precept Master [Jie] ultimately reside? He replied, "Gao'an Dayu; it has now been fifty years.
At that time, Dongpo was forty-nine. Later, he wrote in a letter to Zhenjing: "Precept Master Jie does not recognize people's prejudices."

To force a smile and emerge once more is truly laughable. During the Shaosheng era, when the Master was exiled to Danyang, he carried with him a single scroll of Amitābha Buddha and said, "This is my official warrant for traveling to the Western Paradise.
On the seventh month of the first year of Jianzhong, the Master passed away in Pilin.
At that time, Qian Jiming was by his side and asked, "Throughout your life you have studied Buddhism; how will you fare on this day? The Master—
He said, "I do not accept these words either. Furthermore, when Chan Master Linji of Mount Jing asked about his illness, he said, "Throughout your life, you have practiced with such diligence;
at this moment, you must exert yourself even more. The Official responded instantly, saying, "To exert effort is precisely the error. These words ended, and he passed away immediately.

Su Luancheng, whose given name was Su Zhe, styled Ziyou, and titled Yingbin as well as Luancheng, served successively as Hanlin Academician and Grand Secretary. He was posthumously honored with the title Wending.
In the third year of the Yuanfeng era, the Master was exiled to Gaoyang for his offenses; it was there that he encountered Chan Master Quan of Huangbo.

At the city temple, the Master gazed intently at the official and said, "You are tranquil and wise. If you apply yourself wholeheartedly to the Gate of the School (Zongmen), why should you worry about not accomplishing this Way?
The official recognized this and began practicing seated meditation. He repeatedly sought resolution from Chan Master Wuchu, until suddenly he had an awakening.
Chan Master Cong came to reside at Shoujing Temple. The Duke went there to inquire about this matter. Cong did not answer.
The Duke pressed him further, and Cong spoke slowly, saying: "Yuanzhao has never spoken of the Way to others; I, too, have nothing with which to speak to you."
The Duke thereby attained the meaning beyond words. He once also consulted Chan Master Shun of Hongzhou regarding the Dharma of the mind.

Shun showed him the karmic occasion of "pinching the nose," and the Duke attained great enlightenment upon hearing these words. He presented a verse, saying: "In middle age I heard the Way and realized my former errors;
By chance I met the aged Master Shun. Pinching the nose, I directly entered the true countenance; Shaking my head, I would not accept [anything else]."
A separate pair of tongs and a hammer; what business has the public with withered vines and tattered rags? White wine and green salt—who am I?
I am ashamed before the waning moon over the eastern eaves; a cup of nectar, as smooth as honey.

Mi Xiangyang, whose style name was Yuanzhang, was a native of Wu. He styled himself Haie Waishi (The Outer Historian of the Sea and Mountains). Having served as a district magistrate of Lin’guang, he rose through the ranks to become a Vice Director of the Ministry of Rites.
Mi’s prose was eccentric and daring; he would not borrow a single phrase from his predecessors. He was particularly masterful in calligraphy and ink painting, possessing a profound...
He excelled in the art of calligraphy, capturing the spirit of Xianzhi’s brushwork. After Su Zidan returned from overseas, he once wrote to Yuanchang, saying:
"During my eight years in the mountains and seas, I have been utterly cut off from relatives and friends, yet I never gave them a thought; I only thought of my Yuanchang."

When shall I behold that spirit soaring to the clouds, those elegant and refined writings transcending the mundane, and those calligraphic characters so sublime they enter the divine, to wash away the miasmic poison accumulated over these many years?
Upon obtaining the "Rhapsody on the Baoyue Hermitage," I read it aloud with clear resonance;
I regretted that though we had been companions for twenty years, I did not fully know Yuanzhang. Yuanzhang replied, "There is even more that you do not yet know."

He cultivated the practices of the Yangxu [Immortal] tradition and was destined for the celestial journey of the Azure Void (Biluo). That they would meet again at a later time was something known only then;
such was his lofty self-positioning. In his later years, he studied Chan and attained realization.

While serving as the Military Governor of Huaiyang, he wrote a letter of parting for his friends and relatives one month before his death. He completely incinerated all the books, paintings, and rare objects he cherished, and had a coffin made of fragrant nan wood.

He sat, lay down, ate, and drank within that very space. For seven days prior to his passing, he abstained from pungent vegetables and meat, changing his clothes and bathing, merely sitting in purity while burning incense.
When the appointed day arrived, he invited all the officials of the prefecture. Raising a fly-whisk to show the assembly, he said, "I come from the Land of Universal Fragrance;

I go to the Land of Universal Fragrance. He then cast aside the whisk, joined his palms, and passed away. During his lifetime, he had been fond of rocks; whenever he saw one of peculiar or wondrous formation, he would preserve it.
Those who were refined and upright would take their ceremonial robes and tablets to bow before it, calling it "Stone Master.
Wen Yuke, Wen Yuke—their names being identical—once served as the Prefect of Huzhou. In the eighth month of the third year of the Yuanfeng era, he arrived at Wancheng in Chenzhou.
At the post station, he suddenly stopped and would not proceed further. He bathed, donned his ceremonial cap and sash, sat upright, and passed away.

When Cui Gongdu of the same hostel heard of this, he was startled and said to others, "Yesterday, when I took my leave of Yu Ke at the southern part of the prefecture, Yu Ke asked, 'Will you come again tomorrow?
When I went to see him a second time, Yu Ke said calmly, 'The scriptures state that for one who does not speak falsely, their tongue covers the face. Yu Ke then—" [passed away].

He extended his tongue until it reached above his eyebrows and folded it three times. Gongdu was greatly startled. Hearing now of his passing, he remarked with wonder, "Truly a man who has attained the Way.
He is a successor to Wen Gong of the Han dynasty; his mouth was square and his eyebrows were elegant, and he became famous in the world for his learning.
His character and temperament were lofty and pure, like clear clouds or the autumn moon, untouched by the dust of the mundane world. Sima Guang and Su Zizhan held him in especially high esteem."
He styled himself Master Xixiao (Laughing Laugh). Zizhan once inscribed a eulogy for Master Xixiao’s ink bamboo, saying:
"The Master dwells in leisure, laughing alone without ceasing. When asked what he laughs at, he says: 'I laugh because you are not me.

When things define one another, "me" and "you" are one. The Master laughs again, laughing at that which was laughed at. Beyond this double laughter, he expresses his subtle artistry through bamboo. [The bamboo...]
He also experienced a wind-like sensation and laughed naturally. Alas! This is sufficient to attest to his worthiness.

Cheng Mingdao (Cheng Hao), courtesy name Bochun, was a native of Luoyang. A jinshi degree holder during the reign of Emperor Shenzong, he took the study of the Way as his primary responsibility. The world...
Cheng Mingdao, styled Mr. Xian, once said: "The Buddha spoke of the manifestation of radiance (*prabhāsa*). At first, I could not comprehend its meaning;
later, upon reading the *Huayan Jie lun* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka), I understood it clearly. That which responds to conditions and shatters delusions is called 'radiance' (*guang*);
that which liberates the defilements of the mind is called 'clarity' (*ming*). It is simply the radiance of one's own prior mind, through which one is able to enter the inexhaustible illumination."
Whenever Liu Gong observed the Buddhist monks reading Buddhist scriptures, he noted how dignified and solemn they were.
He then told his students, "When reading any scripture, one must always be like this. Those who read books nowadays have their very countenances already full of indolence;
how can they maintain their inner mastery? One day, while passing through Dinglin Temple, he happened to see a group of monks entering the hall, their every step and movement measured and composed.
Their dignified deportment was majestic; whether sitting or rising, they all conformed to the *qinggui* (rules of purity). Thereupon, Lü Huishu sighed and said:
"The rites and music of the Three Dynasties are entirely contained herein."

Lu Gongchu, courtesy name Huishu, was a jinshi graduate. He served successively as Censor-in-Chief and, at the beginning of the Yuanyou era, was appointed Right Vice President of the Department of State Affairs.

Together with Sima Guang, he collaborated wholeheartedly to assist in the administration. From his youth, Gongchu devoted himself to the study of learning, taking the cultivation of the mind and the nourishment of nature as his foundation.
He had few cravings and regarded rich flavors with disdain. Throughout his life, he never exhibited hurried steps or slothful countenance, nor did he ever indulge in frivolous laughter.
Vulgar or colloquial speech never issued from his mouth. In his later years, he read many Buddhist texts and investigated the principles of Chan.
Although Lord Wen was widely learned and possessed supreme conduct, he alone did not take pleasure in Buddhism. The Master urged him to pay attention to it, saying:

"What is called 'studying Buddhism' simply values its mental discipline as being concise and essential; it does not necessarily require one to adopt its outward practices or become a person beyond the secular world."

At the moment the silk wadding was placed upon his mouth, although his descendants filled the space before him and relatives and friends arrived in great numbers, he did not speak at all of his own life or the management of his funeral affairs.
— Yang Wuweī.
Yang Jie, whose courtesy name was Cigong, served as a Minister of the Board during the Yuanyou era. He styled himself the "Wuweizi" (The Man of Non-action).

Having studied under various renowned masters, he later followed Chan Master Tianyi Huai. Huai frequently cited the spiritual teachings and dialogues of Layman Pang, urging him to investigate them until he reached profound realization.
Later, while serving as a ritual official at Mount Tai, one day upon hearing a cock crow and seeing the sun rise like a platter surging from the earth, he suddenly—
He attained great enlightenment. Dwelling in the Pure Land with self-confidence, he painted an image of a sixteen-foot Amitābha Buddha to carry with him for constant contemplation.
He once said: "If love is not deep, one will not be born in Saṃsāra; if mindfulness is not single-minded, one will not be born in Sukhāvatī. Ordinary beings and sages are of one essence."

The resonance between the spiritual capacity and the response is such that sentient beings dwell within the hearts of all Buddhas; every speck of dust is Sukhāvatī, and within the minds of sentient beings, every thought-moment is Amitābha.
If one abandons one's own numinous spirit, whose fault is it? Furthermore, he once spoke of the Way with a monk, saying:
In general, those who study the Way must constantly maintain vigilance throughout the twelve periods of the day.
Have you not seen Nanquan say: "For thirty years I watched a water buffalo. If it trampled the crops, I would pull its nose and drag it back.
Now it has become a white ox in the open air; I let it roam nakedly, yet it refuses to leave. Everyone must always exert their utmost alertness.

It cannot be said that when one speaks of the Way of Chan, there is immediately some principle of "carrying illumination along. Even when washing vegetables or performing manual labor, one must not be without awareness.
It is like a hen brooding her eggs; if she were to abandon them and leave, the warmth would not be maintained and they would fail to become seeds.
Now, as the myriad phenomena array themselves before us and the six sense-faculties are in constant agitation, if one loses even a moment of care, [the seeds of awakening will perish].
To bring about the loss of body and life is no small matter.
Chao Yi Dao, whose courtesy name was Shuo Zhi, was the grandson of Duke Wenyuan. He once admired the conduct of Sima Guang and Fan Zhongyan.
This man styled himself Jingqian. He passed the jinshi examination. Su Shi (Zi-zhan) recommended him to the court on the grounds that his literary talent was fit for scholarly composition.

He served as an Attendant Censor of the Huigyou Pavilion (*Weiyouge Dazhi*). Throughout his life, he read extensively across all branches of literature, mastered the Six Classics, and was particularly proficient in the *I Ching* (*Yijing*).
His works, including the *Kehua*, were circulated in the world. The Gentleman once supervised the customs at Mingzhou and once traveled to Lake [Hu].
He traveled south to visit Master Mingzhi and heard his exposition on the "Three Thousand Worlds and Contemplation" (*sānqiānjìngguàn*). Delighted, he vowed to study that doctrine.
